Following the election of Donald Trump as the US President, the global economy is facing greater uncertainty. After the new US administration takes office, US policy direction may undergo fundamental changes in two aspects — a shift from monetary easing to fiscal expansion, and a shift from globalisation to anti-globalisation — which could have a profound impact on the global economic landscape. It is worth noting that with the accelerated pace of US interest rate hikes strengthening the US dollar and the possibility of the US adopting trade protectionist measures, the risks faced by emerging market economies have intensified. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has remained broadly stable, while Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates have risen along with US dollar offered rates. Despite this, liquidity conditions remain favourable, and overall loan growth rose further in the second half of 2016. After the implementation of new stamp duty measures, the residential property market showed immediate signs of adjustment but has recently rebounded. Looking ahead, banks should prudently assess the impact of a potentially faster-than-expected pace of US interest rate hikes and, on a broader level, the uncertainty of US policy, particularly the risk of large-scale capital outflows and its potential impact on local interest rates. Following the election of Donald Trump as the US President, the global economy is facing greater uncertainty. Not only was the election result unexpected by the market, but the related market reaction was also surprising. In particular, the expectation that measures introduced by Trump, such as tax reform, increased infrastructure spending, and deregulation, would boost US economic growth, led to a rally in global stock markets. After the new US administration takes office, US policy direction may undergo fundamental changes in two aspects — a shift from monetary easing to fiscal expansion, and a shift from globalisation to anti-globalisation — which could have a profound impact on the global economic landscape. However, the tax cuts anticipated from Trump may not produce the expected stimulus for US economic growth. Particularly as US economic activity is already close to its economic potential, fiscal stimulus measures may only provide a slight cyclical boost to US economic growth, but would exacerbate the upside risk of US inflation. Although it remains uncertain whether the US Federal Reserve (the Fed) will significantly accelerate the pace of monetary policy tightening as a result, long-term bond yields have risen markedly, partly reflecting market expectations of increasing inflation risks. At the same time, rising trade protectionism would be a "lose-lose" situation for the US and the rest of the world. Increased trade barriers would lead to market distortions that harm overall interests, hinder global trade, reduce the efficiency of global supply chains, and pose downside risks to the global economic outlook. Meanwhile, political instability remains a major risk and a headwind, especially for the European economy, where recovery is still weak. For emerging market economies, the risk of capital outflows due to an accelerated pace of US interest rate hikes and further appreciation of the US dollar has increased. This could drag down economic growth and exacerbate the risk of rapid capital outflows. In fact, in anticipation of the Trump administration's large-scale fiscal expansion and concerns about a sharp rise in energy prices, the market has repriced inflation risks, causing long-term bond yields to rise significantly across advanced economies and many emerging market economies. Special Topic 1 (see page 13) assesses the potential spillover effects of US interest rate hike expectations on the sovereign bond markets of 26 selected economies. The findings show that since the "taper tantrum" of 2013, the influence of the US Treasury market on sovereign bond markets has deepened, and US interest rate hikes and tightening financial conditions will have a significant impact on both advanced and emerging market economies. In East Asia, economic growth accelerated slightly in the second half of 2016 as exports picked up, but market volatility, such as currency depreciation and rising sovereign bond yields in the region due to concerns about potential policy changes by the new US administration, only gradually stabilised early this year. Looking ahead, East Asia may maintain steady growth in 2017, but it faces rising risks and uncertainties. US interest rate hikes, currency depreciation in the region, and increased financial market volatility may lead to a tightening of financial conditions. At the same time, the US may implement protectionist policies, which could affect the region's economies, but the actual impact is currently unclear. In Mainland China, overall economic growth accelerated slightly in the second half of 2016, driven by robust growth in infrastructure investment and an improvement in private sector business spending. Although the economy continues to show signs of stabilisation, uncertainties remain in the Mainland's growth prospects. In particular, with the government determined to curb rising property prices, the contribution of the real estate sector to growth may decrease this year if the property market continues to cool down. Meanwhile, the ongoing progress of economic restructuring and changes in Sino-US trade relations may increase uncertainty in the short-term economic outlook. On the external front, although the Renminbi remained stable against the China Foreign Exchange Trade System (CFETS) basket of currencies during the reporting period, capital outflow pressures increased at the end of 2016 with the appreciation of the US dollar and US interest rate hikes, and then appeared to ease slightly in early 2017. Despite signs of stabilisation in private sector economic activity, there are still some concerns in the market about the effectiveness of monetary policy, especially given that M1 growth has accelerated while M2 growth has slowed. Special Topic 2 (see page 24) explores whether the Mainland economy is caught in a liquidity trap, and Special Topic 3 (see page 27) examines the factors that may have caused the divergence in M1 and M2 growth. The findings suggest that there is no evidence that the Mainland has fallen into a liquidity trap, and the main reasons for M1 growing significantly faster than M2 are the reduced opportunity cost of holding liquid money due to monetary easing in recent years, and the possible increase in demand for precautionary money due to rising economic uncertainty. Hong Kong's economic growth accelerated slightly in the second half of 2016. Quarter-on-quarter real GDP growth rose from 0.8% in the third quarter to 1.2% in the fourth quarter. Domestically, private consumption growth continued to strengthen, while buoyant infrastructure activity in the fourth quarter boosted investment growth. Externally, goods export growth rose along with improved trade flows in the region, while services exports grew steadily with the recovery of trade-related and transportation services. As the growth of imports of goods and services was faster, net exports continued to drag on real GDP growth in the second half of the year. With the rise in economic growth, the overall unemployment rate fell slightly to 3.3% in December. Economic growth in 2017 is expected to remain moderate. The government and market consensus forecasts for real GDP growth in 2017 are 2-3% and 2.0% respectively. However, Hong Kong's growth prospects still face significant external headwinds. The protectionist rhetoric of the new US administration has increased the downside risks to global trade and Hong Kong's external demand. With the US dollar facing appreciation pressure and an expected acceleration in the pace of US interest rate hikes, the global financial environment is expected to become less supportive of the real economy, which could lead to a tightening of local financial conditions, especially if tail risks materialise. Special Topic 4 (see page 41) discusses the compilation of a Hong Kong Financial Conditions Index to help monitor local financial conditions. Since the second half of 2016, local inflationary pressures have remained moderate, while quarter-on-quarter inflation momentum picked up slightly in the fourth quarter of 2016, mainly due to fluctuations in food prices and rising housing rents. With stable import prices and moderate local cost pressures, inflationary pressures are expected to remain manageable. Despite market volatility, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained broadly stable, but occasionally weakened after the US interest rate hike in December. The Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered. As the US dollar appreciated, the Hong Kong dollar's nominal effective exchange rate rose further. Due to the large monetary base, Hong Kong interbank offered rates remained low, but have risen since October due to year-end funding demand and catching up with US interest rate hikes. Consequently, after falling to a recent low of 1.71% in October amid intense competition in the mortgage lending business, the average mortgage rate rose slightly to 2.07% in January 2017. Overall loan growth accelerated to 4.2% in the second half of 2016, compared to 2.2% growth in the first half. The growth was supported by strengthening local economic activity and increased financing needs of multinational corporations at year-end. Domestic loan growth accelerated slightly, while loans for use outside Hong Kong rebounded after a slight decrease in the first half of the year. Analysed by currency, Hong Kong dollar loans grew strongly by 5.0% in the second half of the year, while foreign currency loans recorded a 3.2% growth as Mainland borrowers gradually reduced repayment of foreign currency loans. The funding position of banks remained broadly sound. The Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio fell slightly to 77.1% at the end of 2016, reflecting that deposit growth outpaced loan growth. The overall foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio dropped to 59.9% at year-end, and the US dollar loan-to-deposit ratio fell significantly to 63.8% due to strong growth in US dollar deposits. Due to the strong US dollar, both onshore and offshore Renminbi exchange rates weakened. Against this backdrop, Hong Kong's offshore Renminbi liquidity pool (including customer deposits and outstanding certificates of deposit) further consolidated with other offshore Renminbi markets, and the volatility of the offshore Renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate increased significantly. Nevertheless, banks' Renminbi liquidity management remained robust, and the average daily turnover of the Renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained at a high level. Hong Kong's offshore Renminbi business will likely continue to face headwinds from the uncertain trend of the Renminbi exchange rate. As global market conditions improved, the Hong Kong stock market closed significantly higher during the reporting period. Although the US presidential election had an unexpected outcome, the market was only briefly impacted. This was mainly due to investors' anticipation of the Trump administration's fiscal stimulus measures, which pushed global stock markets higher. While benefiting from this, the local market was cautious amidst the optimism, possibly due to concerns about a faster pace of US interest rate hikes, challenges facing the Mainland's economic outlook, uncertainty in Renminbi policy, and controls on capital flows. Looking ahead, although the local market may be affected by external economic conditions, its attractive valuation could provide support to the market. Although Hong Kong dollar bond yields rose sharply at the end of last year, and the spread with US Treasury bonds widened rapidly, the Hong Kong dollar bond market still expanded steadily during the reporting period. At the same time, Hong Kong's offshore Renminbi bond market recovered in the second half of 2016 after contracting in the first half, but new bond issuance for the full year still decreased compared to the previous year. Looking ahead, if global investors reverse their earlier search-for-yield investment strategies, both the Hong Kong dollar and offshore Renminbi bond markets will come under pressure. As US trade policy is not yet clear, the Renminbi exchange rate may remain volatile, and the outlook for these two bond markets in the next six months will continue to be clouded by significant uncertainties. After the government introduced new stamp duty measures, the residential property market showed immediate signs of adjustment, but has recently rebounded. In view of the renewed market exuberance, the government raised the stamp duty to a flat rate of 15% in November. Transaction volumes in both the primary and secondary markets fell in the following two months. However, transaction volume has risen recently, partly reflecting developers increasing the launch of new primary properties. At the same time, property prices continued to rise to new highs, but the pace of increase has slowed.

Following the unexpected election of Donald Trump as US President, policy uncertainty in the United States has increased. Although market focus has been on the short-term benefits of potential large-scale fiscal policies and pro-business measures, US economic activity is now close to its economic potential. Fiscal stimulus measures may only provide a slight cyclical boost to US economic growth, but they will further exacerbate the upside risks to inflation. More importantly, the risks faced by emerging market economies are increasing with the capital outflow pressure brought by a faster pace of US interest rate hikes and a stronger US dollar, while potential US trade protectionist measures will also threaten global trade. In East Asia, real economic activity improved slightly in the second half of 2016, and export volumes have also increased recently. However, against the backdrop of US interest rate hikes, a stronger US dollar, and potential US protectionist measures, financial markets are expected to remain volatile, and downside risks to economic growth have risen. In Mainland China, overall economic growth accelerated slightly in the second half of 2016, amid robust growth in infrastructure investment and an improvement in private sector business spending. The Mainland economy continues to rebalance, with the tertiary industry expanding steadily, but the ongoing economic restructuring and changes in Sino-US trade relations may increase uncertainty in the short-term economic outlook. With the government determined to curb rising property prices, the contribution of the real estate sector to economic growth may also decrease this year if the property market continues to cool down. On the external front, although the Renminbi remained stable against the China Foreign Exchange Trade System (CFETS) basket of currencies during the reporting period, capital outflow pressure increased at the end of 2016 with the appreciation of the US dollar and US interest rate hikes, and then seemed to ease slightly in early 2017. Following the unexpected election of Donald Trump as US President, global financial markets reacted strongly, especially with market expectations that Trump's policies, such as tax reform, a large-scale increase in infrastructure spending, and deregulation, would boost US economic growth and inflation, stimulating major stock markets to rise (Figure 2.1). Consequently, market expectations for US inflation and US interest rate hikes have warmed up, leading to a sharp rise in US Treasury yields and a stronger US dollar. Figure 2.1 Stock Market Indices of Selected Advanced Economies However, the market-anticipated Trump tax cuts may not have the positive impact on US economic growth that the market expects. Although a shift in economic policy to rely on fiscal easing measures will help alleviate the heavy burden on monetary easing policies, the appropriateness of implementing fiscal easing measures at this time is questionable given the current stage of the US economic cycle. Although US economic growth has slowed in recent quarters, the output gap has gradually narrowed, and the unemployment rate in February was in line with the Fed's estimated natural unemployment rate of 4.7%, reflecting that US economic activity is already close to its economic potential. The US economy is currently in an expansionary cycle, and the fiscal multiplier will be lower than during a recession (see, for example, Auerbach & Gorodnichenko (2012))1. In fact, recent estimates of the US Laffer curve suggest that tax cuts on labor or capital may lead to a decrease in tax revenue (see, for example, Trabandt & Uhlig (2012))2. In any case, with reduced excess capacity, any further measures to boost economic growth, even if their real impact on economic growth is limited, may push up inflation. At the same time, other factors such as rising oil and commodity prices, as well as potential trade protectionist measures including the Border Adjustment Tax currently under consideration, may also exacerbate the upside risks to US inflation. Even with the increased risk of rising US inflation, the Federal Reserve has remained cautious about tightening US monetary policy and has tended to maintain an ultra-accommodative monetary policy stance. However, long-term bond yields have risen, partly reflecting the increased risk of US inflation. Since the US election, although market forecasts for the future federal funds rate have been revised upwards to near the Fed's median forecast for 2017 and early 2018, they are still well below the Fed's long-term forecast (Figure 2.2). Therefore, a faster pace of US interest rate hikes could trigger the risk of significant market volatility. While financial markets have focused on the short-term benefits of potential expansionary fiscal policies and pro-business measures driving stronger US economic growth, long-term risks remain, including damaging protectionist trade policies and a further rise in US national debt. In fact, the Trump administration may fulfill its election promises and adopt trade protectionist measures. Increased trade barriers would lead to market distortions that harm overall interests, hinder global trade, reduce the efficiency of global supply chains, and pose downside risks to the global economic outlook. Figure 2.2 Future Federal Funds Rate Forecasts: Fed vs. Market In Europe, political instability remains a major risk and headwind to the European economic recovery. Although the economic environment in the Eurozone has gradually improved, with real GDP growing at a moderate 1.7% year-on-year in the fourth quarter, only slightly lower than the 1.8% year-on-year growth in the third quarter, Eurozone economic activity is still only slightly above pre-global financial crisis levels, relative to the stronger recovery of the US economy (Figure 2.3). Since the Brexit decision last summer, there have been concerns that the Eurozone will eventually disintegrate. Although the economic and political situation in Italy seems to have stabilized after the formation of a new government and the implementation of bank rescue measures, upcoming elections in Germany and France (and possibly Italy) against the backdrop of Brexit negotiations and rising anti-establishment sentiment could become political flashpoints. Partly due to increased political uncertainty, sovereign bond yields in Europe have continued to climb, and corporate bond spreads have also widened, a situation particularly evident in peripheral countries, which could create a vicious cycle for the real economy and potentially put pressure on real business investment in the Eurozone. Figure 2.3 Real GDP of Major Advanced Economies In Japan, real GDP has been revised upwards in recent quarters, with the annualized growth rate in the fourth quarter of 2016 increasing to 1.6% year-on-year, the fastest pace since the third quarter of 2015, indicating a stronger-than-expected economic recovery. However, partly due to structural problems in the labor market, wage growth has been slow, leading to weak consumption growth. At the same time, the recent rapid depreciation of the yen means that the downward pressure on "new core" goods inflation caused by the earlier appreciation of the yen is about to begin to subside. Coupled with a stronger-than-expected recovery, this indicates an improved short-term inflation outlook, and "new core" inflation (excluding fresh food and energy), although falling to 0.1% in December, is expected to bottom out and rebound. Nevertheless, in the face of long-term and structural headwinds, growth may remain slow, and inflation expectations remain at around 0.5% – 0.6%, lower than the level at the launch of Abenomics in early 2014. Therefore, the risk that the inflation rate will fail to reach the Bank of Japan's medium-term target of 2% still exists. For other countries, especially emerging market economies, the benefits from faster US economic growth through trade channels may be smaller due to reduced US imports after the global financial crisis and the potential implementation of protectionist policies by the US. At the same time, a faster pace of US interest rate hikes and further appreciation of the US dollar will lead to tighter financial conditions, exacerbating downside economic risks. This could drag down economic growth and increase the risk of rapid capital outflows. In fact, market expectations of large-scale fiscal expansion by the Trump administration, coupled with concerns about a sharp rise in energy prices, have led to a repricing of inflation risk, causing a significant and widespread increase in long-term bond yields in advanced economies as well as in many emerging market economies. Special Topic 1 assesses the potential spillover effects of US interest rate hike expectations on the sovereign bond markets of 26 selected economies. In East Asia3, real economic activity has recently regained vitality, with a slight increase in regional GDP and rising inflation. Real GDP Growth — In the second half of 2016, economic growth generally remained stable due to steady private consumption in many regional economies. At the same time, exports generally rose slightly from their lows in 2015. This benefited not only from the stabilization of growth in China but also from improved performance in advanced economies such as the US and Europe. For net commodity exporters (e.g., Malaysia and Indonesia), the rebound in commodity prices also provided an additional boost. Other major exporters (e.g., South Korea, Taiwan, and Singapore) also regained momentum due to growth in electronics and semiconductor exports. Inflation — As commodity (especially oil) prices have rebounded, producer price inflation has generally shown an upward trend. While this will push up industrial costs and even consumer spending, consumption and investment growth may be boosted by the reduced risk of long-term deflation. The acceleration of producer price inflation may exert upward pressure on consumer price inflation, with the actual impact depending on the extent to which the increase in producer prices is passed on to consumer prices, which is inconsistent across economies. Consensus forecasts for the Consumer Price Index indicate that while inflation in many regional economies will remain slightly below their central banks' 2017 inflation targets, it will rise to levels closer to the targets (Figure 2.4). With the exception of Indonesia, which cut interest rates twice in September and October last year to boost growth, central banks in the East Asian region have generally maintained an accommodative monetary policy with unchanged interest rates. Figure 2.4 Headline CPI Inflation, Forecasts, and Central Bank Targets in East Asia Despite the improvement in the real economy, the unexpected outcome of the US presidential election in November 2016 led to short-term volatility in financial markets. Foreign Exchange Markets — After the US presidential election, investors expected US inflation to rise, and most regional currencies depreciated against the US dollar. However, on a trade-weighted basis, some regional currencies have depreciated less, or even appreciated slightly, since the US election (Figure 2.5). Figure 2.5 Spot FX Depreciation against USD and Change in Nominal Effective Exchange Rate after US Election Bond and Stock Markets — Asset prices briefly fell after the US presidential election but subsequently stabilized. The spread between sovereign bonds of East Asian economies and US Treasury bonds widened. However, as the market stabilized, yields in some regional economies declined but have not yet returned to pre-election levels (Figure 2.6). Nevertheless, the spread has narrowed compared to pre-election levels. Figure 2.6 Spread between 10-Year Sovereign Bonds and US Treasury Bonds Portfolio Investment Flows — Portfolio investment funds flowed out of the East Asian region in the fourth quarter of 2016, but at a slower pace than during the "taper tantrum" in mid-2013. In the first few weeks of 2017, capital inflows were recorded again, supporting asset prices and financial conditions. Looking ahead, regional growth is expected to remain stable, but at a pace still below the historical average. Financial markets are likely to remain volatile due to increased uncertainty about US government policy and the potential policy response from the Federal Reserve. A sharp rise in the US dollar and yields could attract capital from the region to the United States, causing investors to reduce their holdings of regional assets, especially those with currently high valuations. The tightening of financial conditions in this situation would also put repayment pressure on companies with large amounts of US dollar-denominated debt. On a macro level, a general rise in global interest rates would also reduce fixed capital investment in the region, which would not only drag down aggregate demand in the short term but could also affect potential growth in the long term. Finally, the region's exporting countries face the potential threat of protectionist policies from the new US administration. The US trade deficit with East Asian economies has continued to widen in recent years (Figure 2.7), especially in the region's major export industries, such as electronics, electrical appliances, automobiles, apparel, and textiles. Over the past two decades, as US imports in these industries have increased, a large number of jobs have been lost. Protectionist policies aimed at reducing the trade deficit and revitalizing US manufacturing could pose a significant risk to the region's exporting countries.

Accelerating growth in private consumption and robust activity in the construction and building sector—driven by the public sector—contributed to a slight pickup in Hong Kong’s economic growth during the second half of 2016. Given increasing uncertainties in the external environment, economic growth is expected to remain moderate in 2017. Thanks to stable import prices and moderate domestic growth momentum, inflationary pressures are anticipated to stay under control.  Hong Kong’s economic growth edged up slightly in the latter half of 2016. Seasonally adjusted real GDP grew by 1.2% quarter-on-quarter in the fourth quarter, slightly higher than the 0.8% growth rate recorded in the third quarter (Chart 3.1). Partly owing to improved consumer confidence and a resilient labor market, private consumption expanded at a faster pace, becoming the main driver of GDP growth. Supported by infrastructure projects such as the construction of a third runway at Hong Kong International Airport, activity in the construction and building sector also remained strong. However, weak corporate capital expenditure limited the overall contribution of investment to GDP growth. Externally, both exports and imports accelerated, reflecting rising trade flows within the region (Chart 3.2). Trade-related and transport services further boosted export growth, while import growth rebounded partly due to strong demand for travel among local residents. Nevertheless, net exports continued to weigh on GDP growth.  Chart 3.1: Real GDP growth rate and contributions from major expenditure components   Chart 3.2: Real exports and imports  The labor market remained tight. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate stayed at 3.4% during the first three quarters before edging down to 3.3% in the fourth quarter (Chart 3.3). In fact, unemployment rates declined across several major sectors in the latter half of the year, including retail, accommodation, and food services; this was partly due to a stabilization in the slowdown experienced by the retail sector. Total employment reached a record high of 3.824 million in February 2017, while the labor force participation rate remained stable at around 61%.  Chart 3.3: Unemployment rate and total employment  Economic growth is expected to remain moderate in 2017. On the external front, global economic and trade growth may stay sluggish amid uncertainties surrounding the global macroeconomic and financial environment. Moreover, the strong U.S. dollar has led to an appreciation of the Hong Kong dollar’s real effective exchange rate, which is likely to dampen Hong Kong’s export performance. Domestically, although stable employment and income conditions should support consumption, private consumption is forecast to grow at a moderate pace, constrained by rising interest rates. With increased housing supply and the rollout of various infrastructure projects, construction activity is expected to grow steadily; however, a weak business sentiment and higher interest rates are likely to restrain corporate capital expenditure. Currently, the government forecasts real GDP growth in 2017 to range between 2% and 3%, while analysts from the private sector project an average growth rate of 2.0%. The economic outlook remains subject to numerous uncertainties, particularly those stemming from the external environment. Policy uncertainties under the new U.S. administration could cloud the global economic outlook; potential protectionist trade policies might also hinder global trade flows. The process of Brexit and upcoming elections in several major European countries may trigger volatility in financial markets and affect capital flows into Hong Kong. Additionally, the normalization of U.S. interest rates is expected to tighten domestic monetary conditions, exerting downward pressure on the real economy and asset prices.  Since the second half of 2016, although domestic inflation has shown some quarterly acceleration in recent months, it has generally remained moderate. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying composite CPI remained steady at 2.1% from the latter half of 2016 through January this year (Chart 3.4). The three-month annualized underlying inflation rate—an indicator of inflation momentum—rose from 0.9% in the third quarter to 3.0% in the fourth quarter, before slightly easing to 2.4% in January. The main drivers of this rising inflation momentum were higher prices of traded goods and rising housing rents (Chart 3.5). In particular, inflation for traded goods shifted from negative figures in the third quarter to 3.0% in the fourth quarter, driven primarily by higher prices of basic food items and clothing. Meanwhile, since the third quarter, the housing rent component of the composite CPI has risen—owing to a narrowing decline in private residential rents and an increase in public housing rents implemented in September 2016—though it eased slightly in January (Chart 3.6). Figure 3.4 shows various indicators of consumer price inflation. Figure 3.5 illustrates consumer price inflation broken down by major components. Figure 3.6 presents the rent component of the composite CPI as well as market rents. In the short term, given weak import prices and moderate domestic cost pressures, inflationary pressures are expected to remain under control. The strength of the Hong Kong dollar is expected to offset, to some extent, the rebound in global commodity prices; consequently, imported inflation will likely stay low (Figure 3.7). Domestically, the output gap is estimated to have remained close to zero in the fourth quarter of 2016, which should help alleviate business cost pressures and thus curb inflation in the services sector. Despite a tight labor market, wage growth has remained modest in recent quarters; real per capita wages rose by 1.1% in the first half of 2016 before declining by 0.4% in the third quarter (Figure 3.8). Given ongoing uncertainties in the external environment, which have led to cautious business sentiment, wage growth is expected to remain subdued. Additionally, given the poor retail sales performance in recent months, retail property rents are forecast to increase only moderately. Moreover, the earlier softening in private residential rents is expected to gradually ease inflationary pressures. Overall, the year-on-year inflation rate is projected to decline throughout 2017; the government forecasts the full-year underlying inflation rate at 2.0%, down from 2.3% in 2016.  Figure 3.7: Commodity and import prices  Figure 3.8: Unit labor costs and real per capita wage growth  There are both upside and downside risks to the inflation outlook. On the downside, should inflation rise more rapidly in the United States under the Trump administration, this could prompt faster interest rate hikes there, potentially raising local mortgage rates and increasing downward pressure on property prices and housing rents. Meanwhile, a stronger Hong Kong dollar might keep import prices weak while reducing Hong Kong’s attractiveness to tourists. On the upside, if global economic expansion exceeds expectations, this could accelerate Hong Kong’s economic growth and drive demand-driven increases in international commodity prices, thereby exerting upward pressure on local inflation. Furthermore, the revised statutory minimum wage will take effect on May 1, 2017; this is likely to further boost inflation, though the actual impact of this cost-driven inflation will depend on the extent to which higher wage costs are passed on to consumer prices.

Despite volatility in financial markets, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained largely stable, while Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates rose in tandem with U.S. dollar rates. Partly due to an improving local economic environment, overall lending continued to grow modestly. Looking ahead, with the pace of U.S. interest rate normalization accelerating, uncertainty surrounding the policy direction of the new U.S. administration, and political risks in Europe, volatility in Hong Kong dollar funding flows may increase. Despite financial market fluctuations, the spot exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar against the U.S. dollar stayed largely stable (Chart 4.1). Although market volatility triggered by the November U.S. presidential election led to a general decline in Asian currencies, the spot exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar against the U.S. dollar remained steady. However, the interest rate projections released by the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) at its meeting on December 13–14, 2016, heightened market expectations of faster U.S. interest rate hikes, causing the Hong Kong dollar to weaken briefly thereafter. In early 2017, the Hong Kong dollar strengthened along with other Asian currencies; however, as market expectations of a March 2017 U.S. rate hike gained momentum from mid-February, the Hong Kong dollar began to show signs of weakening. During the reporting period, the exchange rate peg was not tested (Chart 4.2).    Chart 4.1: Exchange rate and funding flow indicators   Chart 4.2: Funding flow indicators    Driven by the strength of the U.S. dollar, the nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar rose 4.9% between August and December, before stabilizing recently (Chart 4.3). Given the minimal impact from narrowing inflation differentials between Hong Kong and its trading partners, the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar closely followed the trend of the nominal index.    Chart 4.3: Nominal and real effective exchange rates    Portfolio investment saw outflows in the second half of 2016. The latest balance of payments statistics indicate that net inflows of investments in equities and debt securities by non-residents occurred in the third quarter, reflecting improved global market sentiment and a surge in initial public offerings (Table 4.A). However, driven partly by Hong Kong banks’ increased purchases of U.S. bonds, there were substantial outflows of debt investments by local residents, which offset the inflows from non-residents. Consequently, cross-border portfolio investment recorded a net outflow in the third quarter. A survey of global mutual funds revealed that portfolio outflows in the final quarter of 2016 were primarily attributable to the unexpected outcome of the U.S. presidential election and expectations of faster U.S. interest rate hikes, which put pressure on both local and other Asian financial markets (Chart 4.4). Nevertheless, the latest data show that portfolio inflows into Hong Kong regained momentum in the first quarter of 2017, partly due to investors’ optimism regarding expansionary U.S. fiscal policies, which boosted global financial market performance.    Chart 4.4: Market survey on equity and bond-related funding flows    Looking ahead, volatility in Hong Kong dollar funding flows may increase. An acceleration in U.S. interest rate normalization would raise the risk of a reversal in Hong Kong dollar funding flows. Meanwhile, uncertainties surrounding the new U.S. administration, the UK’s Brexit process, and elections in EU member states could also heighten funding flow volatility. Additionally, growing demand from mainland investors for Hong Kong dollar assets may exert upward pressure on the Hong Kong dollar. Although initial trading volumes under the Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect in December favored northbound transactions over southbound ones, it is expected that two-way equity investment flows between the mainland and Hong Kong under this scheme will gradually increase. Despite rising U.S. interest rates and financial market volatility, Hong Kong’s monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2016 and more recently. The Hong Kong dollar monetary base remained substantial; driven by growth in certificates of indebtedness and government-issued currency in circulation, it rose a further 1.7% in the second half of the year (Chart 4.5). Given that the exchange rate peg was not tested, the total reserves and outstanding Exchange Fund bills and bonds remained largely at the elevated level of HK$1,222.7 billion. Amid this, the issuance of HK$49 billion worth of additional Exchange Fund bills was undertaken to meet banks’ substantial liquidity management needs; consequently, total reserves contracted while the outstanding amount of Exchange Fund bills and bonds rose accordingly. As shown in Figure 4.5, the components of the monetary base indicate that Hong Kong’s Hong Kong dollar money supply grew at an accelerated pace, reflecting a gradually stabilizing local economy. The growth rate of Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (HKD M3) rose from 2.3% in the first half of the year to 6.5% in the second half. As a major component of HKD M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits posted a relatively rapid growth rate of 6.6% in the second half (Figure 4.7), driven primarily by heightened local economic activity and increased trading demand resulting from a rebound in initial public offering activities. An analysis based on corresponding assets reveals that the growth of HKD M3 mainly reflects increases in Hong Kong dollar loans and banks’ net foreign currency assets (Figure 4.6); these developments correspond respectively to monetary expansion stemming from credit growth and net inflows of Hong Kong dollar funds into the non-bank private sector. Figure 4.6: HKD M3 and changes in its corresponding assets. Meanwhile, growth patterns for foreign currency deposits remained uneven. Following a 10.2% increase in the first half, US dollar deposits recorded an even higher growth rate of 12.8% in the second half, driven by a stronger US dollar (Figure 4.7). Driven by stronger local economic activity and rising cross-border financing demand, total lending expanded by 4.2% in the second half of the year, following a 2.2% increase in the first half (Figure 4.10). With economic growth momentum gaining strength, growth in local lending slightly accelerated from 3.2% in the first half to 4.0% in the second half. Loans used outside Hong Kong rebounded by 4.6% in the second half of the year after a slight decline in the first half, partly reflecting heightened financing needs among multinational corporations at year-end. By currency, Hong Kong dollar loans posted robust growth of 5.0% in the second half; meanwhile, foreign currency loans also saw a modest 3.2% increase, as mainland borrowers gradually reduced repayments on such loans. Overall, total loans grew by 6.5% in 2016, up from 3.5% in 2015.    Figure 4.10: Loan growth by economic sector    Domestic loan performance varied across sectors in the second half of the year (Figure 4.11). Loans to financial services firms and the information technology sector recorded double-digit growth, reflecting stronger financing demand driven by their relatively favorable growth prospects. Loan growth in the construction and property development sectors also accelerated, mirroring rising private construction activity. Conversely, despite signs of improvement in commodity trade and retail sales, loans for trade financing and to the manufacturing, wholesale, and retail sectors declined.    Figure 4.11: Domestic loan growth by sector    Household debt growth accelerated to 4.3% in the second half of the year, compared to 0.5% in the first half. Partly reflecting an improving economic environment, private loans—including credit card balances and other loans for personal use—rose by 7.2% (Figure 4.11). Residential mortgage lending also picked up, growing at 3.1%, largely due to robust housing transactions between July and October. Consequently, the ratio of household debt to GDP rose from 65.8% in the second quarter of 2016 to 67.2% in the fourth quarter (Figure 4.12). Meanwhile, the overall foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell from 61.4% to 59.9% over the same period; notably, the US dollar loan-to-deposit ratio dropped sharply to 63.8% owing to strong growth in US dollar deposits. The HKMA’s “Survey on Credit Conditions Outlook” indicates that loan demand will remain weak in the short run.    The appreciation of the US dollar led to a weakening of both offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates (Figure 4.14). Throughout most of late 2016, the offshore renminbi traded at a discount to the onshore rate, closing the year at an annual low of 6.98 per US dollar. In December, liquidity in the offshore renminbi interbank market tightened once again, partly reflecting deteriorating financial market conditions and banks’ precautionary financing needs ahead of year-end (Figure 4.15). As banks built up liquidity buffers amid deteriorating market sentiment, the overnight offshore renminbi Hong Kong interbank offered rate surged to 61.3% on January 6, 2017.    The subsequent rise in offshore renminbi financing costs prompted liquidation of short positions, prompting a rebound in the offshore renminbi exchange rate in early January 2017; the premium of the offshore rate over the onshore rate also reappeared. Since mid-January, both offshore and onshore renminbi rates have stabilized somewhat, with liquidity conditions gradually improving. By end-February 2017, the overnight and three-month offshore renminbi Hong Kong interbank offered rates had fallen to 2.00% and 4.61%, respectively.
