Global financial markets saw renewed volatility at the beginning of the year as the market reassessed US inflation risks. In February, global stock markets fell sharply from their late-January highs, completely wiping out the significant gains from the start of the year, while the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield rose to a four-year high. The sustained rally in global stock markets over the past two years amid low volatility was driven by market expectations of a continued ideal state of solid economic growth, low inflation, and low interest rates. However, this expectation is facing risks from tightening global monetary conditions, rising trade protectionism, and geopolitical tensions. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, but the market continued to operate in an orderly manner. In the second half of 2017, overall lending continued to increase, but at a slower pace. After a slight slowdown last year, both property price growth and transaction volume picked up in the fourth quarter of 2017. Looking ahead, renewed volatility in global and local financial markets may add to the volatility of capital flows in Hong Kong. Given the uncertainty in the financial markets, as well as the normalization of US monetary policy and ongoing geopolitical risks, banks should remain vigilant against increased interest rate volatility and potential capital outflow risks. In particular, given the continued rise in corporate leverage and high levels of personal debt, banks should assess the potential impact of a larger-than-expected rise in interest rates on asset quality. After the Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index (VIX) hovered at low levels for more than two years, global financial markets saw renewed volatility at the beginning of the year. Global stock markets fell sharply from their late-January highs, with the S&P 500 index once falling by more than 10%, completely wiping out the significant gains recorded in early January. The shift in market sentiment was due to signs that the global economic recovery could put pressure on long-subdued US wages and prices, which could lead the Federal Reserve to accelerate its pace of interest rate hikes. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high. The long-term rally in global stock markets over the past two years was based on market expectations that economic conditions would remain ideal. In the second half of 2017, global economic growth momentum continued to strengthen, with economic activity picking up in both advanced and emerging market economies. Towards the end of the year, the US Congress passed a tax reform package that included tax cuts and a comprehensive overhaul of corporate and personal tax rules, leading to market hopes that the strong US economic recovery would receive an additional cyclical boost in the short term. Despite the strengthening of activity, core inflation in major advanced economies remained moderate, further reinforcing market expectations that global interest rates would remain low for a long time. Against this backdrop, global asset markets rose significantly in 2017, with US stock markets in particular repeatedly hitting new highs. However, with the release of stronger-than-expected US wage growth data for January, global stock markets reassessed inflation risks. After the short-term financial market volatility, the risk of tightening global monetary conditions may continue to cast a shadow over the global economic outlook. In the US, the economy has now reached its potential output, and the cyclical stimulus to domestic demand from the expected tax cuts may accelerate the rebound in inflation, prompting the Federal Reserve to accelerate the tightening of monetary policy. At the same time, as the tax cuts will lead to a rise in the fiscal deficit, the US may issue more government bonds in the future, which is expected to put upward pressure on long-term bond yields as the Federal Reserve continues to advance the normalization of its balance sheet. Outside the US, the strengthening growth momentum in other major advanced economies has led to market expectations that their central banks may scale back their quantitative easing programs. If implemented, this would lead to a synchronized tightening of global monetary conditions. Policy and event risks arising from international political and geopolitical tensions could also cast a shadow over the global economic growth outlook. The US government appears to be increasingly inclined to adopt protectionist trade measures to protect domestic industries from competition, with recent examples including the announcement of import tariffs on solar panels, washing machines, steel, and aluminum. These moves have raised concerns about whether its trading partners will respond with retaliatory measures. In addition, an unexpected escalation of geopolitical tensions could affect global trade and exacerbate volatility in global financial markets. Given the above uncertainties in the global economic outlook, it is questionable whether the current high valuations in global asset markets can be sustained. At a fundamental level, it remains to be seen whether the cyclical growth in global demand and the expected rise in the fiscal deficit from US tax cuts will push up the natural rate of interest (R*); in addition, the normalization of the Federal Reserve's balance sheet is expected to lead to a rise in the term premium, which may push up long-term interest rates, thereby being unfavorable to asset market valuations. In East Asia, the region's economies are also in an ideal environment of solid growth and moderate inflation. With good economic performance and an optimistic outlook, capital inflows have also accelerated, and financial markets have risen at the same time. However, this positive outlook faces downside risks from the tightening of global liquidity due to the synchronized normalization of monetary policy by major central banks; the US government's inward-looking trade policy; geopolitical tensions; and the potential for a squeeze in offshore US dollar liquidity as US companies repatriate large amounts of profits in response to the one-time "deemed repatriation" provision under the country's tax reform. Any shock to credit and financial markets could trigger a reversal of capital flows, and sectors and economies with higher leverage are most vulnerable to the impact of tightening financial conditions. In mainland China, the economy performed well in the second half of 2017, supported by solid consumption, strong infrastructure, and a rebound in industrial spending towards the end of the year. At the same time, signs of the rise of the "new economy" have become more apparent, with industries such as high-value-added manufacturing and services showing strong business expansion momentum in the past few quarters. Looking ahead, the near-term economic growth outlook remains positive, but uncertainties remain. In particular, it remains to be seen to what extent the rapid growth of the "new economy" can help offset the short-term pressure on growth from the further advancement of structural reforms. The mainland authorities announced in 2018 that they would continue to adopt a proactive fiscal policy stance, which may help to mitigate adverse economic developments if necessary. During the review period, some progress was made in structural reforms and the control of systemic risks. In particular, with the introduction of tightening measures, the mainland property market showed signs of cooling during the review period, especially in first-tier cities. At the same time, as banks tightened their loan approval standards, banks' risk exposure to companies in overcapacity industries remained under control, while shadow banking activities also slowed down amid financial deleveraging. In addition to the above positive developments, our analysis also shows that the efficiency of capital allocation in mainland China seems to have improved. In particular, the borrowing constraints faced by state-owned enterprises with weaker repayment capacity seem to have tightened, possibly due to a reduction in the support provided by local governments (for details, please refer to Special Topic 2 on page 28). On the external front, capital outflow pressure remained moderate for most of 2017 amid a stabilizing economic situation and reduced risks. The Hong Kong economy maintained its quarter-on-quarter growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Real GDP grew by 3.8% for the full year of 2017, the fastest growth rate in 6 years. Private consumption remained solid in the second half of 2017 due to favorable employment and income conditions and rising asset prices. Overall investment spending also rebounded due to an increase in corporate capital expenditure. On the external front, benefiting from improved global trade growth and a gradual recovery in inbound tourism, Hong Kong's export performance further improved. Nevertheless, as import growth was faster than export growth, net exports of goods still dragged down GDP growth, while net exports of services made a positive contribution to GDP growth. Economic growth is expected to remain solid in 2018. Private consumption, building and construction activities, and exports will continue to support economic growth. Given that Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually rise, Special Topic 3 examines the impact of a higher mortgage payment burden on private consumption. The government and market consensus forecasts for real GDP growth in 2018 are between 3 to 4% and 3.0%, respectively. However, Hong Kong's growth outlook is still affected by many uncertainties and risks, including the external environment mentioned above, the economic performance of mainland China under tightening financial conditions, and the trend of Hong Kong's asset markets. Although the unemployment rate fell to a nearly 20-year low of 2.9%, local inflation pressure remained under control. However, quarter-on-quarter inflation momentum has shown signs of a slight increase in recent months. Among them, the prices of both traded goods and services have risen. Looking ahead, the underlying inflation rate may rebound slightly to a still moderate level, partly reflecting the pass-through effect of rising rents for newly signed private residential leases. Affected by the funding demand for IPO activities and seasonal funding demand, liquidity conditions tightened, and the unwinding of Hong Kong dollar short positions increased, causing the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate to strengthen between September and November 2017. As liquidity conditions eased and interest rate arbitrage activities became active again, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened again from December 2017. In early 2018, despite the turmoil in global financial markets (especially the stock market), the Hong Kong dollar remained basically stable. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened further in early March 2018, but the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered. Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates were under upward pressure from September to December 2017. This was mainly due to the funding demand for IPO activities and the cautious attitude of banks towards liquidity management towards the end of the year. In December, the average overnight and 3-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates rose by 14 and 50 basis points, respectively, from six months ago, to 0.25% and 1.26%. After a slight decline in early January 2018, the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate remained largely stable and was not affected by the recent adjustment in global financial markets. Despite the fierce competition in the mortgage lending business, the average lending rate for new mortgages of banks still followed the upward trend of short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates, rising to 2.16% in December. On the other hand, the financing costs of retail banks remained generally low after a brief rise in October due to IPO activities, and the composite interest rate closed at 0.38% in December. Looking ahead, as US monetary policy continues to normalize, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure; if global financial market sentiment changes sharply, the volatility of capital flows may increase. For the full year of 2017, total bank loans grew steadily by 16.1%. After a strong growth of 10.2% in the first half of the year, loan growth slowed to 5.3% in the second half. Among them, the growth rate of domestic loans and loans for use outside Hong Kong in most industries declined. The slowdown in foreign currency loan growth was partly due to the rise in US dollar financing costs. On the other hand, due to the favorable local economic environment and the relatively low financing costs of the Hong Kong dollar, Hong Kong dollar loans continued to record rapid growth. As the growth rate of Hong Kong dollar loans was faster than that of deposits, the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio rose in the second half of 2017, rising to 82.7% at the end of the year, the highest level since March 2015. On the other hand, due to the relatively slow growth of foreign currency loans, the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell to 63.1% at the end of the year. The onshore and offshore RMB exchange rates against the US dollar showed signs of stabilization between September and November 2017. Subsequently, as the US dollar weakened significantly against most major currencies, the onshore and offshore RMB exchange rates against the US dollar strengthened from December. Hong Kong's offshore RMB liquidity pool (including total RMB customer deposits and certificates of deposit), after a slight decline in the first half of the year, picked up slightly in the second half, largely reflecting changes in market expectations for the RMB exchange rate. As for other offshore RMB businesses, although RMB loans continued to decrease, the amount of RMB trade settlement handled by Hong Kong banks picked up in the second half of the year. The average daily turnover of the RMB Real Time Gross Settlement system remained at a high level. Looking ahead, Hong Kong's offshore RMB business is expected to benefit from the advancement of the "Belt and Road" initiative and the continued internationalization of the RMB.

The synchronised strengthening of the global economy since late 2016 has continued unabated. The improving growth outlook has driven global equity markets higher in 2017 and early 2018. However, a sell-off and sharp volatility in global equity markets in February, as markets reassessed US inflation risks, marked an end to the calm state of financial markets over the past two years. Looking ahead, the risk of tightening global financial conditions and a range of policy and event risks will continue to cast a shadow over the global outlook. US tax cuts in a tight labour market could accelerate the cyclical rebound in inflation, prompting the US Federal Reserve to tighten monetary policy at a faster pace. As the Fed continues to normalise its balance sheet, an increase in US Treasury issuance to finance the tax cuts could add to upward pressure on long-term bond yields. The shadow of rising trade barriers and an unexpected escalation of geopolitical tensions could also threaten the nascent global trade recovery. In East Asia, real economic growth continued to rise in the second half of 2017, benefiting from strong export performance and stable domestic demand. However, while the economic outlook is optimistic, it also faces a number of downside risks, such as a greater-than-expected tightening of global monetary conditions, US inward-looking trade policies and geopolitical tensions. The materialisation of these downside risks would also increase the risk of a reversal in capital flows. Policymakers are facing multiple challenges, on the one hand, to guard against risks to economic growth, and on the other, to limit the impact of prolonged accommodative financial conditions on inflation and balance sheet vulnerabilities. In Mainland China, the economy performed well in the second half of 2017. During the review period, some progress was made in structural reforms and containing systemic risks. The near-term growth outlook remains positive, but uncertainties remain, which will depend in part on the extent to which the rapid growth of the 'new economy' can offset the short-term pressures on growth from further structural reforms. As economic conditions stabilised and risks abated, capital outflow pressures remained moderate for most of 2017. Growth in advanced and emerging market economies accelerated in tandem in 2017 as the cyclical economic improvement gained momentum since late 2016. Among the major advanced economies, the US saw a solid rise in investment and exports, driven by positive private sector sentiment and a significant depreciation of the US dollar, while the Eurozone and Japan also recorded a broad-based cyclical recovery. Exports from emerging market economies also benefited from stabilising global commodity prices and increased import demand from major advanced economies. In the short term, investment and consumption are expected to be further boosted by corporate and personal income tax cuts following the passage of tax reform in the US. In view of the current cyclical economic upswing and the expansionary effects of the US tax reform, the International Monetary Fund forecast in January that global economic growth would accelerate from an estimated 3.7% in 2017 to 3.9% in 2018 (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 Real GDP Growth Forecasts As growth momentum in the Eurozone and Japan strengthened, market expectations of a narrowing of global monetary policy divergence, coupled with a more optimistic global growth outlook, spurred risk appetite and capital inflows into emerging market economies, which in turn put pressure on the US dollar. Despite the Fed raising interest rates three times during the year and beginning to normalise its balance sheet, the US dollar index still recorded a fall of nearly 10% in 2017. At the same time, despite the broad-based acceleration in economic growth, core inflation in the major advanced economies remained weak and below their central banks' targets, leading markets until recently to expect global interest rates to remain low (Chart 2.2). Against this backdrop, global equity markets continued to rise in 2017 and early 2018, with the S&P 500 index repeatedly hitting new highs, pushing the cyclically-adjusted price-to-earnings ratio to 33.8 in January 2018, its highest level since the 'dot-com bubble' in early 2000. Chart 2.2 Core Inflation in Major Advanced Economies However, since the second half of 2017, concerns that tax cuts would lead to higher fiscal deficits and inflation have caused long-term US Treasury yields to continue to climb, casting doubt on the sustainability of increasingly high asset market valuations. As the US announced a higher-than-expected increase in average hourly wages for January 2018, the market reassessed US inflation risks, triggering a correction in global equity markets in early February 2018. The S&P 500 index once fell by more than 10% from its high on January 26, completely wiping out the significant gains at the beginning of the year, and continued to be under pressure after the US government announced a new round of trade protection measures in early March. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a 4-year high in mid-February. Market volatility rose sharply, with the CBOE Volatility Index once soaring to a two-year high of 37.3, marking the end of the narrow volatility environment that had persisted for the past two years (Chart 2.3). Chart 2.3 CBOE Volatility Index (VIX) Looking ahead, after the short-term stock market volatility, US inflation risks, upside risks to long-term US bond yields, and possible monetary policy tightening by other major central banks could all lead to a tightening of global monetary conditions, which in turn would cast a shadow over the global economic outlook. First, with regard to US inflation risks, the recently passed tax reform includes several provisions that are expected to provide a short-term cyclical stimulus to private consumption and investment. The main measures involved in the tax reform include: (1) lowering corporate and personal income tax rates, (2) temporarily allowing full expensing of capital investment, and (3) a one-time 'deemed repatriation' provision that helps reduce the incentive for US companies to park their overseas earnings offshore. While it is not yet certain how the tax cuts will affect domestic demand and inflation, as the US economy has now reached its potential output, the tax cuts could push US output further beyond its potential, leading to an overheating economy and a cyclical rebound in inflation. A greater-than-expected rise in inflationary pressures could prompt the Federal Reserve to tighten monetary policy at a faster pace. Currently, the path of the federal funds rate expected by financial markets is more gradual than the forecasts released by the Federal Reserve. However, if inflation rebounds unexpectedly, the risk of a sudden readjustment of interest rate hike expectations cannot be ruled out (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 Federal Funds Rate Forecasts Second, given that the tax reform is likely to exacerbate the fiscal deficit, the issuance of US Treasury bonds is expected to increase in the future. At a time when the Federal Reserve continues to implement its balance sheet normalization plan, this is expected to lead to a rise in the term premium; in this situation, an increase in the issuance of US Treasury bonds may exacerbate the upward pressure on long-term bond yields. In addition, as market expectations for the passage of the US tax cut plan have increased, US inflation expectations have continued to rise since the second half of 2017 (Chart 2.5). As a result, the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield, after hovering at a low level for most of 2017, has risen by more than 70 basis points since the third quarter, partly reflecting concerns about increased supply pressure on Treasury bonds and rising inflation expectations. Chart 2.55 5-Year, 5-Year Forward Inflation Expectation Rate In addition, a key issue is whether the natural rate of interest (R*), a major component of long-term interest rates, will remain at a low level for a long time as most people expect. Although estimates of R* vary, it is generally believed that it has fallen sharply since the global financial crisis (Chart 2.6). Nevertheless, the US R* may face upward risks in the future due to (1) an expected decline in the national savings rate due to an increase in the fiscal deficit, and (2) a possible increase in the investment rate due to corporate tax cuts and more favorable tax treatment of capital expenditures. A rise in R*, coupled with the expected rise in the term premium from the Fed's balance sheet normalization, could signal a rise in long-term interest rates, which would pose a headwind to asset market valuations. Chart 2.6 US R* Estimated by the Laubach-Williams Model Third, the strengthening growth momentum in the Eurozone and Japan has led to market expectations that their central banks may scale back their monetary easing measures. Should this occur, it could signal a synchronized tightening of global monetary conditions. In the Eurozone, member economies have recorded a broad-based cyclical expansion (Chart 2.7). As for Japan, the economic recovery has also accelerated, with real GDP recording its eighth consecutive quarter of positive growth in the fourth quarter of 2017. Although the European Central Bank (ECB) and the Bank of Japan have continued to signal that they will maintain accommodative monetary policy in the face of sluggish inflation, the brightening economic growth prospects in Europe and Japan (and the continued tightening of the Japanese labor market) have led some market participants to predict that they will further scale back their quantitative easing programs in the near future. Chart 2.7 Real GDP of Selected Eurozone Member States Policy and event risks arising from international political and geopolitical tensions could also pose a threat to the nascent global economic growth and trade recovery. The US government appears to be more inclined to adopt inward-looking trade policies to protect domestic industries, with recent examples being the announcement of import tariffs on solar panels and washing machines in January 2018, and the announcement of import tariffs on steel and aluminum in early March, raising concerns about whether its trading partners will respond with retaliatory measures. At the same time, negotiations between the UK and the rest of the EU on post-Brexit trade arrangements are currently underway, and the process is fraught with uncertainties. If the above developments lead to increased trade friction, it could hinder global trade flows and reduce global production efficiency. In addition, an unexpected escalation of geopolitical tensions (such as a military conflict on the Korean Peninsula, political turmoil in the Middle East, and the underlying risk of terrorist attacks) could increase volatility in global financial markets. In East Asia, economic growth momentum strengthened further in the second half of 2017, ending the year on a strong note. Real growth in 2017 accelerated to 4.3%, the fastest pace since 2012. External trade remained the main driver of growth, while domestic demand also provided stable support (Chart 2.8). The accelerating recovery in advanced economies, stronger-than-expected growth in Mainland China, and a rebound in global demand for technology products all boosted the region's exports. Chart 2.8 East Asia: Domestic Demand and Exports Inflationary pressures have remained weak so far. In the second half of 2017, overall inflation in East Asia moderated, affected by falling food price inflation and stable energy prices (Chart 2.9). At the same time, due to slow wage growth in several economies, the core consumer price inflation rate (excluding food and energy) remained at a relatively low level. Chart 2.9 East Asia: Overall Core Consumer Price Inflation* Note: Since 2016, South Korea has set its inflation target at 2%, with a range of +/-0.5%. The favorable economic conditions were accompanied by large capital inflows, which led to a significant rise in financial asset prices in 2017 and early 2018 (blue and pink bars in Chart 2.10). The volume of capital flowing into the region's markets rebounded significantly in 2017, with total portfolio investment inflows reaching their highest level since 2010. Valuations of various financial assets in the region also rose with the market rally. In fact, credit risk compensation in the region narrowed further in the second half of 2017, and benchmark stock indices across the region rose across the board. Currencies in the region generally appreciated against the US dollar.

With robust local demand and improved export performance, Hong Kong's economy maintained steady growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Economic growth in 2018 is expected to remain steady. However, Hong Kong's economic outlook remains affected by numerous uncertainties and risks, including the normalization of monetary policies by major central banks, stability in global financial markets, rising protectionist sentiments, and escalating geopolitical tensions. In the short term, although local inflationary pressures are expected to remain moderate, several upside risks persist. Hong Kong's economy maintained growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Seasonally adjusted real GDP grew by 0.8% quarter-on-quarter in both the 3rd and 4th quarters, similar to the average growth rate of 0.9% in the previous two quarters (Figure 3.1). Compared with the first half of the year, private consumption continued to grow steadily and remained one of the main drivers of GDP growth. Consumption growth was robust due to favorable employment and income conditions, optimistic consumer sentiment, and the positive impact of rising asset prices through the wealth effect. Although property and construction activities weakened, an increase in corporate capital expenditure led to a significant rise in overall investment expenditure in the final quarter after three quarters of relatively stable performance. Regarding external factors, Hong Kong's export performance further improved, benefiting from improved global trade growth and the gradual recovery of the inbound tourism industry (Figure 3.2). Nevertheless, as the growth rate of imports was faster than that of exports, net merchandise exports continued to drag on GDP growth, while net service exports contributed positively to GDP growth. Figure 3.1 shows the growth rate of real GDP and the contribution of major expenditure items. Figure 3.2 shows the continued economic growth drivers of real imports and exports, which drove an increase in employment positions in the second half of 2017. During the period, the total number of employed persons increased by approximately 0.7% to over 385 million, with the most significant increases seen in the construction industry, financial and commercial services, and public administration, social and personal services. Since real GDP growth exceeded the growth in the number of employed persons, labor productivity showed signs of further improvement. Economic growth in 2018 is expected to remain steady. Regarding external factors, Hong Kong's export performance will continue to benefit from improved global economic growth prospects and the gradual recovery of the inbound tourism industry. Locally, private consumption is expected to continue growing, mainly due to ideal labor market conditions. Given that Hong Kong Dollar interest rates will eventually rise, Topic 3 studies the impact of higher mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption. As for local fixed capital formation, property and construction activities are expected to grow steadily, benefiting from increased housing supply and the continued rollout of infrastructure projects. While the improving economic environment will stimulate commercial capital expenditure, a potential upward adjustment in interest rates may have a negative impact. The government forecasts real GDP growth between 3 to 4% in 2018, while growth forecasts from international organizations and private sector analysts range between 2 to 4%. However, Hong Kong's growth prospects remain affected by numerous uncertainties and risks, including the external environment mentioned in previous chapters, the economic performance of mainland China under tightening financial conditions, and the trends in Hong Kong's asset markets. Local inflationary pressures remained under control in the second half of 2017, but month-on-month inflationary momentum showed signs of a slight rebound in recent months. On a year-on-year basis, the basic Composite Consumer Price Index rose by 1.7% and 1.6% in the 3rd and 4th quarters respectively, similar to the average increase of about 1.7% in the first half of the year. However, the basic inflation rate, which reflects inflationary momentum and is calculated as an annual rate over 3 months, rose slightly to 2.8% in January 2018 (Figure 3.3). During this period, prices for both traded goods and services rose. The rebound in newly signed private residential rents since mid-2016 may also increase inflationary momentum to some extent (Figure 3.4). Additionally, labor cost pressures in recent quarters have remained moderate (Figure 3.5). Figure 3.3 reflects different indicators of consumer price inflation; Figure 3.4 shows the rent item in the Consumer Price Index and market rents; Figure 3.5 shows unit labor costs and per capita wages. As global inflation remains moderate and local cost increases are stable, inflation pressure in Hong Kong is expected to remain moderate in 2018, but the headline inflation rate may gradually rise from the eight-year low of 1.7% in 2017. For example, due to the pass-through effect of the growth in newly signed private residential rents, inflationary pressure may increase in the second half of 2018. Market consensus predicts a moderate overall inflation rate of 2.2% in 2018, while the government's forecast for the headline inflation rate is 2.5%. Although the inflation outlook is moderate, upside risks still exist. Regarding external factors, if global inflation or commodity prices record an unexpectedly high increase, it could potentially increase local inflationary momentum. Regarding local factors, the labor market has tightened further recently; the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate fell from 3.4% in 2016 to 2.9% in December 2017, the first time it has fallen below 3% in nearly 20 years (Figure 3.6). The current output gap is estimated to be close to zero; if the labor market tightens significantly, it could pose additional upside pressure on inflation. Figure 3.6 shows the unemployment rate. Following the 2008 global financial crisis, interest rates remained low, and mortgage debt for Hong Kong households increased. As the normalization of US interest rates progresses, HKD interest rates will eventually rise in tandem with US interest rates. Consequently, the mortgage repayment burden for households will increase accordingly in the future, thereby dragging down household consumption. Therefore, this thematic study examines the impact of the increased mortgage repayment burden on private consumption in Hong Kong. The mortgage repayment burden refers to the proportion of mortgage debt service payments (i.e., interest payments plus principal repayments) to household income. Figure B3.1 shows the role of the mortgage repayment burden in the process of interest rate shocks transmitting to private consumption. In addition to the substitution effect, income effect, wealth effect, and collateral effect induced by asset price changes mentioned in general economic theory, under the condition of a mortgage repayment burden, an interest rate shock will also affect private consumption by changing the mortgage interest payments, which in turn changes household disposable income. This impact will expand as the outstanding mortgage loan amount increases. Furthermore, the principal repayment amount will vary with changes in the outstanding mortgage loan amount, which will also affect private consumption by changing household disposable income. Figure B3.1: Determinants of Private Consumption To measure the impact of the mortgage repayment burden on private consumption, based on outstanding mortgage debt, we estimate the Outstanding Mortgage Debt to Service Ratio (OMDSR). Unlike the current mortgage repayment burden indicator, which only applies to new mortgage debt, OMDSR covers all outstanding mortgage debts of households, which are more closely related to total private consumption. We roughly refer to the method used by the Bank for International Settlements and use the standard formula for fixed installments to measure OMDSR: where $D_t$ is the outstanding residential mortgage loan amount in the banking sector, $Y_t$ is the total income of owner-occupied households (indexed by the median income of owner-occupied households multiplied by the number of owner-occupied households), and $r_t$ and $s_t$ are the average interest rate and term of the outstanding mortgage loans, respectively. To evaluate whether OMDSR can reliably measure the mortgage repayment burden of the entire household sector, it is appropriate to compare OMDSR with two commonly used repayment burden indicators. Figure B3.2 shows the OMDSR estimates from 1985 to 2017, as well as the median mortgage repayment and loan repayment to income ratios estimated by the Census and Statistics Department based on the five-yearly census. In the early 2000s, both ratios showed a downward trend, which is consistent with the trend of reduced overall household mortgage borrowing following the bursting of the property bubble in 1997 and the significant drop in mortgage rates during the same period. Despite the sharp rise in property prices after the global financial crisis, these two ratios remained stable due to the macroprudential measures taken by the HKMA on bank mortgage lending, which curbed overall household mortgage leverage. Additionally, the extension of the tenure for new mortgage loans also reduced the actual amount of mortgage repayments. Figure B3.2 OMDSR and Median Mortgage Repayment and Loan Repayment to Income Ratios  We also compare the OMDSR with the bank's repayment to income ratio, the latter of which is the actual repayment to income ratio of new mortgage applicants at banks. As shown in Figure B3.3, the OMDSR is lower than the bank's repayment to income ratio, partly because the OMDSR covers not only new mortgages but also existing mortgages. Since property prices were lower when existing mortgages were established, their repayments are correspondingly lower than those of new mortgages. Therefore, the indicator of outstanding mortgage repayment burden covering both existing and new mortgages (i.e., the OMDSR) will be lower than the repayment burden indicator for new mortgages (i.e., the bank's repayment to income ratio). Furthermore, the higher bank repayment to income ratio is also due to banks complying with the HKMA's prudential regulatory requirements to include non-mortgage loan repayments when calculating the repayment to income ratio. After the global financial crisis, both the OMDSR and the bank's repayment to income ratio remained stable, mainly because the HKMA implemented prudential supervision of mortgage lending and set a cap on the bank's repayment to income ratio, a measure that also helped to stabilize the OMDSR. Figure B3.3 OMDSR and Bank's New Mortgage Repayment to Income Ratio  Overall, the OMDSR is basically consistent with commonly used repayment burden indicators, but the OMDSR has stronger immediacy and can reflect the burden of the total outstanding mortgage debt, rather than just the burden of new mortgage debt. Therefore, we believe that the OMDSR can be used to assess the impact of mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption. To assess the impact of mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption in Hong Kong, we estimate an error-correction model following the methods of Lai and Lam (2002) and Kang (2016). In this model, the long-term relationship between real private consumption (measured by real average private consumption per household) and its determinants is presented as an error-correction term in the short-term equation. Based on existing theory and empirical evidence, we use real income (measured by the median household income, deflated by the Composite Consumer Price Index), real housing and financial wealth (measured by residential prices and the Hang Seng Index, respectively, deflated by the Composite Consumer Price Index), and the OMDSR as the long-term determinants of private consumption.

The HKD exchange rate weakened, and the local interbank market continued to operate in an orderly manner. In the second half of 2017, the total amount of loans continued to increase, but at a slower pace than in the first half. Looking ahead, as US monetary policy continues to normalize, HKD interest rates may face greater upward pressure. If global financial market sentiment changes sharply, fluctuations in capital flows may increase. In the second half of 2017, the HKD spot exchange rate against the USD fluctuated between 7.799 and 7.827 (Figure 4.1). The HKD spot exchange rate briefly strengthened and remained around the 7.80 level between September and November 2017. This was mainly due to rising funding demands from new share capital raising activities and the cautious attitude of banks toward liquidity management before the end of the month and year, leading to tighter liquidity conditions, which in turn slowed down arbitrage activities and increased the closing of short positions in HKD. As the tight HKD liquidity conditions eased and US commercial demand rose at the end of the year, the HKD spot exchange rate softened again in mid-December 2017. Entering 2018, despite increased volatility in global financial markets (especially the stock market), the HKD continued to operate in an orderly manner. During the reporting period, the HKD exchange rate against the USD weakened, but the exchange guarantee was not triggered (Figure 4.2). Figure 4.1 HKD Exchange Rate Figure 4.2 Capital Flow Indicators The nominal effective exchange rate index of the HKD fluctuated slightly in the second half of 2017, but has recently faced greater downward pressure as the USD weakened further (Figure 4.3). This is generally consistent with the trend of the USD against most major currencies. Since the inflation rate gap between Hong Kong and its trading partners is very small and has a limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index, the real effective exchange rate index of the HKD continued to track closely with the movements of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Figure 4.3 Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates Securities investments by non-residents recorded inflows in the second half of 2017. The latest balance of payments statistics show that stock securities investments by local and non-local residents recorded inflows in the third quarter, reflecting improving economic prospects in the region and optimistic market sentiment (Table 4.A). Debt securities investments by non-residents recorded inflows in the third quarter of 2017, offsetting the outflows of debt investments by local residents. A survey conducted on global mutual funds also showed that both stock and debt investments recorded inflows in the fourth quarter of 2017, as the market maintained an optimistic view of economic prospects and corporate earnings. In recent weeks, the survey data showed that despite adjustments in global financial markets, stock investments still recorded inflows, while bond investments recorded slight outflows (Figure 4.4). Figure 4.4 Market Survey on Stock and Bond Related Capital Flows Looking ahead, as the normalization process of US monetary policy continues, the negative interest rate differential between the HKD and the USD will widen, which may lead to increased arbitrage activities. Therefore, the possibility of the HKD weak-side exchange guarantee being triggered should not be ruled out. This is a normal process under the Linked Exchange Rate System. At the same time, given that the pace of US monetary policy normalization remains unclear and global macro-financial conditions and market sentiment are volatile, fluctuations in HKD capital flows and the HKD exchange rate may increase. The HKMA will continue to do its utmost to ensure the stability of the HKD exchange rate in accordance with the currency board mechanism. Despite the Fed's interest rate hikes and continued balance sheet reduction, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained loose in the second half of 2017 and recently. In the second half of 2017, the HKD monetary base rose further by 1.4%, mainly due to the growth of liabilities issued for the issuance of banknotes (Figure 4.5). Since the exchange guarantee was not triggered, the total amount of closing balances and outstanding Exchange Fund notes and bonds remained basically unchanged in the second half of the year, maintaining at approximately HK$1,226.8 billion. Among these, the closing balances decreased slightly, while the outstanding Exchange Fund notes and bonds increased correspondingly. This was due to the issuance of additional foreign exchange fund notes (totaling HK$80 billion) to meet the banks' substantial liquidity management needs. Entering 2018, despite market adjustments in the stock market, the monetary base remained stable. Figure 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base At the same time, the Hong Kong dollar money supply further increased in the second half of 2017, but at a slower pace. The growth of the broad money supply of Hong Kong dollars (HKD M3) slowed from 8.9% in the first half of the year to 2.5% in the second half. As a major component of HKD M3, HKD deposits rose slightly by 2.2% in the second half (Figure 4.7). Among these, demand deposits grew faster in the second half, partly due to a thriving asset market and rising investment demand. Corresponding asset analysis shows that the growth of HKD M3 was supported on one hand by the strong growth of HKD loans (Figure 4.6), and on the other hand, was dragged down by the net outflow of HKD funds from the non-bank private sector and the contraction of banks' net foreign currency assets. Figure 4.6 HKD M3 and Corresponding Asset Changes On the other hand, the growth of foreign currency deposits was mixed. Reflecting the depreciation of the US dollar against most major currencies, the growth rate of US dollar deposits fell from 3.0% in the first half of the year to 2.4% in the second half (Figure 4.7). In contrast, other foreign currency deposits, which had been falling for over two years, rebounded significantly in the second half, with an increase of 8.4%. This was mainly driven by the recent recovery in RMB deposits. Due to the slowing growth of HKD and US dollar deposits, the total deposits of authorized institutions increased slightly by 3.0% in the second half, compared to a growth rate of 5.6% in the first half. For the full year of 2017, total deposits grew moderately by 8.7%, which was roughly similar to 2016. Figure 4.7 Deposit Growth During the period from September to December 2017, funding demand for new share capital raising activities rose, while banks maintained a cautious attitude toward liquidity management toward the end of the month and year, which put upward pressure on the HKD interbank interest rate (Figure 4.8). Compared with six months earlier, the overnight and 3-month Hong Kong dollar interbank rates rose by 14 and 50 basis points respectively, reaching 0.25% and 1.26% in December (calculated as monthly averages). The negative interest rate spread between the 1-month to 3-month HKD and USD interbank rates also narrowed accordingly. Figure 4.8 HKD and USD Interbank Rates At the same time, the HKD yield curve shifted upward but flattened, following a trend similar to the USD yield curve. In the second half of the year, the yield on 3-year Hong Kong government bonds rose by 63 basis points to 1.52% at the end of 2017, while the yield on 10-year Hong Kong government bonds rose by a smaller amount of 33 basis points to 1.83% at the end of 2017 (Figure 4.9). Figure 4.9 Government Bond Yields, Composite Interest Rates, and Average New Mortgage Lending Rates Entering 2018, the HKD interbank market continued to operate orderly. As funding demand eased toward the end of the year, the HKD interbank rate fell in early January. Thereafter, despite adjustments in global and local stock markets, the HKD interbank rate remained largely stable. The overnight and 3-month Hong Kong dollar interbank rates stood at 0.43% and 1.08% respectively at the end of February 2018. At the retail level, although banks' lending rates rose somewhat with the spike in the Hong Kong dollar interbank rate, banks' financing costs generally remained low due to the still-large deposit base. Despite fierce competition in the mortgage lending business, the average lending rate for new mortgages by banks rose gradually by 36 basis points to 2.16% in December (Figure 4.9), roughly following the upward trend of the 1-month Hong Kong dollar interbank rate. On the other hand, although the composite interest rate measuring the HKD financing costs of retail banks rose briefly in October due to increased funding demand from new share capital raising activities, it remained relatively soft for most of the second half of the year, closing at 0.38% at the end of December. Looking ahead, as US monetary policy continues to normalize, coupled with the possibility that other major economies may initiate interest rate normalization, HKD interest rates may face greater upward pressure. At the same time, fluctuations in global market sentiment and rapidly changing macro-financial conditions may increase volatility in capital flows. However, the massive HKD monetary base can serve as a buffer, helping to mitigate excessively rapid rises in HKD interest rates. Additionally, banks' prudent liquidity management and the ability to discount via the discount window also help to suppress excessive fluctuations in interbank lending rates.  Bank lending grew strongly throughout 2017. The loan growth rate reached as high as 10.2% in the first half of the year and slowed to 5.3% in the second half (Figure 4.10). In the second half of 2017, the growth of loans used in Hong Kong and loans used outside Hong Kong both slowed down. By currency analysis, due to the favorable local economic environment and relatively lower HKD financing costs, HKD loans continued to grow rapidly by 9.5% in the second half, while foreign currency loans rose only slightly by 0.1%. Among them, the growth of USD loans slowed to 1.8%, partly due to rising USD financing costs. For the full year of 2017, the total amount of loans recorded a robust growth of 16.1%, compared to 6.5% in 2016.  Figure 4.10 Loan Growth: The growth of loans used in Hong Kong (including trade finance) fell from 9.4% in the first half to 5.6% in the second half, with performance varying across major industries (Figure 4.11). The growth rate of loans in the construction and property development and investment sectors slowed in the second half, partly because the authorities required banks to strengthen risk management for loans to property developers starting from June 2017. Despite further improvements in commodity trade and retail sales, loans in trade finance and the transportation industry recorded only relatively slight increases, while loans in the wholesale and retail sectors recorded a decline. In contrast, loan growth for finance and finance-related enterprises remained strong, reflecting the steady expansion of the financial services industry to some extent.  Figure 4.11 Local Loan Growth by Individual Industry: Household debt grew by 6.5% in the second half of 2017, compared to an increase of 5.0% in the first half. Within household debt, the growth of private loans (including credit card advances and other private purpose loans) accelerated further, reaching an increase of 12.4% in the second half. The strong growth in private loans was mainly driven by borrowing from private banking and wealth management clients using financial assets as collateral. The growth of these loans is roughly consistent with the continuous growth of client assets managed by the banks. The risk of such collateralized loans is within a controllable range. Furthermore, the HKMA issued guidelines on private loan risk management to banks in January 2014, requiring banks to adopt prudent risk management measures, including setting caps on loan tenors and borrowers' debt-to-income ratios.  On the other hand, although residential transaction volumes increased, the loan-to-value ratios of newly approved mortgages fell, and the growth rate of residential mortgage loans slipped slightly to 3.8% in the second half. Overall, the ratio of household debt to local GDP rose from 68.2% in the second quarter of 2017 to 70.2% in the fourth quarter (Figure 4.12).

Mainly benefiting from growth in net interest income, the profitability of retail banks in the second half of 2017 improved compared with the same period in 2016. Capital and liquidity positions remained sound. After experiencing strong growth in the first half of 2017, credit growth slowed in the second half, while asset quality, by historical standards, remained solid. Despite a significant rise in Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates, the HKD funding costs of retail banks remained low because retail deposit rates stayed subdued. However, banks should be alert to the risks of increased interest rate volatility and possible capital outflows amid the normalisation of US monetary policy, as well as to geopolitical risks. As corporate leverage has continued to rise and the debt burden of individuals also remains high, banks should assess the impact that larger‑than‑expected interest rate increases could have on asset quality. To enhance banks’ resilience to systemic risks, Hong Kong’s countercyclical capital buffer ratio will be raised to 2.5% with effect from 1 January 2019.  In the second half of 2017, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks increased by 13.6% compared with the same period a year earlier. This was mainly supported by a sharp increase in net interest income and a reduction in loan impairment charges, which more than offset the decline in non-interest income. However, as asset growth outpaced profit growth, the return on assets (ROA) of retail banks edged down from 1.17% in the first half of 2017 to 1.15% in the second half. Nevertheless, the ROA in the second half of 2017 remained higher than the 1.11% recorded in the same period in 2016 (Chart 5.1). For 2017 as a whole, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 15.8%, while the ROA rose from 1.09% in 2016 to 1.16%.  Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks  The net interest margin (NIM) of retail banks further widened to 1.5% in the fourth quarter of 2017 from 1.34% in the same period in 2016 (Chart 5.2). Anecdotal evidence indicates that the improvement in NIM is consistent with the increase in the average interest spreads on Hong Kong dollar corporate loans in the Hong Kong syndicated loan market (Chart 5.3).  Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Chart 5.3 Average spreads on Hong Kong dollar syndicated loans  Since September 2017, Hong Kong interbank offered rates have risen across the board, mainly driven by liquidity needs related to initial public offerings and by banks’ year-end liquidity demand, as well as expectations of US interest rate hikes. Among them, the three‑month Hong Kong interbank offered rate rose to 1.31% at end-December 2017, the highest level since the global financial crisis, up 53 basis points from the end of June, though still low by historical standards (blue line in Chart 5.4). Moving into 2018, as banks’ year-end liquidity needs eased, Hong Kong interbank offered rates appeared to have stabilised.  Although Hong Kong interbank offered rates have risen recently, the HKD funding costs of retail banks have remained stable. This is mainly because retail deposit rates stayed at low levels during the review period. In this situation, the composite interest rate, which reflects the average HKD funding cost of retail banks, remained at around 0.3% for most of the second half of 2017, and only rose slightly to 0.38% by end-December (green line in Chart 5.4).  A similar pattern was also observed in the overall HKD and USD funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong. In the second half of 2017, the average HKD and USD funding costs for banks’ non-deposit market funding rose by 35 basis points, while the average deposit funding cost rose slightly by 12 basis points. Overall, the average aggregate HKD and USD funding costs of licensed banks increased by 22 basis points (red line in Chart 5.5). Chart 5.4 Interest rates Chart 5.5 HKD and USD funding costs and tenors of licensed banks  The increase in Hong Kong interbank offered rates has outpaced the rise in the overall funding costs of the Hong Kong banking sector, which may help improve the interest margins on assets that are priced with reference to HIBOR. However, this improvement may be partly offset by intense competition in the mortgage market. In particular, market information indicates that some banks have reduced the spread between their mortgage rates and the benchmark rates, or have introduced fixed‑rate mortgage terms to attract new customers.  Given expectations of further US interest rate hikes this year, banks may soon face greater upward pressure on funding costs. In light of the keen competition in the loan market, if the higher funding costs cannot be fully passed on to customers, this could put pressure on banks’ net interest margins.  The consolidated capital adequacy ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained well above the international minimum standards, indicating that the capital position of the Hong Kong banking sector remains strong. At end-December 2017, the total capital ratio increased to 19.1% from 18.7% at end-June (Chart 5.6), and the Tier 1 capital ratio54 also rose to 16.6%, of which 15.4% was common equity Tier 1 capital.55  Chart 5.6 Capital adequacy of locally incorporated authorized institutions  The HKMA recently issued a consultation paper to consult on rules to be made under the Financial Institutions (Resolution) Ordinance regarding loss‑absorbing capacity requirements applicable to authorized institutions. While enhancing the loss‑absorbing capacity of authorized institutions helps reduce the likelihood of financial crises and thus benefits society, it will inevitably entail costs. Box 5 provides a cost‑benefit assessment of the potential impact of the loss‑absorbing capacity requirements on Hong Kong. Our assessment indicates that implementing these requirements will generate net benefits for the Hong Kong economy.  Measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) under Basel III, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound during the review period. The average LCR of Category 1 institutions rose from 144.2% in the second quarter of 2017 to 155.1% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 80% applicable in 2017. Although the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of Category 2 institutions edged down slightly from 49.7% in the second quarter of 2017 to 49.4% in the fourth quarter, it still remained well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. The ample liquidity of authorized institutions indicates that the Hong Kong banking sector is capable of withstanding liquidity shocks arising from possible capital outflows from Hong Kong.  Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio  The Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR), one of the Basel III liquidity standards, was implemented in Hong Kong on 1 January 2018. This requirement aims to reduce banks’ medium- to long-term funding risks by requiring them to maintain a sufficient amount of stable funding to support their business activities. Specifically, Category 1 institutions must maintain an NSFR of not less than 100% at all times.57  Customer deposits continue to be the primary funding source for authorized institutions, reflecting a stable funding structure in the banking system. At end-December 2017, the share of customer deposits in the total liabilities of all authorized institutions remained broadly unchanged from six months earlier, staying at 56.2% (Chart 5.8).  Chart 5.8 Liability structure of all authorized institutions  The HKD loan‑to‑deposit ratio of all authorized institutions rose from 77.1% at end-June 2017 to 82.7% at end-December (Chart 5.9), reflecting that HKD loans and advances grew faster than deposits during the review period. Meanwhile, as foreign currency deposits grew faster than loans, the foreign currency loan‑to‑deposit ratio fell from 65.5% at end-June 2017 to 63.1% at end-December. Overall, the loan‑to‑deposit ratio for all currencies combined rose from 71.4% six months earlier to 73.0%. Banks should assess the impact of the rising loan‑to‑deposit ratio on their liquidity management.  Chart 5.9 Average loan‑to‑deposit ratios of all authorized institutions  The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained low. We estimate that, under a shock scenario of a parallel 200‑basis‑point increase in interest rates, the potential decline in the economic value of the interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks would be equivalent to 3.45% of their total capital base at end-December 2017 (Chart 5.10). Nevertheless, in view of expectations that the Federal Reserve will continue to raise interest rates and proceed with balance sheet normalisation, banks should assess the implications of this for their interest rate risk management.  Chart 5.10 Impact of interest rate shocks on locally incorporated licensed banks  In the second half of 2017, in a moderate but still favourable economic environment, the growth rate of total loans and advances of all authorized institutions slowed to 5.3%, from the strong 10.2% recorded in the first half. After two years of slower growth, total loans for the whole of 2017 grew at a solid pace of 16.1%.  The asset quality of banks’ loan portfolios remained sound and continued to improve in the second half of 2017. At end-December 2017, the total classified loan ratio and the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio of all authorized institutions fell to 0.67% and 0.52% respectively, from 0.84% and 0.61% at end-June. For retail banks, the total classified loan ratio and the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio also declined, to 0.54% and 0.4% respectively (Chart 5.11). However, given the rapid growth in loans for use outside Hong Kong in recent years, banks’ asset quality may have become more sensitive to external conditions, and therefore banks should closely monitor their credit risk. According to the HKMA’s Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook in December 2017, 29% of the surveyed authorized institutions expected loan demand to increase over the next three months, while the remaining 71% expected loan demand to remain unchanged (Table 5.A).  During the review period, the credit risk associated with personal lending remained low. Banks’ mortgage loan portfolios stayed healthy, with the delinquency ratio remaining at a low level of 0.03% at end-December 2017. The average loan‑to‑value ratio of newly approved mortgages fell further from 50.1% in the second quarter of 2017 to 48.8% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.12).
