This was mainly due to the slowing growth of private loans (including credit card advances and other private purpose loans), which offset the rapid growth of residential mortgage loans (Table 5. B). Since the growth rate of Hong Kong's nominal Gross Domestic Product (GDP) was slower than that of personal loans, the ratio of household debt to GDP rose slightly from 71.2% in the second quarter of 2018 to 71.9% in the fourth quarter (Figure 5.14).

Since the outbreak of the coronavirus pandemic at the beginning of 2020, both demand and supply have been adversely affected, posing challenges to the global economy unlike those seen in previous crises. Although major central banks and several governments have introduced stimulus measures since early March to mitigate the economic impact of the pandemic, financial markets remain volatile and global financial conditions have tightened. Despite uncertainties in both external and domestic environments, Hong Kong’s foreign exchange and money markets continued to function smoothly and orderly. With a relatively strong Hong Kong dollar, stable total reserves, and modest growth in total deposits, no significant outflows of funds from the Hong Kong dollar or the local banking system were observed during the review period. After a mild rebound in the first half of 2019, the growth rate of total loans slowed down in the second half. The residential property market has generally softened since mid-2019, though its trend has been somewhat erratic. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face multiple downside risks, including uncertainties stemming from the spread of the coronavirus, future Sino-US trade relations, geopolitical tensions, and local social events. Given the ongoing rise in corporate leverage and household debt levels, banks should prudently assess how the asset quality of their loan portfolios might be affected under these potentially heightened risks. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, global economic growth has shown initial signs of stabilization, aided by intensified monetary easing by major central banks, easing Sino-US trade tensions, and a reduced risk of a “no-deal” Brexit. However, since late January, the rising number of global coronavirus infections has raised market concerns and triggered substantial volatility in global financial markets. To address evolving pandemic risks, several major central banks have slashed interest rates and expanded liquidity facilities, while some governments have introduced targeted measures to support the real economy. Nevertheless, credit spreads have widened and equity markets have declined sharply, resulting in tighter global financial conditions. Looking forward, downside risks to the global economic outlook have increased. The coronavirus pandemic is expected to dampen global economic activity, with the extent of its impact depending on the severity and duration of the outbreak. In the medium term, relations between the United States and its major trading partners may tighten once again, while trade negotiations between the UK and the EU following Brexit are likely to prove difficult. Weak global demand continues to weigh on economic growth in East Asia.1 Exports from the region to major destinations such as the United States, European economies, and mainland China remained sluggish in the second half of 2019. Although several major telecommunications equipment exporters in the region recently reported revenue growth, it remains to be seen whether the technology sector cycle will experience a broad-based rebound. Financial markets responded positively to the Phase One Sino-US trade agreement announced in December 2019; the trade truce has somewhat alleviated uncertainties surrounding global trade. That said, East Asia will continue to grapple with weak corporate earnings and high private sector leverage. Meanwhile, the coronavirus outbreak has raised concerns that the region’s economies may face further pressure amid persistently sluggish growth. Travel bans imposed by various economies in the region could adversely affect Asia’s tourism sector, particularly in economies heavily reliant on tourism-related exports. Given the region’s close integration with mainland China’s supply chains, the manufacturing sector may also be impacted by the outbreak. In mainland China, economic growth continued to decelerate in the second half of 2019 due to weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, although the signing of the Phase One trade agreement between China and the US has helped reduce external uncertainties for the Chinese economy in the short term, downward pressures remain amid the coronavirus outbreak, ongoing economic rebalancing, and global economic slowdown. The Central Economic Work Conference held in December 2019 identified economic stability as a key priority for 2020, while also emphasizing the need to control financial risks. The latest consensus forecasts indicate that mainland China’s economic growth will slow to 5.2% in 2020. During the review period, mainland authorities continued to introduce targeted monetary and fiscal policies aimed at supporting the private sector, particularly small private enterprises. Topic 2 examines the factors driving changes in the equity of mainland industrial enterprises by analyzing data from listed companies in 2018; it finds that private or small enterprises are not inherently more prone to downsizing or “regression.” While negative profitability emerged as the primary factor, other elements—especially structural factors—also warrant attention (see Topic 2 for details). Hong Kong’s economic activity contracted significantly in the second half of 2019. Real GDP declined for three consecutive quarters, signaling that the economy had entered a recession. As a result, the economy shrank by 1.2% for the whole of 2019, a marked deterioration from the 2.9% growth recorded in 2018 and the first annual contraction since 2009. The slowdown in domestic demand, particularly a decline in private consumption, was the main factor behind the GDP drop in the latter half of 2019. Local social unrest severely affected consumer activity, dampening economic prospects and eroding both consumer and business confidence. With escalating Sino-US trade tensions, slowing global economic growth, and a sharp downturn in inbound tourism, Hong Kong’s external trade performance remained weak. Given these significant headwinds, the government rolled out multiple rounds of economic stimulus measures between August and December 2019. To give banks greater room to bolster support for the local economy and help smooth out economic fluctuations, the HKMA announced on October 14 that it would lower the countercyclical capital buffer ratio from 2.5% to 2.0%. This move enabled banks to release an additional HK$2,000–3,000 billion in lending capacity for businesses, especially small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). The economic outlook for 2020 is expected to be highly challenging, and the recent outbreak of the pandemic has introduced notable downside risks. Given that sectors such as retail, hospitality, food services, tourism, and transportation have yet to recover from the damage caused by social unrest, the pandemic will deal these industries a double blow. Nevertheless, a series of countercyclical measures outlined in the 2020/21 Budget are designed to provide relief to households and businesses, particularly SMEs; these include a one-off cash payment to adult permanent residents and 100% government-guaranteed low-interest loans for enterprises under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme. 2 On March 16, 2020, the HKMA further reduced the countercyclical capital buffer ratio from 2.0% to 1.0%, thereby granting banks even more capacity to support the local economy, especially sectors and individuals facing heightened pressure in the short term due to the pandemic. Looking at the components of GDP, private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak amid fragile consumer and business confidence. Although government spending will help sustain economic growth, public investment is expected to be relatively subdued as several major infrastructure projects reach completion. On the external front, the Phase One trade agreement between China and the US is anticipated to have a modestly positive impact on Hong Kong’s economy in the short term. 3 However, sluggish global economic growth and trade activity will continue to weigh on Hong Kong’s external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak may disrupt regional supply chains and slow cross-border economic activities such as tourism, thereby constraining Hong Kong’s export performance. The Government forecasts that real GDP growth in 2020 will range between -1.5% and 0.5%, while the average growth forecast among international institutions and private-sector analysts stands at -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is influenced by numerous uncertainties and risks, including the slowdown in global economic growth, Sino-US trade relations, economic performance on the Chinese mainland, and local social events. The labor market faced greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020: total employment declined, the unemployment rate rose, and the real wage index also fell year-on-year. Specifically, the unemployment rate climbed from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.7% in February 2020, partly reflecting the impact of social unrest and the outbreak of the pandemic on the retail, accommodation, and food services sectors. Looking ahead, given the weak economic outlook and the coronavirus outbreak, the unemployment rate is expected to rise further. Topic 3 will examine in greater detail recent developments and short-term prospects for the labor market. Local inflationary pressures continued to build up in the third quarter of 2019, primarily driven by rising fresh pork prices; subsequently, as economic activity weakened, inflation momentum gradually slowed. Given the weak economic conditions, stabilization of private residential rents, and moderate import inflation, inflation is expected to ease in the near term. Consensus forecasts place overall inflation in 2020 between 0.6% and 3.7%, while the Government projects a core inflation rate of 2.5%. Supported by increased demand for Hong Kong dollars linked to equities—including initial public offerings—the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has gradually strengthened since mid-October 2019. In December, this upward trend intensified, partly due to robust IPO activity and partly because tighter liquidity toward year-end prompted the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions. After the Lunar New Year holiday, liquidity conditions eased, and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate edged lower toward the end of February. Overall, during the review period, Hong Kong dollar trading remained smooth and orderly, without triggering any exchange rate guarantees. Total reserves stayed stable at around HK$540 billion. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, short-term Hong Kong interbank rates have fluctuated, reflecting seasonal liquidity demands as well as heightened capital market activity such as IPOs. Topic 4 explores how market expectations regarding future IPO activity influence the 3-month Hong Kong interbank rate. Meanwhile, the composite interest rate gradually rose from 0.94% at the end of July 2019 to 1.01% by end-January 2020, reflecting banks’ continued efforts to raise preferential deposit rates to attract funds. As some banks raised the ceiling rates tied to the prime lending rate, the average interest rate on newly issued mortgages climbed to around 2.6% in October; however, following a cut in the prime lending rate starting in November, this average rate edged down to roughly 2.5% by January 2020. With a stronger Hong Kong dollar, stable total reserves, and modest growth in total deposits, no significant outflows of funds from the Hong Kong dollar or the banking system were observed during the review period. Nevertheless, we must monitor the potential impact of any further deterioration in the coronavirus situation amid an uncertain external environment. Hong Kong boasts substantial foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system; the HKMA possesses the capability, resources, and resolve to manage capital outflows and maintain monetary and financial stability. During the review period, market expectations of a Sino-US trade deal led to a strengthening of both offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates; however, since late January 2020, these rates have come under downward pressure due to the coronavirus outbreak. Later in 2019, the offshore RMB traded at a premium relative to the onshore RMB. At the end of January 2020, the discount widened briefly, yet the price differential remained modest by historical standards. Hong Kong’s offshore RMB pool recovered slightly after a slight decline in the previous review period. As of end-January 2020, the balance of RMB customer deposits and certificates of deposit rose to RMB6374 billion. Other RMB-related activities in Hong Kong also saw growth, with robust increases recorded in RMB bank lending and RMB trade settlement. Throughout 2019, the average daily transaction volume on the Cross-Border Interbank Payment System remained high at RMB1,133.9 billion. Despite uncertainties in the external environment, Hong Kong’s offshore RMB business is expected to benefit from the continued liberalization of China’s capital account, greater allocation of RMB assets by international investors, and deeper regional economic and financial cooperation under the Belt and Road Initiative and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiative.

At the end of 2019, global economic activity showed signs of stabilization, raising hopes for a global economic recovery. However, since late January 2020, the continuous increase in global coronavirus infection cases has dashed these recovery hopes. Investors' concerns about a global economic recession have deepened, triggering a sell-off in global financial markets. To cope with the economic shock, major central banks and some governments have launched stimulus measures since early March. Given the spread of the epidemic, the downside risks to the global economic growth outlook have increased. In East Asia, weak global demand in the second half of 2019 cast a shadow over the prospects of the region's economies. The coronavirus outbreak is expected to drag down the region's economic growth in the short term, with the tourism industry being hit particularly hard. On the other hand, the East Asian region also continues to face challenges of weak corporate earnings and high private sector leverage ratios. As for Mainland China, economic growth continued to slow in the second half of 2019 due to weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, although the signing of the Phase One trade agreement between China and the US has helped to temporarily reduce external uncertainties, downward pressures remain in the face of the coronavirus outbreak, ongoing economic rebalancing, and a global economic slowdown. The monetary and fiscal policies adopted by the authorities will provide some buffer. Under the influence of persistent trade tensions and policy uncertainty, manufacturing and investment remained weak, and global economic growth was still sluggish in the second half of 2019. However, economic growth showed preliminary signs of stabilization in the last quarter (Chart 2.1), partly benefiting from the earlier easing policies of the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank, as well as the easing of global trade tensions after the signing of the "Phase One" trade agreement between China and the US. Chart 2.1 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index However, since the end of January, the continuous increase in global coronavirus infection cases and the subsequent economic impact have caused market concerns, leading to a sell-off in global financial markets (Chart 2.2). Given that Mainland China is a major global export destination and occupies an important position in the global supply chain, disruptions to its production activities and a drag on its economic growth due to the epidemic will have significant spillover effects, potentially affecting the entire world (Chart 2.3). Since late February, the surge in coronavirus cases outside Mainland China may exacerbate supply chain disruptions and pose a direct risk of dragging down local economic activities. 5 Chart 2.2 MSCI All Country World Index and Bloomberg Barclays Global Corporate Bond Index Option-Adjusted Spread Chart 2.3 Exports of Goods and Services to Mainland China by Selected Major Advanced Economies in 2018 (as a percentage of their GDP) In response to the potentially severe economic impact of the epidemic, some central banks (including the US Federal Reserve, the Bank of Canada, and the Bank of England) have cut interest rates since early March, and some governments have also launched targeted measures to support households and businesses. However, financial markets still face huge selling pressure, leading to a significant tightening of global financial conditions, which in turn may exacerbate the downward pressure on the global economy (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 Bloomberg Advanced Economies Financial Conditions Index In addition to the development of the epidemic, other downside risks and uncertainties also cloud the global economic outlook. In particular, regarding trade tensions, although policy risks have decreased after China and the US reached the Phase One trade agreement, subsequent negotiations may be difficult as many thorny structural issues remain to be resolved. In Europe, trade negotiations between the EU and the UK are not expected to be smooth, thus sustaining the post-Brexit uncertainties. In addition, the sharp drop in oil prices since March will put pressure on major oil-exporting emerging economies. In East Asia, due to sluggish global demand, real economic activity remained weak in the second half of 2019. Exports from the East Asian region to various major destinations such as the United States, European economies, and Mainland China remained weak in the second half of 2019 (Chart 2.5). Although there are preliminary signs that the downward cycle of technology products in the region is bottoming out, including a major regional electronics company reporting improved earnings at the end of 2019,6 it remains to be seen whether there will be a substantial rebound in the region's technology product exports. Chart 2.5 East Asia: Goods Exports to Major Destinations Continued weak economic growth and trade uncertainties also troubled investor sentiment, with gross fixed capital investment falling in most East Asian economies in 2019 (Chart 2.6), which could affect the region's potential economic growth in the long run. To support economic growth in an environment of moderate inflation, the central banks of Indonesia, the Philippines, and South Korea lowered their policy rates again in the second half of 2019 after cutting them in the first half, while the Bank of Thailand also lowered its policy rate for the first time since 2015. Chart 2.6 East Asia: Gross Fixed Capital Formation The outbreak of the coronavirus has led to concerns that the region's economies may face further pressure amid continued weak growth. As many economies in the region have imposed entry and exit restrictions on Mainland China, the tourism industry is bearing the brunt, especially those economies that are more dependent on tourists and tourism service exports from Mainland China, which are more affected by this epidemic (Chart 2.7). The continuation and intensification of the epidemic will also affect the supply chains in the region that are closely related to Mainland China. Chart 2.7 East Asia: Tourism Exports and Chinese Tourists In the short term, this epidemic will continue to affect economic activity and investor sentiment. Referring to the experience of the 2003 SARS outbreak, these effects may be short-lived, but the actual situation will depend on the severity and spread of the epidemic, as well as the effectiveness of government actions to contain the outbreak. At the same time, East Asian economies also face multiple headwinds. First, although market expectations are for corporate earnings to deteriorate in the short term (Chart 2.8), the globally accommodative monetary conditions have encouraged yield-chasing activities, thereby pushing up asset prices without fundamental support. Therefore, the region's stock markets are more susceptible to shifts in investor sentiment. Chart 2.8 Expected Earnings of Benchmark Stock Index Constituents Second, weak corporate earnings and economic growth may make it more difficult for private institutions in the region to repay their debts. Although lower local interest rates can provide breathing space for indebted companies and households, they may also sow the seeds for further debt accumulation. In addition, as mentioned in Special Topic 1, when more index-tracking funds flow into the region's financial markets, the risk of debt accumulation in the private sector may also increase, although this impact may be limited to financially sound enterprises and their long-term borrowings. Third, in terms of external factors, East Asian economies may also face increased risks in the face of increasingly protectionist US trade policies. Despite recent progress in the China-US Phase One trade agreement, trade tensions between the two countries persist as fundamental trade issues remain. As seen from the increasing trade surpluses of many economies in the region with the United States (Chart 2.9), multinational corporations may continue to seek more supply channels outside the China-centric supply chain to circumvent tariffs. As of November 2019, the cumulative trade surplus of nine emerging Asian economies (excluding China) with the United States had increased to about US$1670 billion. If the trade surplus with the United States continues to expand, the relevant Asian economies may become the next target of the trade war; for example, the US government imposed huge tariffs of up to 456% on steel imports from Vietnam in July 2019. 7 In view of this, despite the China-US trade truce, the region's trade outlook remains highly uncertain. Chart 2.9 Goods Trade Surplus with the United States Over the past decade, the increasing integration of international financial markets has led to a significant increase in global cross-border portfolio investment flows. A recent study shows that as much as seventy per cent of these cross-border investment flows are driven by index-tracking funds. 8 Index-driven funds include not only funds that closely track investment indices (often called passive funds), but also actively managed funds that reference investment indices. 9 By introducing overseas investors that the relevant economies would not have been able to attract or reach otherwise, these funds help promote the development of financial markets in emerging market economies. Consequently, such funds enable emerging market economies to diversify their investor base, which contributes to the long-term growth and stability of the market. However, is there really such a thing as a free lunch? In the case of passive bond funds, there are concerns that such fund investments may weaken the financial discipline of the corporate bond issuers they invest in, thereby leading to high leverage levels in the relevant companies. 10 In addition, some argue that the growth of index-driven funds in recent years has exacerbated the volatility of global portfolio investment flows, making emerging market economies, which are already very sensitive to global factors and affected by other common factors, even more vulnerable. 11 This special topic assesses the impact of index-driven investment on financial stability based on these two propositions. Passive bond funds allocate their investment funds to the relevant bonds according to the weight of the constituent bonds in the benchmark index. Therefore, compared to actively managed bond funds, the mechanical investment decisions adopted by passive bond funds may reduce the incentive for issuers of index constituent bonds to act in the interests of the fund's investors. 13 Worse, from a financial stability perspective, this behavior may encourage excessive borrowing, posing significant credit and solvency risks to the corporate sectors of emerging market economies, where leverage ratios have risen sharply since the global financial crisis (Chart B1.1). Chart B1.1 Corporate Leverage in Emerging Market Economies Using the weight of companies from various emerging market economies in a mainstream index that tracks emerging market economy corporate bonds as an estimate of their bonds' investment by passive bond funds,14 we find that an increase in such investments will push up the long-term (but not short-term) leverage ratios of the corporate issuers of the relevant bonds. The solid blue bars in Chart B1.2 represent the estimated impact. In addition to promoting the development of the corporate bond market in emerging market economies, the expanded long-term bond investor base due to passive bond funds is also beneficial to the development of companies in emerging market economies. We also find that the above-mentioned effect is only significant for companies in emerging market economies with stronger fundamentals (especially stronger solvency and lower leverage ratios) (solid green bars in Chart B1.2). Faced with higher financial distress costs, highly leveraged or less solvent companies do not seem to be further pushed into a debt trap by the investment of passive bond funds. In summary, the above research shows that the growth of passive bond fund investment may not significantly increase the solvency risk of the corporate sector in emerging market economies.

Due to weakened private consumption, reduced investment expenditure, and poor export performance, Hong Kong's economy contracted in the second half of 2019 and entered its first recession since 2009. Economic performance in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, and the coronavirus pandemic has also recently introduced substantial downside risks. The economic outlook is affected by numerous uncertain factors and risks, such as the slowdown in global economic growth, China-US trade relations, economic performance in mainland China, and the development of local social events. Given the various headwinds facing the economy, the unemployment rate may climb further in 2020. Local inflationary pressures are expected to ease somewhat, though the outlook faces potential risks on both the upside and downside. Hong Kong's economy contracted significantly in the second half of 2019. On a year-on-year basis, real local Gross Domestic Product (GDP) contracted by 2.8% and 2.9% in the 3rd and 4th quarters respectively (Table 3.A). Dragged down by the economic contraction in the second half of the year, the economy contracted by 1.2% for the full year, a sharp contrast to the 2.9% growth in 2018, and marking the first annual contraction since the global financial crisis in 2009. Figure 3.1 shows the quarterly comparison of the real local GDP growth rate and the contributions of major expenditure items; economic activity slowed significantly in the second half of the year (Figure 3.1). Specifically, real local GDP fell by 0.4%, 3.0%, and 0.3% in the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th quarters respectively, indicating that the economy had entered a recession. Locally, private consumption was the main factor dragging down local GDP in the 3rd quarter. Local social events severely affected consumption activities, which in turn weakened the economic outlook and hit consumer confidence; therefore, private consumption contracted significantly starting from the third quarter. 33 Due to increasing economic uncertainties and a deteriorating business atmosphere, total investment expenditure remained weak and dragged down local GDP in the fourth quarter. 34 Externally, as China-US trade frictions intensified, global economic growth weakened, and the number of visitors to Hong Kong plummeted, Hong Kong's foreign trade performance continued to remain sluggish (Figure 3.2). 35 Under the impact of a sharp contraction in services exports, net exports dragged down local GDP in the third quarter but provided support for local GDP growth in the fourth quarter, partially reflecting an improvement in the goods trade balance. Figure 3.2 Real imports and exports Given that the economy is facing huge headwinds, the government launched multiple rounds of measures between August and December 2019 to alleviate the financial burden on citizens, protect employment, and support businesses, particularly supporting small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and industries severely impacted, such as retail, catering services, transport, and tourism. 36 To provide banks with more room to increase support for the local economy and help mitigate economic cycles, the HKMA announced on October 14 that it would lower the countercyclical buffer capital ratio for banks from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby allowing banks to release an additional lending capacity of HK$2,000 billion to HK$3,000 billion to enterprises, including SMEs. Economic performance in Hong Kong in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, and the pandemic has also recently brought significant downside risks. As some industries have yet to recover after experiencing destruction caused by social events, the pandemic will bring a double blow to these industries. However, a series of countercyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 fiscal budget can provide assistance to households and businesses (especially SMEs), including a one-off cash payment to adult permanent residents and providing preferential low-interest loans with 100% government guarantee for businesses under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme." 37 The HKMA further lowered the countercyclical buffer capital ratio for banks from 2.0% to 1.0% on March 16, 2020, which will allow banks more room to increase support for the local economy, especially for industries and individuals facing greater pressure in the short term due to the pandemic. Analyzing the components of the Gross Domestic Product (GDP), private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak due to fragile consumer and business confidence. Although government consumption will support economic growth, public investment expenditure is expected to be relatively sluggish as some major infrastructure projects are completed. Regarding external factors, the first phase of the US-China trade agreement is expected to have a slight positive impact on the local economy in the short term. 38 However, weak global economic growth and trade activity will continue to drag down Hong Kong's foreign trade performance. In particular, the outbreak of the coronavirus may lead to supply chain disruptions in the region and a slowdown in cross-border economic activities (e.g., the tourism industry), thereby limiting Hong Kong's export performance. The government forecasts real GDP growth for 2020 to be between -1.5% and 0.5%, while the average growth forecast from international organizations and private sector analysts is -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is influenced by numerous uncertainties and risks described in the preceding chapters. The labor market faced greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.3% in December 2019, and climbed further to 3.7% in February 2020 (Figure 3.3). Meanwhile, the unemployment rate in the retail, accommodation, and food and beverage services industries rose to a nearly ten-year high of 6.1%, partly reflecting the heavy impact caused by social events. 39 As economic momentum weakened, the total number of employed persons fell by 0.5% year-on-year in the second half of 2019 and continued to decline to 3,768,800 in February 2020. Among these, the decline in the number of employed persons mainly came from the trade, wholesale, retail, accommodation, food and beverage services, and construction industries. Real wages also fell by 0.3% year-on-year in the third quarter. Looking ahead, in response to the aforementioned weak economic outlook, the labor market will continue to face more challenges, and the unemployment rate is very likely to climb further. Topic 3 will explore the recent developments and short-term prospects of the labor market in more detail. Figure 3.3 Labor Market Conditions Local inflationary pressures continued to accumulate until the third quarter of 2019, mainly due to the impact of rising fresh pork prices; thereafter, as economic activity weakened, inflationary momentum also gradually slowed down. On a year-on-year basis, the Headline Composite Consumer Price Index (CCPI) grew by 3.3% in the third quarter, with the increase slowing slightly to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. The Headline Inflation Rate, which reflects inflationary momentum on a three-month annual basis, also softened from a high of 4.7% in August 2019 to 2.1% in January 2020. The slowdown in inflationary momentum was due to reduced price pressures on several items comprising the CCPI. Regarding traded goods, the rise in fresh pork prices caused headline food inflation to remain significant, but price pressures on consumer goods such as clothing and footwear, as well as durable goods, remained moderate. In terms of services, as the growth of rents for newly signed private residential leases slowed down earlier, the growth of the rent component of the CCPI also showed a downward trend (Figure 3.5). Labor cost pressures rose slightly but remained at a moderate level in recent quarters (Figure 3.6). Figure 3.4 Different Indicators Reflecting Consumer Price Inflation Figure 3.5 CCPI Rent Component and Market Rent Figure 3.6 Unit Labor Cost Local inflationary pressures are expected to ease in the short term. Locally, the weak economic conditions and the widening output gap will continue to exert downward pressure on local inflation. As private residential rents continue to slow down, the housing rent component of inflation should ease further. Externally, due to weak global economic growth and soft energy prices, imported inflation is expected to remain moderate. Market consensus predicts the overall inflation rate for 2020 will range between 0.6% and 3.7%, while the government forecasts a core inflation rate of 2.5% and an overall inflation rate of 1.7%. This inflation outlook is influenced by both upside and downside risk factors. On one hand, given that the estimated output gap has widened since the third quarter of 2019, if the economic deterioration is more severe than expected (for example, due to the continued coronavirus pandemic), it could further suppress inflation. On the other hand, if the situation regarding restricted fresh pork supply becomes more severe, it will exert upward pressure on inflation. Despite the significant slowdown in the local economy, the unemployment rate remained at a low level of 2.8-2.9% during the first 9 months of 2019. It was only as social events continued that the unemployment rate rose more noticeably to 3.3% by the end of 2019. Affected by the coronavirus pandemic, the labor market will face greater headwinds in 2020. Against this backdrop, this special report analyzes recent developments and short-term prospects of the labor market, including exploring why the overall labor market remained largely stable (with almost no change in the unemployment rate) during the first three quarters of 2019, and what implications this has for future developments. This article also examines some risk factors that could lead to a sharp rise in the unemployment rate. It is worth noting that unemployment is a lagging indicator because it requires costs to adjust labor demand. In fact, the unemployment rate often lags the year-on-year growth rate of real local GDP by about two to three quarters (Figure B3.1). This lagging nature can explain why the unemployment rate remained low at about 2.9% even when real economic activity deteriorated sharply in the third quarter. Figure B3.1 Real GDP Growth Rate and Unemployment Rate Regarding labor demand, although tensions in China-US trade and local social events dealt heavy blows to employment in trade, retail, and tourism-related industries respectively, some major industries were still able to support the overall labor market. Specifically, employment in finance, business, public administration, and social and personal services continued to grow in 2019, partially offsetting the impact of declining employment in the trade and retail sectors (Figure B3.2). Although the economy entered a recession, Hong Kong's financial system remained robust, and financial activities in fintech development and new share issuances were very active. These factors may have helped support the employment market in the financial and business services sectors. Additionally, the public administration, social, and personal services sectors—including education, healthcare, and social work activities—appear to be less sensitive to economic cycles. Correlation coefficient analysis shows that while employment in many industries is highly correlated with real local GDP, the response of public administration, social, and personal services to economic cycles is more neutral. In other words, even if the economy slows down, employment in these industries may not be significantly affected by cyclicality. Figure B3.2 Changes in Employment by Industry in 2019 Regarding labor supply, the labor force participation rate fell from 61.2% in 2018 to 60.5% in 2019, providing a buffer for the rising unemployment rate. Figure B3.3 shows various supply and demand factors affecting changes in the unemployment rate (blue line). As shown in the chart, the labor force participation rate (green bar) exerted downward pressure on the unemployment rate in 2019. 41 On the other hand, the increase in employment in the first half of 2019 (purple bar) also helped suppress the unemployment rate. However, as the economy contracted significantly in the second half of the year, the decrease in employment exerted upward pressure on the unemployment rate. Overall, although the number of employed persons decreased during the economic recession, the lower labor force participation rate helped alleviate the pressure on the rising unemployment rate in the second half of 2019. Some changes in the structure of the labor market, which contributed to changes in the unemployment rate, are also noteworthy as shown in Figure B3.3. In particular, the increasing proportion of voluntary part-time employees may help companies retain staff. In fact, the proportions of self-employed persons and underemployed persons in the total number of employed persons have fallen to 6% and 1% respectively in recent years, but the number of voluntary part-time employees has continued to rise, becoming the second largest group in the total employed population (approximately 7% in 2017). 42 Therefore, companies may be able to retain or hire more employees by adjusting the working hours of part-time employees. Our calculations show that the average weekly working hours have decreased, falling from a recent high of 48 hours in 2010 to about 44 hours currently, partly reflecting the fact that there are more part-time workers among the current employed population.

The HKD exchange rate has strengthened since October, with upward momentum further intensifying in December, keeping the HKD exchange rate on the stronger side of the Linked Exchange Rate System (LERS) range over the past few months. Strong demand for the HKD stems partly from stock-related demand and partly from the closing of short positions in the HKD due to tightening liquidity as the year-end approached. Overall, the operation of Hong Kong's foreign exchange and money markets continues to be smooth and orderly. Despite the uncertain external environment and the potential for the coronavirus pandemic to trigger market sentiment and lead to heightened fluctuations in capital flows, Hong Kong possesses substantial foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, and is therefore capable of withstanding pressure from capital outflows without affecting the city's financial stability. Supported by increased stock-related demand for the HKD (including initial public offerings), the HKD exchange rate has gradually strengthened since mid-October (Figure 4.1). Entering December, the upward momentum of the HKD further intensified, and from mid-December to February, the HKD exchange rate remained on the stronger side of the LERS range. The strengthening of the HKD exchange rate was partly due to the robust activity of initial public offerings and partly due to the closing of short positions in the HKD caused by tightening liquidity as the year-end approached. After the Lunar New Year holiday, the liquidity situation eased somewhat, and the HKD exchange rate softened slightly, closing at 7.7956 on February 28. Overall, during the review period, HKD trading continued to be smooth and orderly. As neither the stronger nor the weaker side of the LERS was triggered during the review period, the net reserve remained unchanged at approximately HK$540 billion (Figure 4.2). Figure 4.1 HKD Exchange Rate Figure 4.2 Net Reserve and FX Fund Notes and Bonds The nominal effective exchange rate index of the HKD roughly followed the movements of the US dollar and rose slightly during the review period (Figure 4.3). Since the inflation rate gap between Hong Kong and its trading partners is very small, the impact on the HKD real effective exchange rate index is limited, and the trend of the HKD real effective exchange rate index roughly follows that of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Figure 4.3 Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates When measuring capital flows in Hong Kong, it is necessary to distinguish between two distinct but interrelated concepts of capital flows: (1) HKD capital flows; and (2) cross-border capital flows. HKD capital flows focus on the currency dimension of capital flows, which helps assess currency stability, especially under the LERS. On the other hand, cross-border capital flows focus on the movement of funds between regions through the Hong Kong banking system, which helps assess the stability of Hong Kong's overall financial system. The two capital flow concepts require different monitoring indicators. When monitoring HKD capital flows, attention needs to be paid to the HKD exchange rate and the net reserve. If the public or investors convert a large amount of their HKD assets into foreign currency assets, the demand for the HKD will naturally decrease, leading to a weakening of the HKD exchange rate. Under the LERS, if the HKD exchange rate weakens to the weaker side of the LERS at HK$7.85 to US$1, the HKMA would be prepared to purchase HKD upon request by banks, and the net reserve would subsequently decrease. Since April 2019, the net reserve has remained largely unchanged, and the HKD exchange rate has been on the stronger side of the LERS range in recent months; therefore, no significant capital outflows from the HKD were observed during the review period. When monitoring cross-border capital flows, the total amount of bank deposits in Hong Kong is a useful indicator. When there is a large amount of capital outflow from the Hong Kong banking system, bank deposits will inevitably decrease. During the review period, the total amount of deposits grew at a moderate pace, indicating that no significant cross-border capital outflows occurred. The operation of Hong Kong's foreign exchange and money markets continues to be smooth and orderly, indicating that the impact of the coronavirus pandemic on the city's monetary environment remains limited. However, we need to closely monitor the risks brought about by the outbreak of the coronavirus pandemic. Hong Kong possesses substantial foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, and the HKMA has the capability, resources, and determination to address capital outflows and maintain Hong Kong's monetary and financial stability. Despite the uncertain external environment and the slowdown in the local economy, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained relatively loose during the review period. The HKD monetary base remained large, rising by 4.0% since the end of June to HK$1,689.4 billion at the end of January 2020 (Figure 4.4). As no exchange guarantees were triggered during this period, the total balance remained largely unchanged at approximately HK$54 billion. Other components of the monetary base, including outstanding foreign exchange fund notes and bonds, certificates of indebtedness, and banknotes and coins in circulation issued by the government, rose steadily. Figure 4.4 Components of the monetary base During the review period, broad HKD money supply indicators remained largely stable. Broad HKD money supply (HKD M3) grew by 3.5% in the first half of 2019, followed by a slight increase of 0.2% over the seven-month period since the end of June 2019. Corresponding asset analysis shows that the growth in HKD M3 since the end of June primarily reflects an increase in banks' net foreign currency assets and a rise in the monetary base (driven by increases in certificates of indebtedness and banknotes and coins in circulation issued by the government) (Figure 4.5). Over the seven-month period since the end of June, HKD deposits (the main component of HKD M3) remained largely unchanged (Figure 4.6). Within HKD deposits, time deposits continued to grow moderately, partly reflecting the rise in HKD deposit rates. Figure 4.5 Changes in HKD M3 and corresponding assets Over the seven-month period since the end of June 2019, foreign currency deposits grew moderately by 2.3% (Figure 4.6), primarily driven by USD deposits, which increased by 3.5% during this period. Other foreign currency deposits fell by 1.0% during the same period, with RMB deposits denominated in HKD recording a slight decline. Overall, the total deposits of authorized institutions grew steadily by 1.2% since the end of June. Supported by the increase in total deposits, Hong Kong's total broad money supply also rose at a relatively stable pace, with total money supplies M2 and M3 increasing by 1.6% and 1.5% respectively since the end of June (Figure 4.7). As monthly monetary statistics may fluctuate due to various short-term factors (such as seasonal and IPO-related funding demands, as well as business and investment-related activities), the statistics should be interpreted with caution. Figure 4.6 Deposits of authorized institutions by currency Figure 4.7 Total broad money supply (M2) Although the monetary environment remained relatively loose, short-term HKD interbank interest rates experienced fluctuations, reflecting seasonal liquidity demands and increased capital market activity since the fourth quarter of 2019, particularly the active IPO activity in the Hong Kong stock market; the Hong Kong interbank overnight interest rate experienced significant fluctuations in late October and mid-November (Figure 4.8). 44 During the review period, other short-term Hong Kong interbank interest rates generally rose. Large IPO subscriptions exert significant pressure on overnight rates; Theme 4 provides an empirical analysis showing that market attention to future IPO activities also affects the 3-month Hong Kong interbank rate. This situation occurs if market participants anticipate the future closing dates for large IPO subscriptions and prepare medium-term funds in advance for early deployment. Figure 4.8 HKD and USD interbank interest rates As for the HKD yield curve, it shifted downward following the USD yield curve. Compared to the end of June 2019, the yield on 10-year Hong Kong government bonds fell by 60 basis points to 1.04% as of February 28, 2020 (Figure 4.9). At the same time, the yield on 3-year Hong Kong government bonds fell by 50 basis points to 1.00% during the same period. Figure 4.9 Government Bond Yields, Composite Interest Rates, and Average Lending Rates for New Mortgages At the retail level, the composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of HKD funds for retail banks, rose gradually from 0.94% at the end of July 2019 to 1.01% at the end of January 2020. This increase mainly reflects banks continuing to raise preferential deposit rates to attract deposit funds, thereby increasing the weighted deposit rate for HKD. In late October 2019, following the downward adjustment of the US Federal Funds target range, several retail banks lowered their prime lending rates by 12.5 basis points. Consequently, the prime lending rates of retail banks currently range from 5.00% to 5.50%. Regarding mortgage loans, for mortgage loans benchmarked against the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR), major banks raised the interest rate caps determined by the prime lending rate; therefore, the average lending rate for new mortgages in October rose to around 2.63%. 45 The prime lending rate in the market has been lowered since November, and the average mortgage lending rate subsequently fell slightly to 2.53% in January 2020. In response to the evolving risks posed by the coronavirus pandemic to US economic activity and to support the Federal Reserve in achieving its policy goals, the Fed lowered the target range for the federal funds rate by a total of 150 basis points to 0-0.25 on March 3 (US time) and March 15 (US time). Although the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate follows US dollar interest rate movements in the long run, the short-term HIBOR may be influenced by local factors that could affect HKD demand, such as new stock listings in Hong Kong. The total surplus of the banking system has decreased since April 2018, and the sensitivity of the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate to changes in the supply and demand of HKD funds may have increased. However, this does not mean that the current total surplus level of HK$540 billion is insufficient to meet the demand for interbank payment settlements. In fact, Hong Kong's interbank market has continued to operate in an orderly manner. Should liquidity become tight in the short term, banks can utilize the liquidity arrangements provided to banks by the HKMA. Given that the US-China trade conflict could intensify, the offshore and onshore RMB exchange rates weakened significantly in late August and September 2019, with the offshore RMB against the US dollar falling to a ten-year low of 7.19 on September 2 (Figure 4.10). Entering October, with market expectations that China and the US would resume trade negotiations, the RMB depreciation trend reversed, and both offshore and onshore RMB strengthened in the fourth quarter, briefly rising above the 6.9 level in mid-January 2020 after China and the US signed the first phase of the trade agreement. However, since the end of January, due to the outbreak of the coronavirus pandemic, both offshore and onshore RMB have faced pressure to weaken again. The offshore RMB traded at a discount to the onshore RMB for most of the period from May to August, while it traded at a rough premium in the latter part of 2019; the discount widened briefly at the end of January 2020, but the difference between the two remains moderate by historical standards. Figure 4.10 Onshore and Offshore RMB Exchange Rates Despite fluctuations in the RMB exchange rate, liquidity in the offshore RMB interbank market remained largely stable. During the review period, the 3-month offshore RMB Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate continued to hover between 3-4% (Figure 4.11). The overnight offshore RMB Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate experienced brief fluctuations in late August and late November due to the adjustment of A-shares by Morgan Stanley Capital International (MSCI), and again near the end of January 2020 approaching the Lunar New Year holiday.

Due to increasing uncertainties in the global and local economic environment, the profits of retail banks in Hong Kong recorded a slight decline in the second half of 2019. Nevertheless, the capital and liquidity positions of the Hong Kong banking industry remain strong and robust by international standards. By historical standards, asset quality remains at a healthy level. Although the growth rate of total loans slowed down in the second half of last year, it still outpaced deposit growth during the same period of the review period. Accordingly, the average loan-to-deposit ratio for all authorized institutions in all currencies and the HKD loan-to-deposit ratio both rose. However, given that the total surplus of the banking system remains at a stable level and deposits have remained largely steady, the liquidity position of the banking industry remains robust. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking industry will continue to face several downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, future US-China trade relations, geopolitical tensions, and local social events. Given the continuous rise in corporate leverage levels and personal debt burdens, banks should prudently assess the impact on the asset quality of their loan portfolios under conditions where these risk factors may intensify. In the second half of 2019, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banking was 59, representing a slight decline of 1.5% compared to the same period in 2018. Accordingly, the return on assets in the second half of 2019 fell slightly to 1.13%, lower than the 1.23% in the same period of 2018 (Figure 5.1). Although the net interest margin of retail banking narrowed slightly from 1.67% in the second half of 2018 to 1.63% in the same period of 2019 (Figure 5.2), the net interest income of retail banking continued to record moderate growth during the review period. However, both loan impairment provisions and operating expenses of retail banking increased, leading to a slight decline in profits. Figure 5.1 Profits of Retail Banking Figure 5.2 Net Interest Margin of Retail Banking Despite the US Federal Funds target rate being lowered three times by 25 basis points each in the second half of 2019, the HKD wholesale funding market has not yet experienced significant downward pressure. Conversely, influenced by several local factors (including seasonal funding demands, increased liquidity demands due to large initial public offerings, and tighter liquidity conditions in the interbank market), the short-term HKD interbank lending rate has been on an upward trend since the fourth quarter of 2019. At the same time, during the review period, the longer-term HKD interbank lending rate remained largely stable, with the three-month Hong Kong interbank lending rate at 2.43% as of the end of 2019, close to the level six months prior (blue line in Figure 5.3). At the retail level, as HKD savings deposit rates remain near zero, retail banks have limited room to follow interest rate cuts after the US lowered its policy rates. 60 On the other hand, due to the tightening of HKD liquidity in the banking system during the review period, banks continued to compete to absorb long-term stable deposit funds. 61 Reflecting the increase in the weighted cost of HKD deposits, the composite rate (an indicator measuring the average cost of HKD funds for retail banks) gradually rose from 0.95% six months prior to 1.09% at the end of 2019, yet it remains at a relatively low level by historical standards (green line in Figure 5.3). During the review period, the net interest income of banks benefited from the slight decline in their overall cost of funds and the relatively high level of the HKD interbank lending rate, providing support for the banking industry's profits during the same period. Therefore, figures from June 2019 onwards cannot be directly compared with figures from previous months. Looking ahead, several downside risk factors from external and local environments will continue to cast a shadow over the profit prospects of banks. Relevant factors include uncertainties such as the spread of the coronavirus, the future direction of China-US trade relations, and the escalation of geopolitical tensions. The intensification of these risk factors may strike the already weak global economic growth momentum and reduce demand for bank credit. Given that major central banks have widely adopted loose monetary policies, the global low-interest-rate environment is likely to persist, which may put pressure on the future net interest margins of banks. At the local level, local social events since mid-2019 have continued to hit commercial investment and market confidence. Against the backdrop of an already weak economic environment, if the situation continues or further intensifies in the future, it may cause the credit demand outlook and bank asset quality to deteriorate. Regarding overall market developments, following the issuance of eight virtual bank licenses by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the Hong Kong banking industry has begun to launch virtual banking services. As these new market participants may increase their market share by attracting new customers through the launch of more convenient products and more attractive deposit rates, this may exert upward pressure on the funding costs of existing banks. Although the short-term impact may remain mitigated because the current business scale of virtual banks is still limited, the long-term impact may depend on whether existing banks will accelerate the application of financial technology to maintain competitiveness. The results of Topic 5 show that the extent to which Hong Kong banks adopt financial technology is statistically correlated with improvements in cost-effectiveness and increases in profit levels. The capital levels of the Hong Kong banking industry remain robust and are far higher than the minimum international standards. As of the end of 2019, the aggregate total capital ratio of locally registered authorized institutions further rose to 20.7% (Figure 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio also increased to 18.5%, of which 16.5% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. On a semi-annual basis, loan growth (measured by the change in the total amount of loans and advances of all authorized institutions) grew moderately by 4.2% in the first half of 2019, then slowed to 2.4% in the second half (Figure 5.12).
