The rollout of coronavirus vaccines has brought hope for economic recovery, bolstering global growth prospects. Coupled with ongoing fiscal and monetary easing, financial markets have repeatedly reached new highs. Nevertheless, global prospects remain clouded by uncertainties, and the pace of recovery is expected to vary across economies. In the medium term, a disconnect between financial markets and the real economy, high levels of debt, and the long-lasting economic damage caused by the pandemic will pose challenges for policymakers. The Hong Kong dollar foreign exchange and money markets continued to function smoothly. The Hong Kong dollar stayed close to the strong-side convertibility guarantee level against the US dollar, driven primarily by demand related to equities. During the review period, total deposits increased, with no signs of significant capital outflows from the local banking system. Partly reflecting weaker economic activity and reduced credit demand due to recurring pandemic waves, total bank lending edged down in the second half of the year; however, it still posted a modest increase for the whole of 2020. Meanwhile, the residential property market remained largely stable. Looking ahead, uncertainties surrounding the pace of economic recovery and persistent geopolitical risks will continue to pose challenges to Hong Kong’s banking sector. In particular, as the pandemic may impair the repayment capacity of firms and households, banks must remain vigilant regarding the impact of these downside risks on asset quality. Global economic growth rebounded in the third quarter of 2020 as economies reopened, but with new coronavirus infection rates rising again from the fourth quarter onward, global growth slowed once more. Nevertheless, the breakthrough in vaccine development toward the end of 2020 raised market expectations that the pandemic would eventually end, facilitating a return to normalcy and accelerated growth worldwide. Coupled with continued fiscal and monetary easing, global financial markets climbed to new peaks in early 2021, despite emerging signs of a disconnect from the real economy. Against this backdrop, uncertainties will continue to cast a shadow over the global economic outlook. It remains to be seen whether vaccines can be widely distributed. Meanwhile, supply bottlenecks and earlier aggressive easing measures could lead to higher-than-expected inflation, prompting central banks to scale back monetary easing earlier than anticipated and thus shattering market expectations of “prolonged low interest rates.” In the long run, policymakers must assess the costs and benefits of prolonging relief measures and address numerous economic after-effects triggered by the pandemic, including high global debt levels and lasting economic damage. In East Asia, domestic GDP growth improved in the second half of 2020, supported by rebounding export demand. With risk appetite on the rise, inflows of portfolio investment into the region picked up, and yield-seeking activities resumed. Despite these positive developments, East Asia still faces persistent uncertainties stemming from the pandemic. First, in the global race to procure vaccines, less developed economies in the region may lag behind advanced economies in achieving herd immunity, hindering the recovery of their tourism and service sectors. Second, uncertainties regarding vaccine supply, coverage, or efficacy—combined with deteriorating fiscal conditions among regional governments—could dampen market sentiment and trigger capital flow reversals. In mainland China, economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020 as consumer activity gradually returned to normal. For the whole of 2020, the mainland economy grew by 2.3%, making it the only major economy to record positive growth. Looking ahead, the economic outlook will largely depend on the pandemic’s trajectory and developments in Sino-US tensions. The latest consensus forecasts predict 8.4% growth for the mainland economy in 2021. After depreciating for several months at the start of 2020, the Chinese yuan strengthened for the remainder of the year, driven by faster economic recovery, a weaker US dollar, and robust capital inflows into the mainland bond market. Detailed analysis shows that during the outbreak of the novel coronavirus, fundamental factors—rather than market sentiment—played a more significant role in driving yuan exchange rate fluctuations (see Topic 1 for details). Hong Kong’s economy showed some improvement in the second half of 2020, yet real GDP remained well below pre-outbreak levels. Supported by slightly stronger domestic demand and further expansion in goods exports, seasonally adjusted real GDP began to rise in the third quarter, ending five consecutive quarters of contraction. The year-on-year contraction in real GDP also narrowed considerably, from 9% in the first half of 2020 to around 3% in the second half. However, for the full year of 2020, real GDP declined by 6.1%, marking the steepest drop on record and representing the first instance in history of two consecutive years of contraction, following a 1.2% decline in 2019. The latest GDP figures by sector indicate that consumption- and tourism-related industries suffered even greater setbacks than the broader economy amid the pandemic. To combat the ongoing crisis, the government launched two additional rounds (the third and fourth) of the Anti-epidemic Fund in the latter half of 2020, aimed at assisting industries and citizens affected by the pandemic while enhancing Hong Kong’s pandemic response capabilities. In its recent 2021/22 Budget, the government also announced extra countercyclical measures to stimulate the economy, including one-time HK$5,000 electronic consumption vouchers and government-guaranteed loans for unemployed individuals. In March 2021, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, together with the “Banking Industry SME Loan Coordination Mechanism,” extended the “pre-approved interest deferral” scheme until October of the same year and prolonged the repayment period for trade financing loans under this scheme. These extensions are expected to alleviate cash flow difficulties faced by certain corporate borrowers. The rollout of new coronavirus vaccines offers hope for a return to normal economic activity; consequently, the local economy is projected to return to positive growth in 2021 as a whole. Nevertheless, the strength and pace of this recovery hinge on numerous uncertain factors, including the pandemic’s evolution and the progress and effectiveness of vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the local economy is anticipated to encounter significant challenges in the early part of 2021. On the external front, mainland China’s economy is expected to strengthen further, providing support for Hong Kong’s exports of goods and services; meanwhile, the pace of recovery in other major economies will depend on the success of their large-scale vaccination programs. The government forecasts real GDP growth of 3.5–5.5% for 2021, while international institutions and private analysts project an average growth rate of 4.4%. The labor market deteriorated further in the latter half of 2020 and early 2021. The unemployment rate climbed steadily, reaching a 17-year high of 7.2% in February 2021; meanwhile, the underemployment rate rose to 4.0%, the highest level since the SARS outbreak. To address this worsening labor market situation, the government introduced the “Retain Employees Scheme” under the second round of the Anti-epidemic Fund, offering time-limited (June–November 2020) wage subsidies to employers to help them retain staff. Following the conclusion of this scheme, the government rolled out other targeted measures (such as lump-sum grants) under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund to further support industries severely impacted by the pandemic. In the short term, given the weak economic conditions, the labor market is expected to remain under pressure. Topic 2 examines the potential impact of fluctuations in Hong Kong’s tourism sector on the local labor market. Domestic inflationary pressures steadily eased over the eight-month period from mid-2020 to February 2021. The underlying consumer price inflation rate dropped significantly year-on-year to 0.3% and 0.2% in the 3rd and 4th quarters of 2020 respectively; in January and February 2021, it fell further to -0.5% and -0.1% respectively. Although the 3-month annualized underlying inflation rate—a key indicator of inflation momentum—has fluctuated slightly in recent months, it remains at a low level. Given that both global and local economic conditions remain challenging, inflationary pressures in Hong Kong are likely to stay subdued in the near term; in particular, the recent slowdown in private residential rent growth is expected to continue curbing local inflation. Market consensus forecasts an overall inflation rate of 1.4% for 2021, while the government projects underlying and overall inflation rates of 1.0% and 1.6% respectively for 2021. The Hong Kong dollar remained close to the strong-side convertibility guarantee level against the US dollar, driven primarily by equity-related capital demand, including robust new share offerings and inflows of southbound funds via the Stock Connect programs linking Shanghai and Shenzhen with Hong Kong. Active fundraising activities in the first two months of 2021 further bolstered the Hong Kong dollar’s strength. During the review period, the strong-side convertibility guarantee was triggered 47 times in September and October 2020, resulting in an inflow of HK$2633 billion into Hong Kong. Throughout 2020, it was triggered a total of 85 times, bringing cumulative inflows to HK$3835 billion. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to proceed smoothly and orderly. From a geographical perspective, total deposits increased during the review period, indicating no signs of substantial capital outflows from Hong Kong’s banking system. Although uncertainties related to the pandemic’s trajectory, the pace of economic recovery, and ongoing tensions between China and the US may exacerbate fluctuations in capital flows, Hong Kong possesses ample foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, enabling it to withstand such volatility. With the strong-side convertibility guarantee being triggered, the aggregate balance of the banking system rose, and Hong Kong interbank rates remained at extremely low levels. The composite rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funding for retail banks, fell from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 to 0.23% by late February 2021. Thanks to these lower funding costs, the average interest rate on newly issued mortgages dropped from 2.02% in June to 1.56% in January. Meanwhile, the best lending rates offered by major retail banks remained unchanged throughout the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. As the onshore RMB exchange rate strengthened, the offshore RMB (CNH) appreciated against the US dollar since late May 2020. For most of the review period, the offshore RMB traded at a premium relative to the onshore rate; in the fourth quarter, this premium averaged around 100 basis points, a level still considered moderate by historical standards. Hong Kong’s offshore RMB liquidity pool continued to expand in the latter half of 2020; by end-January 2021, the total balance of RMB customer deposits and certificates of deposit had reached RMB 8,263 billion. Regarding other RMB-related activities, RMB bank lending in Hong Kong declined, while RMB trade settlement saw growth; the daily average transaction volume on the RMB Real Time Gross Settlement System remained robust at RMB 11,915 billion throughout 2020. Hong Kong boasts highly efficient financial infrastructure, providing investors with numerous channels for cross-border capital flows to the Chinese mainland. With the gradual liberalization of the mainland’s capital account, rising global demand for RMB-denominated assets, and deepening regional economic and financial cooperation under initiatives such as the Belt and Road Initiative and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area plan, Hong Kong’s offshore RMB business is poised to benefit further. Supported by rising global equity markets and active buying of Hong Kong stocks by mainland investors via the Stock Connect programs, Hong Kong’s stock market rebounded after experiencing a sharp correction at the start of the review period. Global equity markets rose due to unprecedented monetary easing measures implemented by major economies, positive market expectations regarding vaccine development as a catalyst for economic recovery, and a reduction in global geopolitical uncertainties. Against this backdrop, the Hang Seng Index recovered from its 2020 losses, posting a 15.1% increase during the review period; in mid-February 2021, it briefly surpassed the 31,000-point mark, reaching a 32-month high. Backed by steady issuance volumes, both the Hong Kong dollar and offshore RMB bond markets continued to expand in the latter half of 2020. After experiencing substantial net capital outflows in the first half of 2020, market confidence rebounded swiftly following unprecedented economic stimulus measures introduced by governments worldwide; bond funds inflowing into the local market also saw a recovery. Although bond yields experienced a modest uptick during this period, global yields, including those in Hong Kong, remained near historic lows.

With breakthroughs in vaccine development, the market expects that the COVID-19 pandemic will eventually end and global economic growth will accelerate. Coupled with the expectation of a “lower for longer” global monetary policy, investors were not deterred by the rebound of the pandemic at the end of 2020, and financial markets rose to new highs in early 2021. However, the high expectations of the financial markets are disconnected from the still challenging macroeconomic environment. If the economic recovery is not as strong as expected, or if policy support is withdrawn earlier than anticipated (for example, due to higher-than-expected inflation), asset prices could become volatile. Looking ahead, policymakers will face the difficult task of when to withdraw policy support and address the many problems left by the pandemic, including high debt levels and long-term economic scarring. The ongoing uncertainty of the pandemic continues to cast a shadow over the economic recovery in East Asia, where slower-developing emerging market economies may face greater challenges in vaccine procurement and distribution. Any setbacks in the progress of vaccination programs could reverse the current optimism, leading to instability in capital flows and financial markets. As for Mainland China, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020 as consumption activities gradually returned to normal. Looking ahead, the economic growth outlook remains uncertain and largely depends on the development of the pandemic and changes in Sino-US tensions. Therefore, the government has announced that it will continue to maintain a supportive policy stance and emphasized the importance of controlling systemic risks. Benefiting from the purchasing power released by the reopening of the economy, major economies mostly recorded better-than-expected real GDP growth in the third quarter of 2020. However, since the fourth quarter, the number of new COVID-19 infections has climbed again, prompting governments to resume lockdowns and social distancing measures, and global growth momentum has weakened again. At the end of 2020, a more contagious variant of the virus emerged and subsequently spread around the world, making the situation more severe. Nevertheless, with breakthroughs in vaccine development and the approval of several vaccines for use at the end of 2020, the market expects that the pandemic will eventually end, and the global economy will return to normal and accelerate its growth. Another driving force supporting the global economic recovery comes from continuous policy stimulus measures, including the commitment of major central banks to a “lower for longer” monetary policy amid weak inflation, and the continued fiscal easing measures of major advanced economies, especially the fiscal stimulus packages passed by the US Congress in December 2020 and March 2021. Accordingly, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) raised its 2021 global GDP growth forecast to 5.5% in January 2021, 0.3 percentage points higher than the forecast made in October 2020 (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 IMF's real GDP growth forecasts in January 2021 and October 2020. Against this backdrop, market optimism has increased, and the stock prices of cyclical industries that usually benefit from economic recovery have risen, driving global stock prices and valuations to new highs in early 2021 (Chart 2.2). Chart 2.2 12-month forward P/E ratios of major stock indices. However, while the financial markets are performing strongly, the macroeconomic situation remains challenging, and the disconnect between the two may lead to volatility in the asset markets in the face of multiple risks. First, the prospect of controlling the pandemic depends on the widespread distribution of vaccines, which remains to be seen. As of mid-March 2021, the overall global vaccination rate was still low (Chart 2.3). Although there are global mechanisms (such as COVAX) to promote a more equitable distribution of vaccines, due to limited vaccine supply, the problem of low vaccination rates in lower-income emerging market economies is expected to be more severe. If the pandemic is not well controlled, various regions may need to extend social distancing and other restrictive measures, which would in turn dampen the prospects for a global recovery. Chart 2.3: Proportion of the population that has received at least one dose of vaccine in selected economies (as of March 15, 2021). Second, the rebound in financial markets is based on continued monetary and fiscal policy support, especially a "lower for longer" monetary policy. However, there is a risk that support measures may be withdrawn faster than expected. For example, inflation expectations in the United States and Europe have risen due to the combined effects of supply bottlenecks, strong currency and liquidity growth, and aggressive fiscal easing policies (Chart 2.4). If future inflation is stronger than expected, central banks may need to scale back their monetary easing policies, and higher-than-expected inflation data could also lead to greater volatility in financial markets. Chart 2.4: 5-year/5-year inflation-linked swap rates in the US and Eurozone. Third, there is significant uncertainty about the future of Sino-US relations. The wave of Sino-US "decoupling," especially in the financial and technological fields, has intensified since the outbreak of the pandemic. And given the increasingly tough stance of both the Democratic and Republican parties in the United States towards Mainland China, this trend may not be reversed under the Biden administration. An unexpected escalation of Sino-US tensions could trigger financial market turmoil in the future. Looking ahead, policymakers will face the difficult question of whether and when to withdraw anti-pandemic support measures. While premature withdrawal of these measures could jeopardize the economic recovery and create a "cliff effect," these measures are costly in the long run, including creating a fiscal burden and delaying the necessary reallocation of resources after the pandemic, such as allowing "zombie companies" with no longer viable business models to survive with continued government support. In addition, policymakers must also address the many problems left by the pandemic. First, global debt levels rose sharply in 2020 due to falling corporate revenues and soaring government spending (Chart 2.5). Although the problem of soaring debt may not be imminent as global interest rates are currently at extremely low levels, the continued accumulation of debt in the public and private sectors may raise concerns about fiscal sustainability and financial stability. Chart 2.5: Global debt as a percentage of GDP. Another legacy issue involves the potential long-term economic damage or scarring caused by the pandemic. For example, high uncertainty may cause companies to reduce investment, while workers who have been unemployed for a long time may permanently withdraw from the labor market, resulting in a large waste of human resources. In East Asia, real GDP growth stabilized in the second half of 2020 after a sharp drop in the second quarter (Chart 2.6). The main driver of the economic recovery was a rebound in exports, with the strongest demand for exports of electronic and technological equipment. At the same time, the hardest-hit service industries (such as tourism and consumer services that require face-to-face contact with customers) continued to be in dire straits. Chart 2.6: East Asia: Real GDP growth in 2020. Despite the uncertainty surrounding the economic recovery, portfolio investment funds have begun to flow back in. Since the second half of last year, the region has attracted more bond fund inflows due to improved market sentiment and higher yields relative to bonds in advanced economies (Chart 2.7). As the economy showed signs of recovery and vaccination programs were launched, equity fund inflows into East Asia also accelerated in the last quarter of 2020. Regional currencies also appreciated accordingly due to portfolio inflows, causing the Bloomberg JPMorgan Asia Dollar Index to rebound by about 10% from its low in March last year. Chart 2.7: East Asia: Portfolio investment flows. East Asia continues to face ongoing uncertainty from the pandemic. First, although the rollout of vaccines has brought hope to the region's hard-hit service industries and economy, competition for early batches of vaccines around the world has driven up procurement costs, and vaccine distribution also poses challenges to the region's logistics and public health capabilities. As a result, slower-developing economies in the region may achieve herd immunity later than advanced economies, and uneven vaccination rates among economies may prolong border closures and delay the recovery of tourism-related industries. Second, as investor optimism is largely driven by the vaccine rollout, the current capital inflows and rebound in financial asset prices may come to an end if the progress or effectiveness of vaccination is far below expectations. A sudden drop in capital inflows could trigger another wave of market turmoil. With the successful control of the novel coronavirus and the gradual recovery of consumption, the mainland economy recovered rapidly in the second half of 2020. At the same time, benefiting from strong demand for pandemic-related products (such as medical equipment and high-tech products), exports also maintained growth (Chart 2.8). Throughout 2020, despite the unprecedented impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the economy, mainland China's GDP still recorded a growth of 2.3%. Chart 2.8: Mainland China: Contribution of various demand components to GDP growth. Looking ahead, the latest consensus forecast shows that the mainland economy will grow strongly by 8.4% in 2021, with private consumption expected to be the main driver of economic growth. However, the sustainability of the economic recovery still depends to some extent on the development of the pandemic. Although industrial production activities in the mainland have normalized, the service industry is still partially disrupted as the pandemic has re-emerged in several northern provinces. In terms of the external environment, although exports resumed growth in the second half of 2020, global demand remains uncertain due to a new wave of outbreaks in most developed economies. In addition, the tense Sino-US relations are unlikely to ease in the short term, but the previously signed Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) and the agreed-upon EU-China Comprehensive Agreement on Investment will help China further integrate with other economies, which may partially offset the adverse effects of Sino-US decoupling on the economic recovery. Considering the still uncertain economic outlook, the government announced at the Central Economic Work Conference in December 2020 that the existing policy stance will not change significantly in 2021 to support economic growth, while also emphasizing the importance of controlling systemic risks, such as maintaining the stability of macro-leverage and the sustainability of local government debt. In addition, the latest government work report sets the growth target for 2021 at over 6%. In the long run, the "14th Five-Year Plan" prioritizes technological self-reliance and dual circulation, with the aim of achieving a per capita GDP level of a moderately developed country by 2035. The impact of the novel coronavirus outbreak on the repayment ability of bond-issuing enterprises seems to be limited, and the overall default rate in the mainland bond market remained at a low level in the second half of 2020. However, due to a sharp increase in defaults on bonds of state-owned enterprises (SOEs), the total amount of defaulted bonds increased in 2020 (Chart 2.9). Although the increase in SOE defaults mainly reflects the central government's determination to break the "implicit guarantee" of SOEs to promote more rational market risk pricing, the limited fiscal space of some local governments may also be a reason, especially for local governments in less developed regions. Chart 2.9: Mainland China: Onshore bond default scale and ratio. In the second half of 2020, the financing costs of corporate issuers increased, especially for some high-risk issuers. Although the continued economic recovery and the gradual normalization of interest rates have to some extent led to an increase in financing costs for lower-rated issuers, several corporate default incidents in the last quarter of 2020 caused credit spreads to widen significantly (Chart 2.10). Chart 2.10 Mainland China: 5-year corporate bond yields. In the real estate market, housing prices in mainland China continued to rise in the second half of 2020, especially in first-tier cities. In contrast, the pace of housing price increases in lower-tier cities was much slower (Chart 2.11). As for the problem of housing oversupply that had plagued third-tier cities in previous years, it was basically under control in 2020, partly due to strong sales in third-tier cities amid high market sentiment. As of the end of 2020, the inventory-to-sales ratio in third-tier cities remained at around 13 months, far below the peak of 31 months in early 2015.

Although real GDP remains well below pre-pandemic levels, Hong Kong’s economy showed some improvement in the second half of 2020, driven by a rebound in domestic demand and further expansion in goods exports. With hopes that COVID vaccinations will restore normal economic activity, the local economy is expected to return to growth in 2021, following the worst contraction on record in 2020. Nevertheless, the strength and pace of this recovery depend on numerous uncertainties, including the evolution of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of vaccine rollouts. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, Hong Kong’s economy is still expected to face significant challenges in early 2021. Consequently, the labor market is anticipated to remain under pressure in the short term, while domestic inflationary pressures will stay modest. Hong Kong’s economy improved in the second half of 2020 (Table 3. A), yet economic activity remained far below pre-pandemic levels. The year-on-year decline in real GDP narrowed to 3.6% in the third quarter and further to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. Nonetheless, for the whole of 2020, real GDP fell by 6.1%, marking the largest annual decline on record and representing the first instance in history of two consecutive years of contraction, following a 1.2% drop in 2019. Latest figures on sectoral GDP also indicate that economic activity in most sectors declined year-on-year in recent quarters, with consumption- and tourism-related industries experiencing sharper contractions than the overall economy. On a quarter-on-quarter basis, real GDP began to recover from the third quarter of 2020, ending five consecutive quarters of decline (Table 3. A and Figure 3.1). Local private consumption returned to positive growth in the 3rd and 4th quarters; however, consumer confidence remained weak amid the third and fourth waves of the local epidemic, under which the authorities reimposed social distancing measures. With a brief improvement in business sentiment, overall investment spending also rose in the latter half of the year. Partly owing to stronger export performance—particularly to the Chinese mainland—Hong Kong’s merchandise trade expanded further (Figure 3.2). In contrast, services trade remained sluggish due to the ongoing stagnation of global tourism. Overall, net imports (a trade deficit) weighed on GDP growth in the second half of the year, partly reflecting slower growth in imports compared to exports. Novel coronavirus vaccinations are anticipated to facilitate a return to normal economic activity; consequently, Hong Kong’s economy is projected to return to positive growth in 2021 (for the year as a whole). Given that widespread vaccination will require time, the local economy is still expected to encounter considerable challenges in early 2021. On the external front, mainland China’s economy is forecast to strengthen further, providing support for Hong Kong’s exports of goods and services; meanwhile, the pace of recovery in other major economies will depend on the success of their large-scale vaccination programs, thereby influencing both Hong Kong’s merchandise trade and inbound tourism. The government forecasts real GDP growth of 3.5–5.5% for 2021, while international institutions and private analysts project an average growth rate of 4.4%. The labor market deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and early 2021. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate climbed to 7.2% in February 2021, reaching a 17-year high (Figure 3.3). The underemployment rate also rose to 4.0%, the highest level since the SARS outbreak. The total number of employed persons stabilized after dropping to a low level (Figure 3.3), although government figures indicate a continued decline in the number of job vacancies. To address the worsening labor market conditions, the government launched the “Retain Employees Scheme” under the second round of anti-pandemic relief measures, offering time-limited wage subsidies (from June to November 2020) to employers to help them retain staff. Following the conclusion of this scheme, the government introduced additional targeted measures—such as lump-sum grants—under the third and fourth rounds of relief efforts to further support industries severely hit by the pandemic. In the short term, given the weak economic conditions, the labor market is expected to remain under pressure. With the novel coronavirus pandemic raging, inbound tourism has plunged into a swift depression, and there are market concerns that the crisis will have a scarring effect on the future recovery of the labor market. Accordingly, this special topic conducts an empirical analysis of how a thriving tourism sector influences the local labor market, thereby assessing the possible consequences of the current downturn in the industry. Since 2000, Hong Kong’s tourism sector has experienced significant fluctuations (Figure B2.1). Specifically, tourist arrivals declined during the SARS outbreak in 2003. However, following the launch of the “Individual Visit Scheme” in July of that year, tourist numbers surged. Under the initial scheme, mainland residents could individually apply for one or two trips to Hong Kong per year, with each stay limited to no more than 7 days. In April 2009, the scheme was expanded to allow eligible residents with Shenzhen household registration to obtain multiple-entry “Individual Visit” visas valid for one year. Consequently, the number of mainland tourists increased substantially. Driven by new cross-border infrastructure linking Hong Kong and mainland China, tourist arrivals reached record highs at the end of 2018 and early 2019. Subsequent local social events led to a halving of tourist numbers in the second half of 2019, and under the novel coronavirus pandemic, the visitor tourism industry has been stagnant since late January 2020. Figure B2.1: Tourist arrivals and related policies    We examine the impact of a flourishing tourism sector on local employment and income by focusing on the boost brought about by the Individual Visit Scheme. We consider this scheme, introduced in 2003, akin to a random economic shock, as its timing appeared largely exogenous and was unforeseeable to local residents. Our primary data source comprises population statistics drawn from Hong Kong’s population censuses or by-census surveys. Specifically, we utilize the 5% samples from the 1996, 2001, 2006, 2011, and 2016 censuses or by-census surveys. Additionally, we define tourism-related industries as the food and beverage, retail, hospitality, and transportation sectors. First, we employ a “difference-in-differences” analytical framework to compare employment outcomes before and after the implementation of the Individual Visit Scheme between younger workers (aged 20–40) in the “treatment group” and older workers (aged 41–65) in the “comparison group.” We classify the younger group as the treatment group because they are still at the early stages of their careers and can more flexibly make significant changes to their employment decisions in response to exogenous growth in Hong Kong’s tourism industry. Given that the impact of the tourism boom induced by the Individual Visit Scheme on the labor market may evolve over time, we also apply an “event study” approach to identify such time-varying effects. Our empirical findings indicate that, compared to their older counterparts, younger workers—particularly women and those with only secondary education—were more likely to enter tourism-related industries following the implementation of the scheme. Notably, the effect of the scheme on the probability of young women entering these industries was both pronounced and persistent; starting from 2006, this effect remained at nearly 5 percentage points above the average entry probability of older workers (Figure B2.2). We also employed a similar methodology to compare incomes between workers in tourism-related industries (treatment group) and those in non-tourism industries (comparison group). The results show that after the implementation of the Individual Visit Scheme, wage growth among workers in tourism-related sectors outpaced that of employees in other industries. Moreover, compared to their counterparts in other sectors, female workers and those with lower educational attainment experienced even greater and steadily rising income increases—ranging from 3 to 20 percentage points (Figure B2.3). Figure B2.2: Impact of the Individual Visit Scheme on female employment   Figure B2.3: Impact of the Individual Visit Scheme on income of female and low-education workers    These findings are largely consistent with international experience, underscoring that the tourism industry serves as a vital source of employment, especially for young people, women, and workers with lower educational levels. In the context of Hong Kong, our results align with prior analyses indicating that robust growth in tourism has heightened demand for low-skilled labor, thereby enhancing labor market stability among this demographic. However, as the tourism sector experiences a downturn, these worker groups may be disproportionately affected and thus warrant close monitoring.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained close to the strong-side convertibility undertaking level, which was triggered multiple times between September and October 2020. Strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar was primarily driven by equity-related capital needs, including robust initial public offering activities and southward capital inflows via the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect. As the aggregate balance rose to over HK$4,500 billion, Hong Kong interbank interest rates declined across the board. Although uncertainties related to the COVID pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and ongoing tensions between China and the United States may exacerbate capital flow volatility, Hong Kong possesses ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system capable of withstanding such pressures. The proximity of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate to the strong-side convertibility undertaking level was mainly driven by equity-related capital needs, including active IPO activities and southward capital inflows via the Shanghai-Hong Kong and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connects (Figure 4.1). Although some funds raised through IPOs were repatriated, buoyant sentiment in the local stock market and expectations of heightened capital demand toward year-end kept the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate within a narrow range of 7.7505 to 7.7544 in November and December. With continued robust fundraising activities in the first two months of 2021 (Figure 4.2), the Hong Kong dollar closed at HK$7.7568 against the US dollar on February 26, 2021. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading remained smooth and orderly. During the review period, multiple triggers of the strong-side convertibility undertaking led to an increase in the aggregate balance, indicating substantial capital inflows into Hong Kong. In September and October 2020 alone, the undertaking was triggered 47 times. Under the linked exchange rate system, the HKMA sold a total of HK$2,633 billion, raising the aggregate balance from HK$1,931 billion at end-August to HK$4,575 billion at end-February (Figure 4.3). Throughout 2020, the strong-side convertibility undertaking was triggered 85 times, resulting in cumulative capital inflows of HK$3,835 billion. From a cross-border perspective, total deposits increased, indicating no signs of significant capital outflows from Hong Kong’s banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance of payments data showed that direct investment by non-residents continued to flow into Hong Kong in the fourth quarter of 2020, with no abnormal capital movements observed. As an international financial hub, Hong Kong hosts numerous fundraising activities, including IPOs, resulting in substantial capital inflows and outflows. On one hand, these activities attract international investors to transfer funds into Hong Kong; on the other hand, funds raised by listed companies may later be transferred out of Hong Kong to meet business needs. Hong Kong’s ample foreign exchange reserves and robust banking system ensure that such capital flow fluctuations do not compromise financial stability. With continuous inflows of capital into Hong Kong dollars, the monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2020 and recent months. Over the eight months since end-June 2020, Hong Kong’s monetary base expanded by 20.8% (Figure 4.5). This growth was primarily driven by multiple triggers of the strong-side convertibility undertaking, which boosted the aggregate balance. Meanwhile, other components of the monetary base—including certificates of indebtedness, government-issued currency, and outstanding Exchange Fund bills and bonds—remained relatively stable. Entering 2022, the global economy showed weak performance, while inflationary pressures continued to rise worldwide, particularly in the United States. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook faces significant uncertainties, including the risk of another major wave of infections, and the possibility that monetary policy tightening may be more pronounced than expected if inflation in the U. S. proves more persistent and widespread. Should the Federal Reserve implement substantial monetary tightening, leading to tighter global financial conditions, this would put pressure on the recovery of more vulnerable emerging market economies. Recently, the outbreak of military conflict between Russia and Ukraine may have a notable impact on the global economy through trade and financial channels, further complicating the global monetary policy outlook. During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, yet trading remained smooth and orderly. Total deposits saw modest growth, with no significant signs of capital outflows from Hong Kong’s banking system. For the full year of 2021, the growth rate of total bank lending accelerated. Meanwhile, the residential property market has softened since mid-2021. Looking forward, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant could threaten the ongoing economic recovery; coupled with the possibility of a faster-than-expected pace of monetary policy normalization in the U. S., these risks pose challenges to banks’ credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of these risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. The global economy began to slow down in late 2021, a trend that persisted into 2022. This slowdown was driven by heightened restrictions on mobility worldwide due to the highly contagious Omicron variant, as well as ongoing supply bottlenecks that constrained production. Concurrently, global inflationary pressures intensified amid imbalanced supply and demand and labor shortages; inflation has now spread to a wide range of goods and services in major advanced economies, especially the U. S. Recently, the outbreak of military conflict between Russia and Ukraine has led to a sharp rise in commodity prices, which may further exacerbate global inflation risks. Increased volatility in financial markets could also prevent global financial conditions from tightening as expected, further complicating the monetary policy outlook. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook remains highly uncertain. In the short term, should another major wave of infections occur, there is a risk of renewed lockdowns and worsening supply bottlenecks. In the U. S., as the risk of inflation being more persistent and widespread grows, the Federal Reserve has adopted a more hawkish stance, accelerating its timeline for tapering asset purchases and raising interest rates, while also beginning discussions on reducing its balance sheet. Should the Fed need to implement substantial monetary tightening, global financial conditions may also tighten, impairing borrowers’ ability to service debt and triggering disorderly capital outflows that would weigh on the recovery of vulnerable emerging market economies. The recent conflict between Russia and Ukraine may also keep global commodity prices elevated, exacerbating shortages of industrial goods and increasing financial market volatility. Heightened market volatility could also lead to redemption pressures on open-ended funds, raising their liquidity risks. Topic 1 examines whether swing pricing—a liquidity management tool for open-ended funds—can help mitigate such risks during periods of market stress, as well as its potential limitations. In emerging Asia, the economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021; however, in some Southeast Asian economies, strict pandemic control measures reintroduced in the third quarter temporarily slowed down the recovery. Meanwhile, export-oriented economies in the region reliant on technology products—South Korea and Singapore—continued to benefit from strong global demand for such goods. Although most market participants anticipate broad-based recovery across emerging Asia in 2022, the short-term economic outlook faces multiple headwinds. First, new virus variants remain a concern, particularly for economies with low vaccination rates and limited public health resources. Second, the Fed’s accelerated policy normalization could trigger capital outflows from the region and intensify currency depreciation pressures; for economies still needing accommodative monetary policies to support recovery, striking a balance between curbing capital outflows and sustaining economic activity will become more difficult. Third, a slowdown in major economies, coupled with a potential shift in demand from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens, could dampen prospects for trade growth. Fourth, rising prices of various commodities triggered by the Russia-Ukraine conflict are likely to feed into regional inflation while curbing consumer spending. With heightened global economic uncertainties, decisions regarding monetary policy normalization by central banks in the region will become increasingly complex. Central banks in certain economies within the region—those experiencing relatively weak growth and where inflation is highly sensitive to energy price fluctuations—will face particularly difficult policy choices. In the long run, to foster sustainable and robust growth patterns, investors must place greater emphasis on environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors in their investment decisions. Topic 2 examines how sensitive stock returns are to changes in climate risks, and how this sensitivity is influenced by firms’ environmental performance. In mainland China, economic growth slowed in the second half of 2021, affected by a new wave of COVID infections, power rationing measures, and tightening regulations in the real estate sector. Looking ahead, given the continued sluggishness of the property market and the spread of the Omicron variant, the mainland economy is likely to face downward pressure in the short term. Consequently, authorities have made stabilizing growth their top priority this year and introduced a series of fiscal and monetary support measures. The total value of onshore bond defaults, as well as defaults by state-owned enterprises, declined in the latter half of 2021; Topic 3 explores whether pricing of SOE bonds has improved in recent years. Overall banking sector risks remain manageable, as mainland banks—particularly systemically important ones—have limited exposure to developer-related lending, coupled with low non-performing loan ratios and high provision coverage ratios. In Hong Kong, the economy continued its recovery in the second half of 2021, though at a slower pace compared to the first half. Seasonally adjusted real GDP posted modest growth, driven by sustained global economic recovery boosting merchandise exports and private consumption, an improving local labor market, and the government’s consumption voucher scheme. Year-on-year, economic growth stood at 5.1% in the second half of 2021, compared to 7.8% in the first half. To ease cash flow constraints, enhancements were made to the “Fully Guaranteed Personal Special Loan” and various guarantee products under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme; these include higher maximum loan amounts, extended application periods, and longer repayment terms. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority, in collaboration with the banking sector, also extended the “Pre-approved Interest-only Repayment” scheme until the end of October 2022. This scheme further offers borrowers a one-year option to partially defer principal repayment, applicable also to loans under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme. It is anticipated that Hong Kong’s economy will continue to recover throughout 2022, albeit at a slower pace than in 2021, reflecting both a moderation in global growth amid ongoing pandemic concerns and a higher base effect. Specifically, merchandise exports are expected to benefit from global economic expansion, while various infrastructure and public works initiatives promoted by the government will also provide support. S. monetary policy normalization. Since September 2021, amid risk-averse sentiment in the local stock market, the Hong Kong dollar has gradually weakened against the U. S. dollar. Although it saw a brief rebound in October 2021, the HKD’s upward momentum subsequently faded, primarily due to weak net southbound inflows via the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect, as well as market expectations of a stronger U. S. dollar amid the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy normalization. Overall, the HKD remained mostly on the strong side within the currency peg band, and market operations proceeded smoothly. Total deposits posted modest growth during the review period, with no significant signs of capital outflows from the local banking system. Trading in Hong Kong’s interbank market also remained orderly. Ample interbank liquidity kept Hong Kong’s interbank rates at low levels throughout the period. Looking ahead, Hong Kong’s offshore RMB business is expected to benefit from the city’s efficient financial infrastructure, the north-south connectivity provided by the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect, Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect, Bond Connect, and Cross-border Wealth Management Connect, the ongoing liberalization of China’s capital account, rising international demand for RMB assets, and deeper regional economic and financial cooperation under the Belt and Road Initiative and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area development plan. Driven by expansionary monetary and fiscal policies, global economic recovery, and robust corporate earnings, major global stock markets continued to rise in the final quarter of 2021, helping the MSCI World Index reach a record high of 3,262 points on 4 January 2022. However, growing market concerns over tightening stances by major central banks in advanced economies amid rising inflation risks, surging commodity prices, and escalating tensions between Russia and Ukraine have led to a period of consolidation among major global stock indices since early January 2022.

Due to the rapid global spread of the variant viruses (Delta and Omicron), coupled with persistent production bottlenecks, the global economy slowed significantly in the latter part of 2021, and growth momentum remained weak as it entered 2022. Global inflationary pressures continued to intensify and have spread to a wide range of goods and services in the major advanced economies (especially the United States). Heightened inflation concerns prompted the Federal Reserve to adopt a more hawkish monetary policy stance, increasing the risk that an overly early tightening of global financial conditions could put pressure on currently elevated asset valuations, and would also be unfavorable for emerging markets where the recovery is still generally lagging. Recently, the conflict between Russia and Ukraine pushed up energy and other commodity prices and triggered volatility in global financial markets, exacerbating some of the aforementioned risks. In emerging Asia, although the Delta variant had once spread across the region, economies continued to recover in the second half of 2021, and the major technology-exporting economies in the region continued to perform better than other economies. At present, although the Omicron variant does not severely hinder the region’s economic recovery, any uncertainty related to new variants will continue to cast a shadow over the region’s economic outlook. In addition, the normalisation of the Federal Reserve’s policy may trigger an adjustment in regional asset prices, and the slowdown in major economies may also drag down the growth of the region’s goods exports. The conflict between Russia and Ukraine has on the one hand driven up commodity prices and increased inflation risks, and on the other hand weakened consumption and heightened global economic uncertainty, which will make decisions on monetary policy normalisation by central banks in the region more complex. In Mainland China, economic growth slowed in the second half of 2021, affected by a new wave of coronavirus outbreaks, power rationing, and tightening measures in the real estate market. Looking ahead, the mainland economy may continue to face downward pressure arising from a cooling real estate market and outbreaks of the Omicron variant. In light of this, the government has set stabilising growth as its top priority for this year, and macroeconomic policies will also provide greater support. Global economic recovery slowed noticeably in the last quarter of 2021, as the highly contagious Omicron variant overlapped with the spread of the Delta variant, triggering a new wave of infections and leading to tighter mobility restrictions worldwide. In addition, supply chain problems (such as shipping bottlenecks and shortages of key production inputs like semiconductors) continued to weigh on production. Entering 2022, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) projected in January that global GDP growth would slow from 5.9% in 2021 to 4.4% in 2022, reflecting the continued drag from the pandemic and supply constraints, reduced policy support in the United States and other major advanced economies, and the slowdown in growth momentum in Mainland China offsetting the expected rebound in growth in the rest of Asia (Chart 2.1). Core inflation (excluding food and energy prices) rose significantly in major advanced economies, especially in the United States, which had adopted larger-scale policy stimulus since the outbreak of the pandemic. Amid supply bottlenecks, the release of pent-up demand, and labour shortages, inflationary pressures have spread to a wide range of goods and services (Chart 2.2). Furthermore, the recent military conflict between Russia and Ukraine has pushed up the prices of many commodities and may further intensify already elevated global inflationary pressures. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook faces significant uncertainties, with considerable downside risks, and will depend on how the pandemic and related supply chain disruptions evolve, how geopolitical tensions affect global trade, inflation and financial market sentiment, and how major central banks respond to inflation through their policies. Regarding the pandemic, most governments have so far adopted targeted measures in response to the recent surge in Omicron cases, focusing on restricting high‑risk activities, encouraging remote work, and promoting vaccination. Compared with previous lockdown policies, these more relaxed measures should help reduce supply chain disruptions, and there have already been initial signs of improvement in supply chain bottlenecks since the end of 2021 (Chart 2.3). However, if large-scale outbreaks occur, lockdown measures may again be implemented, which would lead to a renewed worsening of supply bottlenecks. Chart 2.3 Purchasing Managers’ Index – subindex of suppliers’ delivery times  If the pandemic remains under control, supply bottlenecks can be expected to gradually ease, providing some relief for goods inflation. However, several developments may cause currently elevated global inflation to persist longer than expected, including: the risk that the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine and sanctions on energy imports from Russia will push up commodity prices; rising production costs being passed on to final prices with a lag; the earlier sharp increase in global residential property prices potentially driving rental increases later on; tight labour markets posing upside risks to wage growth; and rising inflation expectations. In particular, given that US inflation has recorded the largest increase in decades, the Federal Reserve adopted a more hawkish policy stance at the December 2021 FOMC meeting, no longer characterising high inflation as “transitory”, and doubling the pace of tapering asset purchases from a reduction of US$150 billion per month to US$300 billion per month, with the aim of ending the asset purchase programme by March 2022, and began discussing balance sheet reduction. In fact, recent market pricing suggests that the Federal Reserve may raise interest rates multiple times in 2022. In contrast, given the euro area’s closer trade and financial links with Russia and Ukraine, the European Central Bank may face more significant policy trade-offs. Against this backdrop, and with global debt levels and asset valuations remaining elevated under prolonged accommodative policies, if persistent inflationary pressures force the Federal Reserve to tighten policy faster than expected, borrowers’ debt-servicing capacity could deteriorate and financial market volatility could be triggered. Recently, as geopolitical tensions in Eastern Europe have intensified, risk aversion in financial markets has increased and signs of US dollar shortages have emerged, including a widening of cross-currency basis swap spreads. Under a scenario of a premature tightening of global financial conditions, emerging market economies with weaker fundamentals and still affected by the pandemic may be more vulnerable to renewed growth slowdowns, currency depreciation and capital outflow pressures. Heightened market volatility could also trigger redemption pressures on open‑ended funds, increasing their liquidity risk. Box 1 discusses whether swing pricing – a liquidity management tool for open‑ended funds – can reduce the liquidity risks of these funds under market stress, and examines the potential limitations of this tool. In emerging Asia, economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, but the spread of the Delta variant weakened growth momentum in the third quarter, especially in some Southeast Asian economies (Chart 2.4). At the same time, as major exporters of technology products in the region, South Korea and Singapore continued to benefit from strong global demand for technology goods, further widening the unevenness of the recovery across the region. In addition, inflationary pressures in many emerging Asian economies remained moderate. Chart 2.4 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index  Market consensus expects emerging Asian markets to experience a broad-based recovery in 2022, but the region’s short-term economic outlook is facing multiple headwinds:  First, although the Omicron variant has spread within the region since the end of 2021, its economic impact has so far been milder than previous waves of infection. However, some economies in the region where vaccination rates still lag behind and public health resources are relatively constrained will continue to face the threat posed by new variants. Second, the normalisation of the Federal Reserve’s policy may trigger capital outflows and exert depreciation pressure on regional currencies. For economies in the region that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policies to support economic recovery, the trade-off between containing capital outflow pressures and supporting economic activity will become more difficult. At the long end of the yield curve, because long-term yields in the past have been highly correlated (Chart 2.5), the risk of a sudden surge in long-term US Treasury yields could spill over into long-term bond yields in emerging Asia, increasing the risk of adjustments in regional asset markets. Chart 2.5 Correlation between ten-year sovereign bond yields in Asia and corresponding US Treasury yields  Third, the outlook for the region’s merchandise trade faces uncertainties arising from the slowdown in major economies and the potential shift in global demand from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens, which may weaken export growth in the region. Chart 2.6 United States: Imports from emerging Asia and real GDP  Fourth, although economies in the region generally have limited trade and financial linkages with Russia and Ukraine, the rise in commodity prices triggered by the conflict will feed through into regional inflation while at the same time weakening consumption. Coupled with increased global economic uncertainty, decisions by regional central banks on monetary policy normalisation will become more complex. Central banks in some economies in the region with weaker growth momentum and inflation that is more sensitive to energy prices will face particularly difficult trade-offs. The pandemic has also highlighted the need for economies in the region, over the longer term, to rebuild more sustainable and resilient growth models in order to prepare for other risks such as climate change. To this end, investors need to place greater emphasis on environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Box 2 examines whether changes in climate risk affect stock market returns, and how such sensitivity is influenced by firms’ environmental performance. The COVID pandemic caused a massive shock to global financial markets in March 2020. During this period of market turmoil, some open‑ended funds experienced large capital outflows (Chart B1.1), putting pressure on their liquidity management. Chart B1.1 Capital outflows from selected open‑ended funds during the March 2020 episode  Apart from investors’ liquidity needs, another reason for large capital outflows may have been that investors exercised a “first-mover advantage” by redeeming fund shares early in order to avoid bearing the potentially sharply higher redemption costs under stressed market conditions. To curb outflows caused by the first-mover advantage, some open‑ended funds adopted swing pricing – a pricing rule for open‑ended funds aimed at reducing investors’ first-mover advantage. Although many open‑ended funds used swing pricing during this episode, there has been no empirical study showing whether swing pricing can effectively reduce outflows from open‑ended funds. Against this background, this box conducts an empirical study to examine whether swing pricing was able to reduce capital outflows from open‑ended funds during the March 2020 episode, thereby lowering their liquidity risk. In addition, this box also seeks to identify factors that may limit the effectiveness of swing pricing under market stress. Based on these assessments, we offer policy recommendations from a financial stability perspective. The first-mover advantage refers to investors redeeming earlier than other investors and thereby shifting redemption costs onto them. The first-mover advantage mainly exists in open‑ended funds that use traditional pricing rules, under which the subscription and redemption costs of fund investors (such as transaction costs arising from portfolio rebalancing) are reflected in the price of the open‑ended fund only after the transactions take place. Under this pricing mechanism, investors who redeem their shares first do not have to bear these transaction costs. This gives them an incentive to redeem their fund holdings early, especially when large redemption costs are anticipated. Therefore, in times of market stress, the first-mover advantage becomes more pronounced because redemption costs are expected to rise. This amplifies the redemption pressure and liquidity risk faced by open‑ended funds.

With the continued growth in merchandise exports and private consumption, Hong Kong’s economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, registering its first full-year positive growth since 2019. Entering 2022, a new wave of local infections and the resulting tightening of social-distancing measures put pressure on Hong Kong’s economic activities. It is expected that the overall economy will continue to recover in aggregate for the whole of 2022, but the strength and pace of the recovery will be affected by uncertainties and risks such as the pandemic and the normalisation of US monetary policy. These adverse factors may also affect the labour market outlook, which had improved significantly in 2021. Although local inflation may edge up slightly in the short term as import prices rise, weak local rents and labour costs should help contain overall price pressures. Hong Kong’s economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021. In year-on-year terms, real GDP grew further by 5.5% in the third quarter and by 4.8% in the fourth quarter (Table 3. A), though the pace of growth slowed compared with the first half of the year. For 2021 as a whole, real GDP expanded by 6.4%, marking the first full-year positive growth since 2019. Domestically, improving labour market conditions, together with the Government’s Consumption Voucher Scheme, boosted private consumption. However, overall investment spending retreated in the last quarter after having rebounded strongly for two consecutive quarters. Externally, with the global economy continuing to recover, Hong Kong’s merchandise trade performance remained strong, while trade in services stayed weak, partly because inbound tourism remained at a standstill (Figure 3.2). In net terms, external trade dragged on GDP in the third quarter, but contributed to GDP growth in the fourth quarter. The Government launched the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund and introduced additional countercyclical measures under the 2022–23 Budget to support the economy. To support cash flow, the “100% Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme” and various guaranteed products under the “SME Financing Guarantee Scheme” will be enhanced, with higher maximum loan amounts and extended application and repayment periods. The HKMA, together with the banking sector, also extended the “Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme” to end-October 2022. The scheme also provides borrowers with an option of partial principal repayment for one year, which likewise applies to loans under the “SME Financing Guarantee Scheme”. It is expected that Hong Kong’s economy will continue to recover in aggregate for the whole of 2022, but the pace of growth will be slower than in 2021, partly reflecting a slowdown in global economic growth amid the ongoing pandemic and the effect of a higher base. The Government’s promotion of various major works and infrastructure projects will also provide support to the economy. The Government forecasts that real GDP will grow by 2.0% to 3.5% in 2022, while the average growth forecast by international organisations and private-sector analysts is 1.6%. However, the strength and pace of Hong Kong’s economic recovery are affected by numerous uncertainties and risks discussed in earlier chapters. In particular, the recent developments of the pandemic, the faster pace of US monetary policy normalisation, and heightened geopolitical tensions (such as the Russia–Ukraine situation) have cast a shadow over the near-term economic outlook for Hong Kong and the world. On the other hand, if quarantine-free cross-boundary travel between Hong Kong and the Mainland can resume earlier than expected, it could stimulate local economic growth. With the economic recovery, the labour market further improved in the second half of 2021, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling to 3.9% by the end of the year (Figure 3.3). Overall employment in December 2021 also rebounded by 2.0% from the recent low in February 2021, though it remained below its pre-pandemic level. In early 2022, official data indicated that pressures in the labour market re-emerged amid a new wave of local infections. In addition, the decline in the number of online job advertisements also reflected a decrease in new job vacancies. Looking ahead, the new wave of local infections and the tightening of anti-epidemic measures will exert some short-term pressure on the local labour market, especially in sectors involving face-to-face contact. In the longer term, labour market conditions will depend on the evolution of the local epidemic and the pace of local economic recovery. In year-on-year terms, the underlying consumer price inflation rate edged up to 1.1% and 1.2% in the 3rd and 4th quarters of 2021 respectively, and stood at 1.2% in January 2022 (Figure 3.4). The three-month-on-three-month underlying inflation rate, expressed at an annualised rate and indicative of inflation momentum, also picked up in recent months. Specifically, as local demand recovered and external prices rose (Figure 3.5), prices for eating out and some energy-related items increased at a faster pace. At the same time, the housing rental component in the Composite Consumer Price Index continued to decline broadly, thereby restraining overall inflation momentum (Figure 3.6). Although real unit labour costs remained weak, they edged up slightly in recent quarters, partly due to some improvement in real average wages (Figure 3.7). The Hong Kong dollar (HKD) exchange rate softened during the review period amid risk-off sentiment in the local stock market and concerns about the normalisation of US monetary policy. Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) remained low amid abundant HKD liquidity. Overall, the HKD foreign exchange and money markets continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. Looking ahead, while uncertainties surrounding US monetary policy, the pandemic and escalating geopolitical tensions could heighten fund flow volatility, Hong Kong is well positioned to withstand the shocks from fund flow volatility with its ample foreign currency reserves and robust banking system. While the HKD rebounded slightly in 2021 10 on improved market sentiment, the rally lost steam thereafter, mainly due to weak net southbound fund inflows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connects (Chart 4.2) and market expectations of a stronger US dollar on the back of a more hawkish monetary policy outlook of the US Federal Reserve. IPO activities continued to provide support to the HKD during the review period (Chart 4.3). Total deposits grew moderately during the review period, with no obvious signs of fund outflows from the banking system. Meanwhile, the latest Balance of Payments figures showed that direct investment from non-residents continued to flow into Hong Kong in the second half of 2021, and there were no signs of abnormal cross-border fund flows. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant may pose a threat to economic recovery, coupled with the risk that the pace of normalization of U. S. monetary policy may be faster than expected; both factors will pose challenges to the credit risk management of banks. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of relevant risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios.
