Climate change affects every aspect of life, and everyone has a responsibility to contribute to mitigating its impacts. To this end, the HKMA has invested significant effort in promoting Hong Kong's climate goals and contributing to enhancing global climate resilience and sustainable development. Following the inclusion of our first sustainability report as a chapter in the HKMA's Annual Report last year, we are publishing the Sustainability Report separately for the first time this year. I hope this report allows readers to gain a deeper understanding of the HKMA's work strategies and priorities in strengthening the banking system's ability to cope with climate change, building a green finance ecosystem, and fulfilling our role as a responsible investor and a sustainable development institution. During the year, we made significant progress in advancing sustainability work across the HKMA's major functions. Readers will learn about our specific measures and work in this report, with key highlights including the following:  Banks' daily operations face climate risks. As the banking regulator, the HKMA has taken specific measures to strengthen the ability of banks to cope with climate change. In 2022, we formulated a two-year plan to incorporate climate risk factors into regulatory procedures and researched how to leverage the power of technology to assist banks in assessing the impacts of physical risks. Recognizing that banks are launching more green and sustainable products, we also shared best practices with the industry on how to properly manage these products to facilitate banks in enhancing their climate risk management capabilities. The HKMA actively participates in various collaborative initiatives related to addressing climate risks and promoting sustainable finance development. Locally, we are working with other financial regulatory authorities through the "Inter-agency Working Group on Green and Sustainable Finance" (the Working Group) to develop a local green taxonomy; the framework will increase transparency in the financial markets and make green finance policies more consistent. Internationally, we are actively participating in several different international organizations to assist in formulating policies to address climate change and assessing its impact on financial stability. Hong Kong is well-positioned to meet the demand for green and sustainable financing in the Asian region. Despite 2022 being a challenging year for the global bond market, the amount of green and sustainable debt issuance in Hong Kong continued to record robust growth, with an increase of 42%, bringing the total issuance amount to US$805 billion, making it the largest hub in Asia for arranging international green and sustainable bond issuances². Relevant issuers include the People's Government of Shenzhen Municipality and the People's Government of Hainan Province, whose issuances once again demonstrate Hong Kong's unique role in facilitating the flow of green and sustainable finance between the Mainland and the international community. The flourishing of Hong Kong's green bond market is partly attributed to the government's green bond program. Since 2019, the HKMA has assisted the government in issuing green bonds totaling nearly US$160 billion, with the proceeds allocated to more than 40 green government projects, including green buildings, waste management and resource recycling, energy efficiency, and energy saving. We also assisted the government in achieving "firsts" in two areas, including assisting the government in May 2022 to issue the first batch of government green retail bonds worth HK$200 billion, which was the largest green retail bond issuance globally at that time. Additionally, we assisted the government in issuing the first batch of tokenized green bonds in February 2023. This was the world's first batch of tokenized green bonds issued by a government, and this issuance also marked a milestone in our successful integration of strengths in the bond market, green and sustainable finance, and financial technology. Standards, data, and talent are indispensable elements for the healthy development of the climate finance ecosystem, and they rely on the efforts and cooperation of different sectors to be established. To this end, the HKMA primarily expands the aforementioned elements through cooperation with the Supervisory Team and other relevant government departments, regulatory bodies, academic institutions, and the financial industry. In addition to the development of a local green taxonomy as mentioned above, the Supervisory Team also promotes industry skills training and improves Hong Kong's data resources through the "Green and Sustainable Finance Centre" established under it. Furthermore, the Supervisory Team has made good progress in other areas, such as the mandatory disclosure of climate-related information and carbon market opportunities. In 2022, the HKMA further strengthened the work of the Exchange Fund in terms of responsible investment, specifically setting a target for the Exchange Fund's investment portfolio to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. At the same time, we have optimized risk management to enhance the climate resilience and risk-adjusted long-term returns of the Exchange Fund. Additionally, to fully seize the opportunities that climate change may bring, we are committed to promoting sustainable investments for the Exchange Fund, identifying investment opportunities that help support climate transition and mitigate climate change to improve the long-term returns of the portfolio. By the end of 2021, the weighted average carbon intensity of the Exchange Fund's equity portfolio had decreased by 43% compared to 2017 levels. In fact, the Exchange Fund's risk exposure to high-carbon assets remains consistently lower than that of the overall market. In the future, we will continue to move towards the net-zero emissions goal by constantly strengthening the integration of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors into the investment management process, actively exercising asset ownership, continuing to cooperate with various stakeholders, and focusing on the decarbonization and transition of the investment portfolio. At the HKMA, the "Institutional Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee," chaired by me, is responsible for formulating the HKMA's sustainability strategy. Our strategic direction is based on three pillars: environment, employees, and social responsibility. Regarding the environment, we are committed to promoting a green working environment and promoting more environmentally friendly markets to the general public; regarding employees, as a responsible and caring employer, we actively create a healthy and inclusive work environment; and regarding social responsibility, we are committed to improving the public's level of financial literacy, promoting financial inclusion, and actively giving back to society. Compared to the levels when we began tracking our carbon footprint in 2015, our per capita greenhouse gas emissions, energy consumption, and paper usage in 2022 achieved double-digit reductions. More importantly, we have formulated a roadmap to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. In the short term, our goal is to completely eliminate Scope 1 emissions and, using 2015 as a baseline, reduce Scope 2 emissions by 63% by 2030 or earlier. Addressing climate change and promoting sustainable development requires continuous efforts and cooperation from all parties. On this important global issue, we understand that we must lead by example and work together with like-minded peers and international organizations. In the next section, we will outline the HKMA's short-term plans and work priorities in addressing climate change under its major functions. Achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier is a daunting task, and we will do our utmost to achieve this goal. We are confident that with the collective efforts of all colleagues, the financial industry, and the general public, we can successfully respond to future climate challenges. Chief Executive, Christopher Cheung

In 2023, the HKMA will continue to promote the sustainable development of Hong Kong's financial industry and fulfil its responsibilities as a responsible investor and a sustainable organisation. At the same time, through participation in international and regional organisations, the HKMA will also strive to promote the broad development and best practices of green and sustainable finance. As the regulator of the banking industry, we will work to strengthen the climate resilience of the banking sector and further improve our green finance ecosystem to support the green transition of banks. Specifically, the HKMA will communicate with banks to understand their progress in implementing regulatory requirements for climate risk management, incorporate climate factors into our supervisory review process, and revise the banking industry's Common Assessment Framework for Green and Sustainable Banking. At the same time, the HKMA will support banks in their efforts to enhance climate resilience and risk management capabilities, such as exploring different measures and technological solutions to help banks identify, measure, and monitor their climate risk exposures. The HKMA will also collaborate with banks to conduct the next round of climate risk stress tests as part of the regular supervisor-led stress tests for the 2023 to 2024 period. Participating banks will be required to assess their ability to cope with climate risks under an enhanced stress testing framework that covers a variety of stress scenarios, including extreme weather and adverse economic conditions. To promote the healthy development of banks in providing green and sustainable investment products, the HKMA will keep abreast of local and international market and regulatory developments, and maintain communication with the industry to provide guidance on the sales process in a timely manner. We will also conduct off-site thematic reviews to gain a comprehensive understanding of the green and sustainable investment products offered by banks. Meanwhile, to enhance the development of the green finance ecosystem to support the green transition of the financial industry, the HKMA is planning to consult the industry on the structure and core elements of a local green classification framework. In terms of market development, to promote Hong Kong as a green and sustainable finance hub in the region, the HKMA will assist the Government in expanding the issuance size of green bonds under the Government Green Bond Programme and broadening the scope of the programme to cover sustainability bonds; at the same time, it will attract more green financing activities to be conducted in Hong Kong through the Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme. The HKMA is also assisting in the implementation of the Government-funded Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Support Scheme to expand Hong Kong's green finance talent pool. In addition, the HKMA will continue to encourage more Mainland local governments, institutions, and enterprises to conduct green financing through Hong Kong, and explore the feasibility of combining green finance and technology. On the other hand, we will continue to collaborate with other institutional departments on cross-sectoral issues such as skills training and data, green taxonomy, climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, and carbon market opportunities through the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group. Through the Alliance for Green Commercial Banks, the HKMA will jointly launch various special projects with the International Finance Corporation in Asia, including conducting green finance research, providing unique market analysis, offering targeted professional training for banks, and providing practical guidance to help banks develop roadmaps to make green finance a core business. Looking ahead, the Alliance will work closely with its cornerstone members, global partners, and knowledge partners to launch a membership programme to expand the Alliance's influence in the Asian region. At the same time, the Alliance will also enhance the professional capabilities of industry practitioners, promote the sharing of green finance knowledge, and lead the development of project plans in new areas. As a responsible investor, the HKMA has set a target for the Exchange Fund's investment portfolio to achieve net-zero emissions by or before 2050, as part of its commitment to participating in global climate action and implementing the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures. Looking ahead, the HKMA will continue to incorporate environmental, social, and governance factors into its investment management process, strive to achieve its net-zero emissions target, and fully support global climate action efforts. As a responsible and sustainable organisation, the HKMA cares for its employees as well as the wider community and the surrounding environment. We have developed a sustainability roadmap and set climate targets for our own operations as part of our commitment to participating in global decarbonisation and climate action efforts. The HKMA will continue to prioritise carbon reduction and encourage full support from its staff to save energy and reduce waste. In addition, we will provide further guidance to our staff on incorporating sustainability principles into the procurement process. To achieve digital transformation and enhance operational flexibility, the HKMA will explore ways to modernise its internal systems and applications to further improve work efficiency while minimising potential risks that may arise during the digital transformation process.

Climate change represents a significant risk for the financial system. The HKMA has been striving to strengthen Hong Kong’s financial system to foster a greener and more sustainable future, thereby contributing to Hong Kong’s climate goals as well as the global sustainable development agenda. Banks are exposed to various sustainability- and climate-related issues in their day-to-day operations. To continue fulfilling their vital role in the financial system and to channel more funds toward green and sustainable projects, banks must proactively manage climate risks. As the banking regulator, the HKMA places special emphasis on building banks’ capacity to respond to and manage climate risks, as well as accelerating their efforts to support the transition to a low-carbon economy. The HKMA also supports banks in enhancing their ability to detect environmental crimes, and participates in the recently published Hong Kong Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Risk Assessment, which covers areas such as environmental crimes and illegal wildlife trafficking. In 2022, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (Basel Committee)1 issued principles for the effective management and supervision of climate-related financial risks, addressing common questions and clarifying how the existing Basel framework applies to such risks. In response to these international developments, the HKMA remains committed to integrating climate-related factors into its regulatory framework. Following the issuance of Module GS-1 “Climate Risk Management” in its Supervisory Policy Manual in 2021, the HKMA has maintained ongoing dialogue with banks to exchange views on expectations, progress, and challenges related to implementing relevant regulatory requirements. To further strengthen oversight of banks’ climate risk management, the HKMA has devised a two-year plan to incorporate climate risk factors into banking supervision procedures, which was communicated to the banking sector in June. As part of this two-year plan, the HKMA issued a revised version of Module SA-1 “Risk-Based Supervision” in its Supervisory Policy Manual, enhancing the CAMEL rating system by integrating climate risks into risk-based supervision processes. Meanwhile, drawing on lessons learned from a pilot programme in 2021, the HKMA has refined climate risk stress test scenarios and evaluation frameworks. The HKMA also plans to incorporate the next round of climate risk stress tests into regular supervisory stress tests, enabling a more comprehensive assessment of the banking sector’s resilience under extreme climate scenarios. Under this two-year plan, the HKMA is also strengthening its green assessment framework for banks to reflect recent developments in sustainability-related issues, including climate risk management and transition planning. Concurrently, the HKMA is reviewing its supervisory review process used to assess and monitor banks’ capital adequacy levels and determine their Pillar 2 capital requirements, with the aim of encouraging banks to enhance their risk management frameworks to address climate change and risks associated with the transition to carbon neutrality. Given the growing popularity of green and sustainable products issued by banks, the HKMA conducted a thematic review focusing on banks’ development and ongoing management of such products. During this review, several good practices were identified, and a circular was issued in December to share these practices with the industry, helping banks gradually improve their climate risk management capabilities. The application of technology can improve data availability and strengthen banks’ ability to manage climate risks. The HKMA has begun developing a common platform for banks to assess the impact of physical risks on real estate. Additionally, in collaboration with other central banks and regulators, the HKMA completed a project under the Innovation Hub of the Bank for International Settlements, exploring how technological solutions can facilitate physical risk assessments. The HKMA also attaches great importance to promoting sustainable and globally leading anti-money laundering practices; this involves the use of advanced analytics and regulatory technology, supported by fully automated regulatory data collection. Over the past 12 months, the HKMA has streamlined its anti-money laundering regulatory data collection process to reduce administrative burdens and paper usage for banks. To enhance transparency across financial markets and promote greater consistency in green finance policies, the Monetary Authority is collaborating with other financial regulators to develop a local green taxonomy. Commonly referred to as a green classification system, this taxonomy categorizes economic activities as green or sustainable, providing authorities and market participants with a reference point for determining whether a particular activity or its related products are genuinely green or sustainable. To this end, the Monetary Authority maintains close contact with industry players and other relevant stakeholders to thoroughly examine the characteristics and challenges of such a framework. It plans to put forward recommendations on the framework’s structure and core elements and conduct consultations in the first half of 2023. Recognizing that climate change may pose potential risks to the financial system, the Monetary Authority incorporates a broader range of climate-related factors and scenarios into its financial risk analysis and research, thereby strengthening its ongoing monitoring efforts. In its continuous assessment of financial stability risks, the Monetary Authority takes climate change into account and includes analyses of climate-related risks in its various financial stability reports. Through active participation in the Scenario Design and Analysis Working Group under the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), the Monetary Authority helps to further enrich climate scenarios, enabling central banks and regulators to better understand the macroeconomic and financial impacts of climate change. In terms of research, the Monetary Authority conducted several applied research projects in 2022, focusing on two main topics: greenwashing practices in the corporate green bond market and the role of disclosure in mitigating climate risks. The findings from these studies contribute to the formulation of policies and regulatory measures aimed at addressing the impact of climate risks on financial stability. Locally, they assist the Monetary Authority in continuously monitoring and evaluating how climate risks affect financial stability. Internationally, the Monetary Authority has shared these research findings with various stakeholders through multiple channels, including international central banking research seminars and its semi-annual “Monetary and Financial Stability Report.”  The Monetary Authority’s “Liquidity Arrangement Framework” is a collateralized standby funding facility designed to provide timely liquidity support to banks in need. The Authority is currently exploring the possibility of incorporating sustainability considerations into the assessment of eligible collateral under this framework. The Monetary Authority actively participates in international and regional discussions on addressing climate risks and mainstreaming sustainable finance. Through such engagement, it helps foster policy dialogue on climate change and its implications for financial stability at both international and regional levels, while also drawing valuable insights to enhance the climate resilience of Hong Kong’s financial system.

To strengthen Hong Kong’s position as a regional hub for green and sustainable finance, the HKMA has stepped up efforts to raise market awareness and participation, provide necessary infrastructure and incentives, and support international initiatives to align with global standards. The Inter-Agency Steering Group on Green and Sustainable Finance (the Steering Group), co-led by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), coordinates responses within the financial sector to climate and environmental risks, accelerates the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong, and supports the Government’s climate strategy1. The Steering Group’s work is guided by its strategic plan, which outlines 6 key focus areas and 5 action pillars aimed at strengthening Hong Kong’s financial ecosystem and fostering a greener, more sustainable future (Figure 1). These include: strengthening climate-related financial risk management to reinforce Hong Kong’s status as a global risk management hub; promoting the flow of climate-related information at all levels to facilitate risk management, capital allocation, and investor protection; enhancing relevant skills among industry professionals and raising public awareness; encouraging product innovation and research initiatives to channel funds toward green and sustainable projects; seizing business opportunities arising from the Mainland to develop Hong Kong into a green finance hub within the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area (GBA); and strengthening regional and international cooperation. To date, the Steering Group has made good progress in advancing sustainable finance in Hong Kong. Its current priorities include skills training and data collection under the Green and Sustainable Finance Centre (see below), the development of a green taxonomy (see “Establishing a green classification framework to facilitate green financing” in the chapter “Building a sustainable financial system” on page 9), climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, as well as opportunities in the carbon market. Specifically, in March the Steering Group released a preliminary feasibility assessment on opportunities in Hong Kong’s carbon market, pledging to support Hong Kong’s development as a regional carbon trading hub—including the creation of a high-quality international voluntary carbon market—and to capitalize on collaboration opportunities within the GBA. In December, the Steering Group announced a partnership with CDP2 to improve data availability in Hong Kong and enhance sustainability reporting. As part of this collaboration, both parties developed a questionnaire on climate and environmental risks targeted at non-listed companies and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). This tool not only facilitates corporate sustainability reporting but also helps financial institutions collect and analyze company-level data for risk assessment and related business decisions. This marks a significant step by the Steering Group in expanding its data initiatives to include SMEs—an important yet previously under-served segment of the economy. The Steering Group established the Green and Sustainable Finance Centre in July 2021 to coordinate efforts among financial regulators, government departments, industry stakeholders, and academic institutions in training and policy development, while also building resource platforms and databases. In the first half of 2022, the Centre launched three (3) information portals focusing on data, training resources, and internship opportunities, respectively, to help the financial sector and other industries access relevant data and learning materials on green and sustainable finance. One of these portals provides data sources for assessing physical risks in Hong Kong. To support talent development, the Centre assisted the Government in December in launching the “Pilot Scheme on Green and Sustainable Finance Training,” which offers financial assistance to practitioners, students, and graduates participating in relevant training and skill enhancement programs. Additional measures to promote skills development include the “Sustainable Finance Internship Scheme,” which creates more internship opportunities for students, and the introduction of a new “Green and Sustainable Finance” module under the HKMA’s “Professional Qualifications Framework for the Banking Industry”3 for banking professionals. The HKMA has also been actively supporting the development of green and sustainable finance throughout the region. In November 2020, the International Finance Corporation and the HKMA launched the “Green Commercial Banking Alliance”4, bringing together regional financial institutions, banking industry associations, research bodies, and technology providers to foster collaboration in green commercial banking. The Alliance aims to help commercial banks and other financial institutions fully realize their potential in making green finance a core component of their operations, thereby encouraging greater participation of the financial system in efforts to address climate change. The Alliance operates as a one-stop learning platform for financial institutions, enabling them to access essential knowledge, tools, and information needed to develop their own green finance roadmaps and transition into credible green financial institutions. It also serves as a gathering place for green finance leaders, connecting green finance institutions across emerging markets to facilitate communication and discussions on cutting-edge issues, thereby advancing the global green finance agenda and unlocking countless green and climate-related investment opportunities. In June, five leading global financial institutions5 became founding members of the Alliance. They collaborate closely with the International Finance Corporation and the HKMA to encourage clients to adopt green strategies, promote best practices in green products and services, and unlock new business opportunities—all contributing to the transition toward a green economy. Additionally, three global partners and one knowledge partner6 pledged in 2022 to provide climate expertise in areas such as innovation, standardization, and academic research. Detailed information on the Alliance and its membership structure can be found on its official webpage (English version): Founding Members. Meanwhile, the International Finance Corporation and the HKMA signed a Memorandum of Understanding. Since March 2021, the Alliance has organized 18 training sessions and roundtable discussions, attracting over 6,000 participants from across the Asia-Pacific region, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and the Americas. In June 2022, the Alliance, together with the Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s Research Institute7, released its first research report on a cutting-edge topic: “Climate Risks: Definition, Measurement, Current Practices, and Regulation.” The HKMA has consistently promoted the issuance of green and sustainable debt while fostering a local ecosystem of related professional services. In 2022, the total value of green and sustainable debt issued in Hong Kong—including bonds and loans—reached USD 805 billion, marking a 42% increase. +42% Value of green and sustainable debt issued (USD 805 billion) To demonstrate its commitment to tackling climate change and to promote green finance while striving to develop Hong Kong into a more sustainable and livable city, the Government launched the “Government Green Bond Programme” in 2018, with the HKMA assisting in the issuance of related green bonds. To date, the Government has issued green bonds equivalent to nearly USD 160 billion, with proceeds allocated to over 40 green government projects covering areas such as green building, waste management and recycling, energy efficiency, and energy conservation. To enhance transparency and accountability, the Government publishes an annual “Green Bond Report” detailing how funds raised through green bonds are allocated and their anticipated environmental benefits. To enable the general public to participate in Hong Kong’s sustainable development through investment and share in its benefits, the first batch of retail green bonds worth HKD 200 billion was issued in May. These bonds received enthusiastic response from the public, making them the largest retail green bond issuance globally at the time. This issuance also expanded the range of green and sustainable financial products available in Hong Kong, further cementing its status as a leading green finance hub both regionally and internationally. During the 2022–23 fiscal year, the Government continued its regular issuance of institutional green bonds, issuing bonds equivalent to USD 57.5 billion in January 2023. This multi-currency issuance involved USD, EUR, and RMB, with maturities ranging from 2 to 30 years, thereby providing an important benchmark for potential issuers in Hong Kong and the wider region. The issuance was well received by global investors and successfully attracted new investors who had not previously participated in any Government green bond offerings, reflecting strong confidence in Hong Kong’s long-term creditworthiness and economic fundamentals. Responding to investor demand, the Government doubled the RMB-denominated bond issuance volume to RMB 100 billion. Both international investors and Mainland investors participating via the Bond Connect “Southbound Channel” saw their share increase, underscoring Hong Kong’s role as a premier offshore RMB hub and further reinforcing its position as a leading international financial centre. In February 2023, the HKMA also assisted the Government in issuing tokenized institutional green bonds, serving as a test case for utilizing distributed ledger technology in bond issuance and settlement. These were among the world’s first tokenized green bonds issued by a government. The primary issuance was settled on a T+1 basis via a private blockchain network, with subsequent processes—including coupon payments, secondary market transactions, and redemption at maturity—also digitized. The Government’s experience with this issuance serves as a valuable reference for other market participants interested in similar bond offerings in the future. To provide the industry with credible and accessible market information, the HKMA continues to collaborate with the Climate Bonds Initiative and the International Capital Market Association to publish annual reports on Hong Kong’s and the region’s green debt markets. According to the report by the International Capital Market Association, Hong Kong emerged in 2022 as the leading hub in Asia for arranging international green and sustainable bond issuances. The total value of bonds issued through Hong Kong reached USD 278 billion, accounting for over one-third of the regional total. Following its inaugural issuance in 2021, the Shenzhen Municipal People’s Government issued another RMB 50 billion in offshore local government bonds in Hong Kong in November 2022; this issuance included RMB 26 billion worth of green and blue bonds8. In the same month, the Hainan Provincial People’s Government also made its debut in Hong Kong by issuing RMB 50 billion in offshore bonds, which comprised blue and sustainable bonds. These bond issuances once again highlight Hong Kong’s unique role in facilitating the flow of green and sustainable financing between the Chinese mainland and the rest of the world, as well as its enduring status as the region’s premier fundraising platform. The HKMA continues to promote and implement the “Green and Sustainable Finance Subsidy Scheme” launched in 2021, utilizing it to attract more relevant professional service providers—including financial institutions, green consultancy firms, and external review agencies—to establish or expand their operations in Hong Kong. The Scheme has been widely welcomed by the industry. By the end of 2022, it had subsidized external review costs for over 180 issuers of green and sustainable debt instruments, both prior to and following issuance, thereby helping these issuers ensure compliance with market best practices and international standards. Starting in March, the Scheme was enhanced by lowering the minimum loan amount threshold for eligibility for external review subsidies from HKD 200 million to HKD 100 million, thereby facilitating access to green financing for smaller enterprises. Following the successful completion of a proof-of-concept for tokenized retail green bonds under Project Genesis in 2021, the HKMA and the Hong Kong Centre of the Bank for International Settlements Innovation Hub collaborated once more under Genesis 2.0 to explore the technical feasibility of digitizing mitigation outcome benefits (MOI), with the aim of enhancing transparency, objectivity, and environmental integrity within the green bond market. This project was completed in October 2022, resulting in the development of two prototypes capable of tracking, delivering, and transferring digitized MOI by leveraging blockchain and related technologies.

As one of the world’s largest asset owners and managers, the HKMA plays an important role in promoting the development of green and sustainable finance to support the global climate change agenda. The HKMA is also a pioneer in responsible investment. As early as 2015, it took the lead in investing in green and sustainable assets, requiring its external investment managers to adopt the Principles of Responsible Ownership issued by the Securities and Futures Commission, and integrating environmental, social and governance factors into the investment management of the Exchange Fund. The HKMA invests prudently in accordance with the principle of “capital preservation first, long-term growth thereafter”, and believes that attaching importance to environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors can unlock long-term sustainable value for investments and mitigate related risks. In the face of mounting climate change challenges, the HKMA continues to advance on its responsible investment journey, including setting a “2050 net-zero emissions” target in 2022, and enhancing risk management strategies to strengthen the resilience of the investment portfolio, thereby striving for better risk-adjusted long-term returns for the Exchange Fund. The HKMA also actively participates in building a green and sustainable finance ecosystem, working with like-minded investors and regulatory authorities to jointly promote responsible investment, and cooperating with international organisations to develop ESG investment standards. The transparency of climate-related information plays a pivotal role in managing climate risks. To fulfil its commitment in support of the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) and its “Glasgow Declaration”, announced at the United Nations Climate Change Conference in 2021, and to the greening of the global financial system, the HKMA makes climate-related disclosures in respect of the Exchange Fund in accordance with the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) under the Financial Stability Board.  a. FCLTGlobal — Focusing Capital on the Long Term b. PRI — Principles for Responsible Investment c. NGFS — Network for Greening the Financial System d. TCFD — Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures  The Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Financial Secretary, sets the responsible investment framework and guiding principles, which are implemented by the Exchange Fund Investment Office in the investment management of the Exchange Fund. The primary guiding principle is for the HKMA to give priority to ESG investments that are comparable to other projects in terms of risk-adjusted long-term returns, thereby upholding the investment objectives of the Exchange Fund. Details of the HKMA’s responsible investment framework are available on the HKMA website.  The Investment Committee under the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, is responsible for overseeing ESG- and climate-related risks involved in the Exchange Fund’s investment activities. The Investment Committee reviews the responsible investment framework and risk management approach, and monitors the progress of integrating ESG factors into investments and the ESG profile of the Exchange Fund through regular meeting reports from the Risk Management and Compliance Department of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. As shown in Diagram 1, the ESG Committee set up under the Exchange Fund Investment Office, chaired by the Chief Risk Officer, is responsible for coordinating and overseeing various ESG initiatives of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. The motions discussed and progress made at each meeting of the ESG Committee are reported to the Chief Executive Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office.  Oversight and governance framework for responsible investment  The dedicated team of the Risk Management and Compliance Department works closely with the various investment teams of the Exchange Fund Investment Office on the integration of ESG factors, and assists the senior management of the Exchange Fund Investment Office in managing ESG- and climate-related risks and opportunities across different investment activities:  Public market investments  The Credit, Regulatory and Compliance Committee, which is composed of the senior management of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, oversees the ESG profile of the fixed-income portfolios through regular reports from the Risk Management and Compliance Department. In addition, from an ESG perspective, the Risk Management and Compliance Department also participates in the selection, appointment and monitoring of external investment managers for equity portfolios (see the section “Striving to exercise asset ownership actively” in the “Risk Management” chapter on page 27 for details).  Private market investments  The Investment Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, considers ESG-related assessments made by the Risk Management and Compliance Department and the private market investment team for each investment proposal.  Concrete evidence² continues to show that the impact of climate change and related risks is significant. According to the latest report 3 of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), even on the assumption that the “Nationally Determined Contribution” targets announced by different jurisdictions are fully met, the global temperature increase is still estimated to reach as high as 2.1 to 2.4 degrees Celsius by 2100, making it difficult to achieve the goal under the Paris Agreement of limiting the increase in global average temperature to well below 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. If jurisdictions adopt more ambitious policy measures to narrow the temperature gap, the resulting transition risks⁴, together with the repricing of assets by markets based on anticipated future trends, and the inherent physical risks, will further intensify pressure on asset valuations.  In view of updates in the global warming trajectory and model assumptions, with the help of external consultants’ expertise, the HKMA, in addition to the scenarios assessed in 2021, conducted further assessment of the resilience of the Exchange Fund “Investment Portfolio” under an “accelerated transition” scenario (Diagram 2). The “accelerated transition” scenario incorporates higher transition risk factors over the short, medium and long terms, assuming that policy changes and technological developments jointly drive a rapid reduction in carbon emissions, while a wide range of assets are abruptly divested in order to keep the average temperature increase within 1.5 degrees Celsius before 2100. This scenario broadly aligns with the disorderly scenario recommended by the NGFS for forward-looking climate impact assessments. The “Investment Portfolio” can remain resilient over the medium to long term because a larger portion of its asset allocation is in sovereign bonds, which are less sensitive to transition impacts. Sectoral distribution is key. Low-carbon power and renewable energy assets can benefit from the associated transition. Transition risks and asset repricing may affect performance in the short term (especially equity assets). Overall, the “Investment Portfolio” will be increasingly affected by physical risks that materialise gradually over time. The energy and traditional utilities sectors remain the most vulnerable sectors.  Climate scenarios, like other modelling approaches, have their limitations. The analysis is based on sector distribution in market benchmarks at the strategic asset allocation level, and does not take into account the effect of active security selection within a given sector. More in-depth study shows that investments within the “Investment Portfolio” generally have stronger resilience to transition shocks, or are less affected, compared with the market benchmarks used for strategic asset allocation. This result once again confirms that the HKMA’s responsible investment efforts focused on combating climate change can enhance the resilience of the asset portfolio.  The trajectory of climate change remains uncertain, and scenario analysis methodologies will continue to evolve as data quality improves and policies develop. The HKMA will regularly review the relevant scenarios and refine the assessments to gain a clearer understanding of the Exchange Fund’s resilience to climate change.  As a long-term investor, the HKMA fully understands the risks and opportunities brought about by climate change. The HKMA is committed to further expanding sustainable investments and seizing opportunities that support climate transition, mitigate climate risks and enhance the long-term returns of the asset portfolio. In 2022, the HKMA continued its positive momentum and further increased its holdings of green, social and sustainable bonds by 50%. In terms of equity investments, the HKMA invests in an actively managed equity portfolio with a governance theme and adopts decarbonisation strategies for passive equity portfolios that tilt towards companies with lower carbon emissions. In addition, the HKMA is exploring with the dedicated general partners of the Exchange Fund’s “Long-Term Growth Portfolio” the establishment of a dedicated private equity portfolio to promote green and sustainable development in Asia (Diagram 3).  Diagram 3 Continuing measures to increase ESG investments  The HKMA has invested in a pan-African wind farm operator which, in addition to producing clean energy, places great emphasis on social factors and biodiversity in nature. Before the wind farms were set up, local villagers used poisoned bait to prevent predators from attacking their livestock, but this inadvertently endangered certain vulture species that are classified as endangered. Livestock is an important asset for local villagers. To help them protect their livestock, the operator built livestock shelters within the wind farms to protect animals from natural predators. In addition, the operator hired a bird monitoring team to issue alerts when vultures are attracted by animal carcasses occasionally left by predators, so that the wind turbines can be shut down to avoid the birds being struck by the blades. Reducing livestock predation creates a win–win situation: on the one hand, it safeguards villagers’ livelihoods, and on the other hand, it reduces cases of vultures being killed by wind turbines, thereby protecting endangered species.  Good ESG practices can bring more business opportunities and open up revenue sources for companies, as illustrated by the supply-chain-related operations below. The investee company is a Mainland China integrated logistics and warehousing operator specialising in cold-chain pharmaceutical, chemical product and high-end consumer goods logistics services. The company faces increasingly stringent ESG operating standards, mainly from multinational corporate clients that require their service providers to meet ambitious carbon reduction targets in line with the Paris Agreement. In response, the company engaged external consultants to help formulate a “three-year ESG plan” to reduce carbon emission intensity by 50% by or before 2030. This comprehensive decarbonisation plan had already delivered significant results in just 2021. These ESG measures enabled the company to receive the “Low-carbon Green Management Case” award from the China Federation of Logistics and Purchasing. These achievements and recognitions have allowed the company to secure considerable business opportunities from multinational corporate clients in the consumer and chemical products sectors that place particular emphasis on ESG practices.  The growth of ESG investments is closely related to the development of the green and sustainable finance ecosystem. The HKMA actively collaborates with like-minded investors and partners to promote responsible investment and enhance industry capabilities. In 2022, the HKMA successfully organised the 4th annual ESG workshop, exchanging good ESG practices with the 9 participating private market institutions (including general partners, limited partners and corporates), and promoting sustainable investment opportunities in the Asia-Pacific region and the Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macao Greater Bay Area. In the public markets, the HKMA has urged trading partners (mainly investment banks) to expand their ESG staffing and research capabilities, especially in Hong Kong.  Mr Howard Lee, Chief Executive Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, delivering the opening remarks at the HKMA ESG Workshop in 2022  At the international level, the HKMA actively participates in work to develop industry ESG investment standards and practices:  As one of the earliest central bank signatories to the Principles for Responsible Investment (PRI), the HKMA has taken part in a PRI-coordinated collaborative initiative among signatories to develop a standardised responsible investment due diligence questionnaire for private equity and venture capital investments 5, 6, in order to help private market investors conduct ESG assessments of general partners and investment proposals. The HKMA also participates in several working groups to support FCLTGlobal’s research, which aims to explore market-leading practices for long-term investment portfolios and decarbonising private assets, as well as the application of these practices by long-term investors. As a member of the NGFS and a supporter of the TCFD, the HKMA contributed to drafting the NGFS “Guide on Climate-Related Disclosure for Central Banks”, demonstrating its commitment to adopting good ESG practices. The HKMA also leads a workstream under the NGFS “Central Banks and Net Zero” taskforce, participating in the formulation of sustainable and responsible investment principles for the central banking community. The HKMA continues to take part in various industry forums and seminars to share its views on responsible investment and climate change strategies.  Ms Selina Liu, Chief Risk Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office (centre), speaking at a sharing session on ESG investment opportunities  Building internal capabilities is crucial for progressing further along the ESG journey. In addition to encouraging staff to take relevant courses on sustainable development and obtain related qualifications, since 2021 the HKMA has also gained knowledge and practical experience through the process of engaging external consultants to advise on leading industry practices for climate transition of investment portfolios. At the same time, the HKMA uses ESG data compiled by reputable external information providers to complement its ongoing analysis of the asset portfolio, thereby helping to strengthen the ESG resilience of the Exchange Fund.

The HKMA is committed to reducing its own carbon footprint, aiming to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier, thereby contributing to Hong Kong’s overall climate goals. While striving to promote environmental sustainability, the HKMA also fulfills its commitments to safeguarding employees’ physical and mental well-being, promoting financial inclusion, and fulfilling its social responsibilities. The HKMA endeavors to conduct its day-to-day operations in a responsible and sustainable manner. To this end, it implements the principles of sustainability under three key pillars: the environment, employees, and social responsibility (Figure 1). The Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee leads the HKMA in formulating and implementing its sustainability strategy. Chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, the Committee comprises three Deputy Chief Executives as well as representatives from the Risk Management and Supervision Department and the Corporate Development and Operations Department; it submits regular reports to the Governance Committee under the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee. Under the Committee’s guidance, various teams and working groups are responsible for planning and executing measures within their respective areas. In 2022, the Committee approved the HKMA’s climate goals for its operations and reviewed the transition roadmap towards achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. Throughout the year, the Committee continued to monitor progress on the HKMA’s green initiatives, including proposals to strengthen its sustainable procurement policies, procedures, and practices.  **Governance framework for sustainability**   In recognition of the HKMA’s dedication to environmental protection, employee welfare, and broader societal well-being, the Hong Kong Council of Social Service awarded the HKMA the “15 Years and More of Caring” badge for the 16th consecutive year. The HKMA pays close attention to its own carbon footprint and has developed internal “Green Office Guidelines” to manage the environmental impact of its operations. Environmental considerations have been integrated into the interior design, operations, and maintenance of its offices. In 2022, the Hong Kong Green Building Council awarded the HKMA a Gold rating under its BEAM Plus Indoor Certification 1.0 for certain renovated office areas. This marked the HKMA’s second green building certification following its Gold LEED certification in 2021.  **Energy consumption and greenhouse gas emissions**   The HKMA has implemented multiple energy-saving measures. In 2022, total energy consumption amounted to 4,996.4 terawatt-hours (2.8 terawatt-hours per employee), representing a 24.4% decrease compared to 2015 (Figure 1). The combined Scope 1 and Scope 2 greenhouse gas emissions totaled 2,996.4 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (1.7 tCO2e per employee), a reduction of 38.2% from 2015 levels (Figure 2).   Figure 1   Figure 2   Greenhouse gas emission intensity (Scope 1 and Scope 2)  **Paper usage and waste management**   The HKMA encourages paperless operations internally. It has also implemented a print management system requiring employees to log in to printers to confirm each print request, thereby minimizing unnecessary printing and toner usage. When printing is unavoidable, double-sided printing and black-and-white printing are encouraged. Additionally, the HKMA is currently preparing to implement an internal electronic record-keeping system. In 2022, total paper consumption stood at 20.5 tonnes (0.0114 tonnes per employee), a 65.3% drop from 2015 levels (Figure A).   Figure A: Paper consumption intensity    The HKMA continues to adhere to the “4R” principles in its waste management efforts. Apart from conventional waste, it also seeks to reduce electronic waste by adopting technological solutions such as server virtualization and private cloud infrastructure. In 2022, the HKMA engaged an external firm for the first time to conduct a waste audit, analyzing the composition of waste generated in its offices. The audit revealed that food waste constituted a significant proportion of total waste; consequently, the HKMA launched a food waste recycling program (see “Enhancing waste management” on page 41). The total volume of non-hazardous waste generated in 2022 (including general waste and recyclables) amounted to 242.0 tonnes (0.135 tonnes per person), representing a 4.8% decrease compared to 2015 (Figure 3). This fluctuation in trends was primarily caused by the implementation of work-from-home arrangements during the peak period of the COVID-19 pandemic, followed by a return to office operations after the fifth wave of infections.  Figure 3: Density of non-hazardous waste  The HKMA places great emphasis on waste reduction at the source, striving to minimize, reuse, and recycle waste. In 2022, the HKMA engaged a company for the first time to conduct a waste audit, aiming to gain a clearer understanding of the composition of waste generated in its daily operations—such as plastics, paper, metals, glass, wood, and electronic products—and to obtain recommendations for waste reduction. Based on the audit results, the HKMA launched a food waste recycling programme in November, installing food waste collection bins in all staff kitchens. The collected food waste is transported daily to an organic waste recycling centre in Hong Kong, where it is converted into renewable energy. The residues generated during this process can also be turned into compost for use in landscaping and agricultural purposes. Additionally, recycling bins have been conveniently placed throughout the office premises. The HKMA shares recycling tips with staff and pays greater attention to improving source segregation of recyclables, as well as providing guidance on handling recyclable items such as cardboard boxes, food containers, and beverage bottles. Moreover, the HKMA continues to organize activities aimed at raising staff awareness of environmental protection, explaining waste management policies, and encouraging staff to make full use of on-site recycling facilities.  Plastic items are also recycled at the organic waste recycling centre.  The HKMA operates two data centres—one for daily operations and one as a backup. Given that these centres account for a significant portion of the organization’s total energy consumption, the HKMA has adopted green design principles and various energy-saving measures, including rack-mounted air conditioning systems, LED lighting, and round-the-clock monitoring of energy efficiency. Following the completion in 2022 of a consultancy study on enhancing the environmental performance of these data centres, the HKMA is now preparing to implement the recommended measures to further improve overall energy efficiency. It has also begun preparations for obtaining green data centre certification.  Recognizing the importance of fostering a culture of sustainability, the HKMA regularly introduces programmes and activities designed to educate and motivate staff to adopt sustainable habits and green, digital working practices. The HKMA shares tips on green living and publishes annual statistics on office-wide energy consumption and paper usage, reminding staff of their individual roles in addressing environmental issues; it also encourages staff to submit suggestions related to sustainability. Under the leadership of a Senior Manager from the Administration Division, a task force comprising staff from various departments collaborates to generate ideas and concrete measures for promoting a greener working environment. Members of this task force also serve as ambassadors when new green initiatives are launched.  The HKMA encourages the wider community to adopt more environmentally friendly practices, implementing multiple measures to enhance operational efficiency across the HKMA, the financial sector, and the broader economy while minimizing resource consumption. The HKMA’s “System for the Electronic Transmission of Returns” (STET) serves as a one-stop platform enabling banks to submit various periodic reports—weekly, monthly, quarterly, or annually—electronically to the HKMA. Another system, “e-Delivery”, provides a secure electronic communication channel through which the HKMA disseminates circulars, guidelines, and other information to banks. Both systems contribute to substantial paper savings each year. In handling bank complaints and enforcement activities, the HKMA has also taken steps to support paperless document submission; bank customers can now lodge complaints via electronic channels by filling out online forms. Additionally, the HKMA is currently developing a next-generation management information system to streamline complaint handling and facilitate the transition from paper-based to digital records. To reduce paper usage, the Central Moneymarkets Unit (CMU) has adopted digital signatures in its daily communications with participants, including the issuance of circulars, account opening and closure letters, and responses to audit confirmations. Looking ahead, the CMU will continue to explore further green initiatives, such as implementing automated electronic processes for both internal and external communications. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) promotes the use of the Faster Payment System (FPS) and stored value payment instruments to encourage the public to adopt electronic payment methods as alternatives to cash and physical cheques. More information on FPS and stored value payment instruments can be found in the “Hong Kong as an International Financial Centre” chapter of the HKMA’s 2022 Annual Report. Sending electronic red envelopes is simple and convenient; it also reduces the need for physical red envelope covers and cash, thereby contributing to Hong Kong’s sustainable development. To this end, the HKMA continues to actively promote this practice across various social and traditional media platforms, encouraging the public to use FPS or other e-wallet services via online or mobile banking during the Lunar New Year to send electronic red envelopes. Major banks and e-wallet operators have also launched various campaigns to attract users to use electronic red envelopes, such as offering festive user interfaces, enhancing functionality for greater convenience, and running prize draws or cash rebates. While promoting electronic red envelopes on social media, the HKMA still encourages those who prefer to give physical red envelopes to use “new-old notes”—that is, banknotes that are old but still in good condition—for this purpose. The use of such notes helps reduce the need for printing new banknotes, thereby minimizing environmental impact. Feedback from note-issuing banks indicates that the public has increasingly accepted the use of new-old notes in recent years. The Coin Collection Programme reflects the HKMA’s efforts in promoting coin recycling. Coins collected through this programme are returned to circulation to meet public demand, improving coin circulation efficiency and reducing the need for minting new coins. The programme operates two coin collection vans; to date, they have served over 1 million people, collecting more than 800 million coins with a total face value of approximately HK$1.3 billion. In 2022, around 78% of users chose to convert part or all of their collected coins into credit for their stored value payment accounts. The HKMA maintains close cooperation with the Hong Kong Council of Social Service by deploying coin collection vans on the NGO Flag Day to support social welfare initiatives. Launched in 2014, the Coin Collection Programme is the world’s first systematic coin collection programme utilizing mobile vans; over the years, it has received numerous local and international awards in recognition of its innovative and environmentally friendly approach to coin processing. Each of the two vans is equipped with two high-speed coin counters to collect coins exchanged by the public. Individuals may opt to exchange their coins for cash, add them to their stored value payment accounts (such as Octopus cards or e-wallets), or donate them to charitable causes. Besides coin collection, the vans are occasionally utilized for various educational activities, such as school visits.

The purpose of this verification was to confirm whether the Climate Targets were developed in compliance with the SBTi Corporate Handbook. The verification procedures were designed to provide reasonable assurance through the issuance of an opinion and conclusions. The verification process followed all requirements outlined in the SBTi Corporate Handbook. The HKMA was responsible for data collection and reporting. Our verification work was completely independent and impartial. Based on the results of this verification, the Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency can provide reasonable assurance and concludes that:   • The Climate Targets were formulated in accordance with the SBTi Corporate Handbook. Shen Xiaoyin   Head of Assurance   Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency   March 2023    The Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency also conducted an independent verification of the HKMA’s environmental data for 2022 (“2022 Data”). The 2022 Data includes total energy consumption in 2022, greenhouse gas emission intensity under Scope 1 and Scope 2, paper consumption intensity, non-hazardous waste generation intensity and recycling rates, as well as changes in these figures compared to 2015 levels. The HKMA’s greenhouse gas emission data was compiled in accordance with the Greenhouse Gas Protocol jointly developed by the World Resources Institute (“WRI”) and the World Business Council for Sustainable Development (“WBCSD”). The verification covered data from January 1, 2022, to December 31, 2022, as well as relevant data from January 1, 2015, to December 31, 2015, used for annual performance comparisons. The verification scope covered a total of 6 office and warehouse assets: 4 offices at 1) Two International Finance Centre, 2) Hopewell Centre, 3) One Pacific Place, and 4) Kowloon Trade Centre, and 2 warehouses at 5) Lok Sing Industrial Centre and 6) Chong Lee Centre, located in Kwai Chung and Tsuen Wan respectively. The purpose of the verification was to provide reasonable assurance regarding the accuracy and reliability of the 2022 Data, as well as to assess the adequacy of the HKMA’s data collection mechanisms. Within the verification scope, the Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency examined representative data and supporting evidence drawn from 6 assets. This verification was conducted in accordance with the “Assurance Engagements Other Than Audits or Reviews of Historical Financial Information” provisions of the International Standard on Assurance Engagements 3000 (Revised) issued by the International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board. The procedures were designed to yield reasonable assurance through the issuance of an opinion and conclusions. The verification process adhered to all requirements stipulated in the Greenhouse Gas Protocol. To test data integrity and accuracy, the process involved tracing selected sample data back to their sources; it also evaluated basic procedures related to data collection, aggregation, estimation, calculation, and internal checks, while conducting reliability tests. Additionally, the internal data collection and management mechanisms were assessed, and interviews were held with personnel responsible for preparing the 2022 Data; representative data and documentation were then examined. All relevant raw data and supporting evidence underwent thorough review during the verification process. The HKMA remained responsible for data collection and reporting. Our verification work was completely independent and impartial. The verification team from the Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency had no involvement whatsoever in the preparation of the 2022 Data. Based on the results of this verification, the Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency can provide reasonable assurance on the 2022 Data and concludes that: • The 2022 Data is substantially accurate and reliable; • The HKMA’s overall data collection mechanisms are adequate. Shen Xiaoyin   Head of Assurance   Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency   March 2023

Scaling up and accelerating climate action has become the most urgent task at hand. Nearly half of the critical 10-year period for addressing the climate crisis has already elapsed. To keep global warming within 1.5 degrees Celsius, we must reduce global carbon emissions by over 40% during this 10-year period. Yet greenhouse gas emissions continue to reach new highs. Recent climate science research indicates that the window of opportunity to limit global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius is rapidly closing. The effects of a 1.1-degree increase in temperature are already evident worldwide: record-breaking heatwaves and droughts, as well as severe flooding and storms, are occurring more frequently and with greater intensity across the globe. Hong Kong is no exception; last September, following a powerful super typhoon, we experienced a once-in-a-century downpour. Despite having robust infrastructure and rapid disaster-response capabilities, the impact was still severe—widespread flooding, disrupted transportation, and extensive road damage. All these events serve as a stark reminder that decisive and proactive climate action is imperative. Asia faces particularly significant challenges in its low-carbon transition, especially in balancing economic development with sustainability. We need credible transition strategies that appropriately reconcile climate action with economic growth and social inclusiveness. This is no easy task. Given the region’s rapid economic growth and burgeoning population, it accounts for over half of global carbon emissions. Moreover, Asia-Pacific’s high population density and geographical characteristics render it highly vulnerable to rising sea levels and extreme weather events. As economies within the region develop at varying paces, while low-carbon transition offers new opportunities for some, it poses a major challenge for others in securing the necessary funding. Market estimates suggest that Asia-Pacific will require over $3 trillion annually in low-carbon transition investments over the next 30 years. As an international financial hub, Hong Kong possesses both the capability and responsibility to leverage finance to support low-carbon transition across Asia. As a banking regulator, market facilitator, and responsible investor, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has consistently dedicated substantial efforts to advancing the sustainability agenda. Readers will find details of specific measures and initiatives undertaken by the HKMA over the past year in the subsequent chapters of this report. To strengthen internal governance and better coordinate sustainability efforts across various functions, we established the Green and Sustainable Development Steering Committee last year. Further information on this committee can be found in the newly added chapter on “Governance of Sustainable Development.”  Hong Kong’s banking sector plays a pivotal role in supporting Asia’s transition to net-zero emissions. Beyond fulfilling its traditional regulatory duties by ensuring banks properly manage climate risks, the HKMA also acts as a facilitator, helping the banking sector provide financing for low-carbon transition. One example is the development of a green taxonomy designed to assist banks and other financial institutions in identifying environmentally sustainable activities, thereby aligning their business decisions with global climate goals. In May, we released a prototype of this taxonomy for public consultation, and we are currently refining it based on feedback received. Additionally, given the growing demand for higher-quality and globally comparable sustainability disclosures, the HKMA is collaborating with other regulators to develop a clear roadmap for Hong Kong to adopt the disclosure standards issued in June by the International Sustainability Standards Board—a comprehensive global benchmark for sustainability reporting. The HKMA’s role as a facilitator extends beyond crafting frameworks and rules; we also strive to address practical challenges faced by the industry. Currently, many banks struggle to conduct physical risk assessments due to data limitations. To address this, the HKMA will soon launch a cloud-based physical risk assessment platform. By simply entering a property address, banks will be able to evaluate how physical disasters might affect residential and commercial buildings in Hong Kong under various climate scenarios, thereby aiding them in managing related climate risks. As a leading international financial center and hub for sustainable finance in Asia, Hong Kong continues to serve as a bridge, channeling international investment toward sustainable development projects in the region and supporting its low-carbon transition. In recent years, international green and sustainable bonds issued in Hong Kong have accounted for over one-third of the total volume in the Asian market, placing us well ahead of other regions. Notably, in 2023, the Shenzhen Municipal Government and the Hainan Provincial Government issued green and sustainable bonds in Hong Kong for the 3rd and 2nd consecutive years respectively, reaffirming Hong Kong’s vital role as a green gateway linking the Chinese mainland with the rest of the world. The robust growth of sustainable bond activities in Hong Kong can be partly attributed to the exemplary role played by the Government Green Bond Programme. Since 2019, the HKMA has assisted the government in issuing green bonds worth approximately US$250 billion, which were sold to both institutional and retail investors. We have seized every issuance opportunity to continuously innovate and expand the features of green bonds—including currency options, tenors, and distribution channels—thereby laying the groundwork for other public and private green bond issuers in the region. Following the issuance of the world’s largest government retail green bond in 2022, we launched the world’s first batch of tokenized government green bonds in February 2023. In February 2024, we completed the issuance of a second batch of tokenized green bonds; denominated in four major currencies and issued in a digital-native format, these bonds represent the world’s first multi-currency digital green bonds. Simultaneously, we have proactively introduced various measures to enhance the vibrancy and competitiveness of Hong Kong’s sustainable finance ecosystem. These efforts span multiple areas, including skills training, data enhancement, green fintech, and transition finance. In particular, regarding talent development, we introduced a new “Green and Sustainable Finance” module under the Banking Professional Qualifications Framework in 2023, offering bank professionals systematic training to deepen their understanding and expertise in this field. Transition finance constitutes another key priority area; it aims to provide funding for decarbonization efforts in high-carbon and hard-to-abate industries, thereby preventing these sectors from being left behind due to lack of financial support. To foster the healthy development of transition finance, the HKMA will expand its Green Taxonomy to include transition activities. We will also broaden the scope of the Green and Sustainable Finance Subsidy Scheme—which provides financial assistance to eligible bond issuers and borrowers—to cover transition bonds and loans, thereby encouraging regional enterprises to raise transition financing in Hong Kong. Furthermore, we will strengthen engagement with relevant stakeholders, leveraging public-private partnerships and blended finance models to attract private investment toward sustainable development projects that have historically faced financing difficulties. Certain aspects of these initiatives necessitate cross-sector collaboration and are primarily coordinated by the Inter-Agency Steering Group on Green and Sustainable Finance, co-chaired by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission. Regional cooperation remains equally important. Beyond our long-standing partnership with the International Finance Corporation under the Green Commercial Banking Alliance, the HKMA’s Infrastructure Financing Facilitation Office became a founding member in 2023 of both the Sustainable Investment Capacity Building Alliance and the Green Development Investment and Financing Partnership. Additionally, the Glasgow Net Zero Financial Alliance has announced plans to establish a regional chapter in Hong Kong. Through these collaborations, we aim to promote skills development and knowledge sharing, ultimately facilitating the flow of capital toward sustainable projects both regionally and globally. To foster new business opportunities and knowledge exchange, the HKMA helped organize the inaugural “Hong Kong Green Week” earlier this year, attracting over 1,600 participants from nearly 30 regions, including top decision-makers from the global business and financial communities. The event served as a platform for discussing ways to expand climate financing in the region and forging new partnerships. In his keynote address at the “Asia-Pacific Climate Business Forum”—a flagship event of the Green Week—Mr. Eddie Yue, Chief Executive of the HKMA, emphasized that as custodian of Hong Kong’s official reserves and a major global asset owner, the HKMA leads by example as a responsible investor. Since 2015, the HKMA has been at the forefront of investing in green and sustainable assets, gradually expanding the Exchange Fund’s ESG and green portfolios in both public and private markets. In pursuit of its goal to achieve net-zero emissions across its portfolio by 2050, the HKMA launched last year an active global equity portfolio focused on sustainability and climate transition, while also extending the application of a customized low-carbon equity index to another public market portfolio. Moreover, the HKMA’s investments in green, social, and sustainability bonds have consistently outperformed benchmarks, embodying the principle of “doing well by doing good.” In the private markets, we continue to pursue green-related investment opportunities, having become an anchor investor in two Asia-focused transition investment funds. By end-2022, the weighted average carbon intensity (WACI) of the Exchange Fund’s equity portfolio had declined by 6% and 46% compared to 2021 and 2017 levels respectively, remaining consistently below the overall market average. As a sustainability-oriented institution, the HKMA remains committed to continuous improvement, setting our sustainability goals and initiatives based on three core pillars: the environment, employees, and social responsibility. Specifically, on our journey toward a low-carbon transition, we continually strengthen our capacity to address climate change by evaluating our environmental performance and implementing various internal measures. These measures encompass emissions reduction, energy efficiency enhancement, and waste management, all aimed at fulfilling our commitment to achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. We have formulated plans to completely eliminate Scope 1 emissions in the near term, and we are making good progress toward our mid-term target of reducing Scope 2 emissions by 2030. To attract and retain top talent for fulfilling the HKMA’s vital functions, we also prioritize promoting employees’ physical and mental well-being alongside our green objectives. Additionally, through collaboration with various stakeholders, we strive to advance financial inclusion, improve public financial literacy, and raise awareness of financial fraud prevention, thereby contributing to the creation of a caring society. The challenges posed by climate change are immense and highly urgent. Economies worldwide are moving toward a more sustainable future, a transition expected to bring profound changes to financing activities and asset allocation. While this shift entails considerable risks, it also presents unprecedented opportunities. As a leading global hub for sustainable finance, Hong Kong bears the responsibility of spearheading efforts to tackle these challenges. We are also well-positioned to capitalize on this trend. The HKMA will fully support the industry in financing the low-carbon transition; as a responsible investor and sustainability-focused institution, we will lead by example and collaborate with like-minded partners to advance this critically important global agenda. Eddie Yue, Chief Executive

Climate change risks and other sustainability issues are of global concern. The HKMA’s objective in its sustainability efforts is to play a leading role through its policies and operations, ensuring that Hong Kong’s financial system and the HKMA itself can withstand climate change risks and supporting the transition to a more sustainable economic development path. By actively participating in international and regional organizations, the HKMA also aims to contribute to the formulation of regional and global policies and standards for green and sustainable finance. As a banking regulator, the HKMA will further strengthen the banking sector’s climate resilience and climate risk management capabilities.
