Specifically, key priorities include: conducting a new round of thematic reviews on banks’ climate risk management practices and holding further consultation sessions as part of monitoring banks’ progress in complying with regulatory requirements on climate risk management; continuing efforts to integrate climate considerations into the HKMA’s regulatory review processes; completing the second round of industry-wide climate risk stress tests, providing guidance to participating banks throughout the process, and sharing insights and lessons learned with the industry; enhancing sustainability disclosures by collaborating with local authorities to ensure relevant regulations align with the International Financial Reporting Standards’ sustainability disclosure standards, which serve as a global benchmark, and preparing for the implementation of Pillar 1 of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision’s framework on climate-related financial risks; and sharing guidelines on best practices for transition planning with the industry. To foster the healthy development of banks in offering green and sustainable investment products, the HKMA will continue to monitor local and international market and regulatory developments while maintaining close contact with the industry to ensure banks adopt appropriate sales procedures. Additionally, the HKMA will act as a facilitator, promoting the development of a green finance ecosystem and supporting banks in financing the economic transition. We are set to publish a local green taxonomy and will continue expanding its scope to include more activities, such as transition activities. Meanwhile, we will also continue exploring technological solutions to help banks identify, measure, and monitor their climate risk exposures; one example is an upcoming cloud platform designed to facilitate banks’ physical risk assessments. To enhance staff expertise, in 2024 we will introduce a professional-level module on “Green and Sustainable Finance” under the “Banking Professional Qualifications Framework.” Hong Kong is well-positioned to serve as a regional and international hub for sustainable finance. To fulfill this role, the HKMA is assisting the government in implementing the proposals outlined in the 2023–24 Budget, namely expanding the scope of the Government Green Bond Programme to cover sustainable finance projects, thereby further developing Hong Kong’s green and sustainable bond market; it is also leveraging the Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme to attract more green financing activities, including transition finance, to Hong Kong. We will continue to encourage more governments, institutions, and enterprises to raise green funds through Hong Kong and explore potential synergies between green finance and technology. Furthermore, we will continue supporting the implementation of the government-funded “Pilot Training Programme on Green and Sustainable Finance” to expand Hong Kong’s pool of green finance talent. As co-chair of the Inter-Agency Steering Group on Green and Sustainable Finance, we will continue working closely with other agencies to coordinate cross-sectoral policies and initiatives aimed at promoting the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong. In 2024, the Steering Group will focus on three key areas: sustainability disclosures, technology applications, and transition finance. As another key priority, through the Green Banking Alliance, the Monetary Authority of Macao and the International Finance Corporation will continue to jointly launch various initiatives in Asia. These include conducting research on green finance, providing insightful market analyses, offering targeted professional training for banks, and delivering practical guidelines to help financial institutions develop their own distinctive green transition pathways. In 2024, we will also strive to deepen cooperation with the Glasgow Net Zero Finance Alliance, the Sustainable Investment Capacity Building Alliance, and the Green Development Investment and Financing Partnership.    As a responsible investor, the Monetary Authority of Macao is committed to achieving net-zero emissions for its Exchange Fund portfolio by 2050 or earlier. We will continue to enhance the sustainability of the Exchange Fund’s investments through a three-pronged approach to responsible investing, ensuring the resilience of our asset portfolio throughout the transition to net zero. Recognizing that achieving the goals of the Paris Agreement requires a broader economic transformation, we are refining our net-zero strategy to focus on assets that deliver positive climate benefits to the real economy, while still meeting the investment objectives of the Exchange Fund.    As an environmentally conscious organization, our carbon reduction strategy will continue to evolve in line with the latest developments in the market, regulatory frameworks, technology, and other climate-related areas. To further strengthen our climate resilience and risk preparedness, we will explore the feasibility of using technological solutions to assess the impact of physical risks on our operations. Additionally, we will continue to actively encourage staff participation in our sustainability efforts, including launching campaigns to foster sustainable habits and optimizing office processes and practices.    The Monetary Authority of Macao will also maintain consistent, efficient, and sustainable procurement practices, which include evaluating suppliers’ ESG practices during contract selection and renewal. Building on our achievement of Green Data Centre certification in 2023, we remain committed to adhering to the stipulated certification standards. Moving forward, any upgrades to our data centre facilities will incorporate green design and operational practices alongside the latest technological advancements. At the same time, we will continue to minimize electronic waste through technological applications and convergence efforts, while actively modernizing our internal systems to improve efficiency and mitigate potential risks.    Finally, in terms of social responsibilities, the Monetary Authority of Macao will seek additional community service opportunities for our staff. We will also collaborate with industry stakeholders to promote financial inclusion and financial literacy, as well as raise public awareness regarding the prevention of financial fraud.

Climate change affects every aspect of human life, and everyone can contribute to mitigating its impacts. Leveraging its multiple roles as a central bank, banking regulator, market facilitator, responsible investor, and sustainability advocate, the HKMA plays a part in promoting and accelerating the transition to net-zero emissions in Hong Kong and across Asia. The HKMA has established a robust governance framework for sustainability, which guides the formulation of relevant strategies and policies, oversees implementation efforts, and ensures that sustainability considerations are integrated into the HKMA’s own operations. Committed to sound corporate governance, the HKMA has put in place a well-structured governance framework for sustainability featuring clear accountability mechanisms and high transparency. This framework ensures that sustainability factors are effectively incorporated into the HKMA’s strategic planning and decision-making processes, while also providing effective mechanisms to monitor and evaluate progress and outcomes in sustainability efforts. The HKMA’s sustainability governance framework comprises several key components: the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee and its relevant subcommittees, which oversee the HKMA’s work—including its sustainability initiatives—and provide recommendations; the Green and Sustainable Development Steering Committee (the Steering Committee), chaired by the HKMA Chief Executive, which provides leadership at the management level for the HKMA’s overall environmental, social, and governance (ESG) strategies and policies; in the realm of responsible investment, the ESG Committee under the Exchange Fund Investment Office coordinates and oversees all ESG-related activities within the Office; and across other functional areas, various teams and working groups are responsible for planning and implementing sustainability measures related to banking and market development as well as the HKMA’s own operations. At the cross-sectoral level, the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) jointly established the Inter-Agency Steering Group on Green and Sustainable Finance (the Steering Group), which coordinates efforts among financial regulators, government departments, industry stakeholders, and other parties to accelerate the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong. Given the significant expansion of the HKMA’s sustainability initiatives over recent years, we established the Steering Committee in October as a central platform to lead and better coordinate all sustainability efforts across the HKMA’s various functional areas.1 The Steering Committee provides guidance on the formulation of strategies, policies, and plans related to ESG matters within the four key areas of banking, market development, Exchange Fund investments, and internal operations; monitors implementation of ESG-related initiatives by various HKMA departments; evaluates the HKMA’s performance and achievements in attaining its ESG objectives; and oversees external communication strategies. Chaired by the HKMA Chief Executive, the Steering Committee includes three Deputy Chief Executives as permanent members. Additionally, Assistant Chief Executives responsible for key functions related to green and sustainable development are invited to attend Steering Committee meetings to report on major achievements and future plans. Regular meetings are held, with support provided by relevant working groups under the HKMA’s Banking Department, Institutional Development and Operations Department, External Relations Department, and the Exchange Fund Investment Office. Apart from developing and implementing its own sustainability measures, the HKMA and the SFC jointly launched the Steering Group in May 2020. Acting as a cross-agency platform, the Steering Group provides strategic direction and coordinates cross-sectoral efforts among the financial industry to address climate and environmental risks, thereby reinforcing Hong Kong’s position as a leading green and sustainable finance hub in Asia and globally. For further details on the Steering Group’s work, please refer to the chapter “Strengthening the Development of a Green and Sustainable Financial Ecosystem.”

Climate change is a significant risk facing the financial system. The HKMA has been committed to strengthening Hong Kong's financial system to build a greener and more sustainable future, contributing to Hong Kong's climate goals as well as the global sustainability agenda. Banks face impacts from various sustainability and climate-related matters in their daily business operations. To continue to perform their important functions in the financial system and guide more funds toward green and sustainable projects, banks must proactively manage climate risks. As the banking regulator, the HKMA places special emphasis on building the capacity of banks to respond to and manage climate risks, and accelerating the efforts of banks to support the transition to a low-carbon economic model. The HKMA is committed to formulating various policy measures to strengthen the banking system's capacity to respond to climate risks. In August, the HKMA issued the Net Zero Transition Planning Circular, which lists high-level principles to assist banks in remaining safe and sound during the economic transition to net-zero emissions. Following the issuance of the circular, we conducted a questionnaire in the fourth quarter for some banks to understand their transition planning measures. Based on the survey results, we will share observations and best practices regarding transition planning with the industry and will hold seminars or workshops to facilitate the exchange of experiences within the industry. Regarding disclosure requirements, in response to the latest international developments, including the International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) standards published in June and the consultation launched by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) in November on the disclosure framework for climate-related financial risks, the HKMA is intensifying its work to improve the sustainability-related disclosure framework for Hong Kong banks. Specifically, the HKMA is collaborating with relevant local authorities and stakeholders to develop a comprehensive roadmap for Hong Kong that aligns with the ISSB standards. During the year, the HKMA strengthened its supervision of banks' climate risk management and provided recommendations to help banks further enhance their climate resilience and climate risk management capabilities. The HKMA has made significant progress in implementing the two-year plan to incorporate climate risk factors into the banking supervision process. Climate risk management has now been included as a standing agenda item in the prudential supervision meetings held with bank management. Banking supervisors have also adopted the enhanced CAMEL rating system, which incorporates climate risk factors, to assess the risk profile and risk management systems of banks.1 As part of the implementation of the two-year plan to incorporate climate risk factors into the banking supervision process, the HKMA revised the "green" assessment framework to focus on the transition planning measures of banks. The HKMA is also reviewing the supervisory review process used to assess and monitor the capital adequacy levels of banks and determine their Pillar 2 capital requirements, in order to encourage banks to strengthen their risk management frameworks to respond to climate risks. Following the conclusion of the 12-month implementation period for compliance with Unit GS-1 "Climate Risk Management" of the Supervisory Policy Manual under the 2023 two-year plan, the HKMA conducted a round of thematic reviews on climate-related risk governance in the second quarter. The thematic review covered four major areas, including the governance framework for climate-related risks, oversight of climate strategies, oversight of climate-related risk management, and institutional culture, awareness, and communication. The HKMA made several improvements to the climate risk stress testing framework, including the introduction of new 5-year scenarios to assess the potential impact on banks from the simultaneous occurrence of economic and climate change shocks. Following these improvements and as part of the HKMA's regular regulator-led stress testing program, the second round of climate risk stress testing was launched in June to conduct a comprehensive assessment of banks' climate risk exposures and further enhance the capacity of banks to manage climate risks. A total of 44 banks participated in this round of stress testing, an increase of over 60% compared to the first pilot program in 2021. The HKMA also organized a Climate Risk Stress Testing Forum in November, which was attended by as many as 300 banking practitioners. By facilitating the sharing of experiences among banks, the event helped deepen the industry's overall understanding of climate risk measurement. The HKMA also conducted a series of consultation meetings to review the progress of banks in implementing Unit GS-1 "Climate Risk Management" of the HKMA's *Supervisory Policy Manual*. The HKMA held meetings with bank management to discuss their work in climate risk management and the common challenges faced by the industry, and reviewed the information and other public disclosures provided by the banks to assess their relevant progress. The HKMA provided targeted advice to the banks, encouraging and supporting them to continue strengthening their climate risk management capabilities in line with the HKMA's supervisory expectations. As global attention on climate change grows and efforts to address related issues intensify, the HKMA has noted a steadily increasing demand for green and sustainable investment products, with some banks offering relevant products to meet customer needs. In view of this, the HKMA completed a thematic review of banks' sales of green and sustainable investment products and issued a circular in November, listing the standards the HKMA expects banks to achieve and sharing observed best practices. This circular covers multiple areas, including product due diligence, disclosure, governance and controls, staff training, and record-keeping, aiming to mitigate potential greenwashing risks and strengthen investor confidence, thereby promoting the sound development of relevant investment activities. The HKMA will continue to monitor the latest trends and market developments. The HKMA is committed to promoting the application of technology in green and sustainable banking. For example, technology can improve data availability and risk analysis, enhancing the ability of banks to manage climate risks. The HKMA will soon launch a beta version of a cloud platform for banks to assess the impact of physical risks on residential and commercial buildings under different climate scenarios. Additionally, the HKMA continues to collaborate with other central banks and regulatory authorities to explore how technology solutions can assist in physical risk assessments. On the other hand, the HKMA also encourages the adoption of sustainable anti-money laundering (AML) practices through the application of advanced analytics and artificial intelligence to reduce the consumption of compliance-related resources. In 2023, the HKMA launched an online shared data submission platform, fully automating the data collection process for financial crime risks, thereby strengthening the operational workflows for banks to submit AML-related data in a sustainable manner. In September, the HKMA organized the "Green Fintech Competition," aimed at seeking market-ready solutions to help the banking industry address challenges in the following areas: (i) net-zero transition or transition planning; (ii) climate risk management; (iii) green and sustainable finance; and (iv) sustainability or climate-related disclosure and reporting. The competition attracted over 85 entries from approximately 70 companies. In December, the HKMA held the "Green and Sustainable Banking Seminar," providing a platform for the banking and technology sectors to explore the roles of low-carbon technology and green fintech in the net-zero transition of Hong Kong and Mainland China, while also announcing the results of the "Green Fintech Competition." The event attracted about 400 participants from the banking, technology, regulatory, and academic sectors. To improve transparency among financial markets and make green and sustainable finance decisions more consistent, the HKMA developed a local green taxonomy framework with the assistance of a consultancy firm. In May, the HKMA published a discussion paper on the "Hong Kong Green Taxonomy Prototype," seeking stakeholder views on establishing and implementing a green taxonomy catalog. Based on the consultation results, the HKMA is fine-tuning the prototype framework and identifying other areas for the next phase of framework development. The Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) participates in the work of the Task Force on Financial Actions; this organization has identified environmental crimes as predicate offenses for money laundering, and due to the interconnectedness between anti-money laundering and Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) issues, this scope is receiving increasing attention from more regulatory bodies. The FSC fully understands that climate change may pose potential risks to the financial system; therefore, it has incorporated a broader range of climate factors and scenarios into financial risk analysis and research to strengthen current supervisory work. In the process of continuously monitoring financial stability risks, the FSC takes climate change into account and includes analyses of climate-related risks in various financial stability reports. By actively participating in the scenario design and analysis working groups under the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), the FSC assists in further enriching climate scenarios, allowing central banks and regulatory bodies to better understand the impacts of climate change on the macroeconomy and finance. As a member of the Transition Planning Working Group under the Financial Stability Board, the FSC participates in analyzing the interactions between the transition planning of financial and non-financial companies and financial stability, enabling policymakers to examine climate-related financial risks from a forward-looking and dynamic perspective. In terms of research, the FSC conducts several applied research projects exploring the impacts of climate change and broader ESG issues on the financial industry and the economy. Research topics include climate risk exposure of the banking industry and investment funds, ESG capital flows, the impact of climate change on property prices, and the ripple effects of corporate ESG performance in global supply chains. The aforementioned research results enhance the FSC's understanding of the impacts of climate change and ESG issues on financial stability, aiding in the formulation of relevant policies. Locally, these studies help strengthen the FSC's continuous monitoring and assessment of the impacts of climate risks on financial stability. Externally, the FSC also shares research findings with a wide range of stakeholders through various channels, such as international activities on climate-related matters and the "FSC Research Memoranda." The FSC's "Liquidity Arrangement Framework" is a collateralized liquidity arrangement that provides timely liquidity support to banks in need. Following NGFS recommendations, the FSC has incorporated sustainability considerations when assessing eligible collateral under this framework. The FSC actively participates in international and regional discussions on addressing climate risks and promoting sustainable finance as the mainstream. Through participation in these areas, the FSC helps facilitate international and regional policy dialogues on addressing climate change and its impacts on financial stability, and draws insights from these dialogues to help strengthen the climate resilience of Hong Kong's financial system.

To strengthen Hong Kong’s position as a leading regional hub for green and sustainable finance, the HKMA is committed to raising market awareness and participation, providing necessary infrastructure and enabling factors, and supporting international initiatives to align with global standards. Throughout the year, the HKMA worked closely with local and international partners to foster a richer ecosystem and further advance green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong. The Inter-Agency Steering Group on Green and Sustainable Finance (the Steering Group), co-led by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), coordinates responses within the financial sector to climate and environmental risks, accelerates the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong, and supports the Government’s climate strategy. Since its establishment, the Steering Group has made good progress. In January 2024, it announced key measures aimed at helping Hong Kong seize opportunities in sustainable finance; these measures primarily cover sustainable disclosure, ecosystem development, transition finance, and green fintech. Specifically, a Sustainable Disclosure Working Group has been set up to develop a roadmap for Hong Kong’s adoption of the IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Standards. This roadmap will address 4 key areas: sustainable reporting, verification, data and technology, and skills training. Additionally, a Transition Finance Working Group has been established to explore ways of supporting financial institutions and enterprises in transition planning and reporting. The Steering Group also works to strengthen the sustainable finance ecosystem through cross-sectoral skills training and data enhancement. In particular, regarding data, we continue to promote the use of the Climate and Environmental Risk Questionnaire for Non-Listed Companies 2, jointly launched by the Steering Group and CDP in 2022. Moving forward, the Steering Group will stay abreast of latest developments in green and sustainable finance and further consolidate Hong Kong’s role as a regional and global hub for this sector. In January 2024, the Steering Group unveiled three (3) new key initiatives designed to help Hong Kong capitalize on investment and financing opportunities arising from the low-carbon transition in the Asia-Pacific region. To facilitate skills development within the industry, the Green and Sustainable Finance Centre under the Steering Group implements the Government’s “Pilot Scheme on Green and Sustainable Finance Training,” which provides financial assistance to practitioners, students, and graduates undertaking relevant training or pursuing qualifications in green and sustainable finance. As of December 2023, a total of 46 international and local training programs or qualifications had been registered under the scheme, with over 560 funding applications approved. The HKMA has also introduced a foundational level of the “Green and Sustainable Finance” module under the “Banking Professional Qualifications Framework.” This module aims to foster talent development within the banking sector and enhance overall professional capabilities. In 2024, the HKMA will continue collaborating with the banking industry to develop an advanced level of this module, responding to the growing demand for specialized professionals in green and sustainable finance. To help financial institutions and enterprises—particularly SMEs—better understand key climate and sustainability-related issues such as climate risk management, sustainable reporting, greenhouse gas emissions calculation, and transition planning, the HKMA partnered throughout the year with relevant government bureaux and departments, as well as global partners including CDP, the Glasgow Financial Alliance for Net Zero (GFANZ)3 and the Partnership for Carbon Accounting Financials (PCAF)4 to organize a series of seminars and workshops attended by participants from both the financial services and corporate sectors. Among students, following the launch of the “Sustainable Finance Internship Programme” in 2022, training sessions were held in January and February 2023 to deepen interns’ and university graduates’ understanding of sustainable finance. Recognizing technology’s potential in addressing climate-related data gaps and improving data quality, the HKMA strives to make such data more accessible and reliable, thereby supporting sound decision-making and effective climate action. In February 2024, the Steering Group rolled out several website enhancements designed to serve as a one-stop information portal on green and sustainable finance for financial institutions, enterprises, and the general public. Key improvements include an electronic platform for sustainable disclosure, tools for calculating and estimating greenhouse gas emissions, and more focused, user-friendly data and resource sections. During “Hong Kong Green Week,” the Steering Group, together with Cyberport and Invest Hong Kong, co-hosted an event titled “Leveraging Technology to Accelerate Sustainable Finance,” showcasing leading green innovations and Hong Kong’s strengths in green technology. “Hong Kong Green Week – Financial Theme” took place from February 26 to March 1, 2024. Throughout the event, various activities centered on sustainable development attracted over 1,600 participants from nearly 30 regions, including representatives from financial institutions, corporations, central banks, international organizations, government agencies, academia, and consultancy firms. The flagship event of “Hong Kong Green Week” was the “Asia-Pacific Climate Business Forum,” jointly organized by the HKMA and the International Finance Corporation. The forum brought together more than 400 participants, including top decision-makers from the global business and financial sectors, to discuss ways of unlocking climate finance opportunities in the Asia-Pacific region. Over the two-day event, a wide range of topics were explored, such as energy transition, decarbonization in heavy industries, the circular economy, future trends in sustainable finance, and emerging climate technologies in Asia-Pacific’s emerging and developing markets. Numerous public and private sector organizations joined forces to host over 10 roundtables, seminars, and other networking events. Topics covered climate finance, carbon markets, electric vehicle supply chains, financing for net-zero transitions, green finance taxonomies, and green development financing within the Belt and Road Initiative. Additionally, on February 29, 2024, the HKMA and the International Monetary Fund co-hosted the “Asia Climate Finance Roundtable,” which examined key measures for scaling up climate finance and the roles of central banks and regulators in climate risk management. These events form part of the HKMA’s broader efforts to promote and enrich Hong Kong’s green and sustainable finance ecosystem. They serve as valuable platforms for participants to foster new business opportunities, exchange knowledge, and explore innovative solutions to climate finance challenges in the Asia-Pacific region. The HKMA has also been actively supporting the development of green and sustainable finance across the region. In November 2020, the International Finance Corporation and the HKMA launched the “Green Commercial Banking Alliance”5 as a collaborative platform aimed at uniting financial institutions, banking industry associations, research bodies, and technology providers in the region to advance green commercial banking. Since March 2021, the Alliance has organized 22 training sessions and roundtables, drawing over 7,300 participants from across the globe, including the Asia-Pacific, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and the Americas. In October, the Alliance and Crédit Agricole CIB jointly released a cutting-edge research report titled “Developing Ambitious Climate Strategies for Green Banking: Case Studies.” Throughout the year, the HKMA’s Infrastructure Financing Facilitation Office joined the newly established “Capacity Building for Sustainable Investment Alliance” (CASI) as well as the “Green Development Investment and Financing Partnership” (GIFP) initiated by the Belt and Road Green Development International Alliance. Collaborations with CASI and GIFP will facilitate capacity building, knowledge sharing, and channel greater financial resources toward green and sustainable projects in Asia and beyond. In August 2023, GFANZ announced the establishment of its Hong Kong chapter, which aims to support local and mainland financial institutions in their net-zero transition efforts. The HKMA serves as an advisor to GFANZ in its operations. Demonstrating its commitment to tackling climate change, promoting green finance, and developing Hong Kong into a more sustainable and livable city, the Government launched the “Government Green Bond Programme” in 2018. The HKMA assists in the issuance of green bonds under this programme. To date, the Government has issued green bonds equivalent to approximately USD 250 billion, with proceeds allocated to over 70 green government projects, including green building initiatives, waste management and recycling, energy efficiency, and energy conservation. To enhance transparency and accountability, the Government publishes an annual “Green Bond Report” detailing how bond proceeds are utilized and their anticipated environmental benefits. In fiscal year 2023–24, the Government continued its regular issuance of green institutional bonds, releasing green bonds worth around USD 6 billion in June. This multicurrency issuance featured bonds denominated in US dollars, euros, and Chinese yuan across various maturities, attracting broad investor interest; total subscriptions reached nearly USD 30 billion. The issuance volume of RMB-denominated bonds rose from RMB10 billion in January to RMB15 billion, with the introduction of 10-year RMB bonds for the first time. This move helps extend the government’s RMB yield curve and further diversify offshore RMB financial products. Global investors responded enthusiastically to the issuance of green bonds by the government, reflecting their recognition of Hong Kong’s commitment to promoting green and sustainable development. In October, the government issued a second batch of green retail bonds worth HKD20 billion, further advancing market development and fostering inclusive finance. This issuance provided members of the public with an investment opportunity offering stable returns, enabling them to participate in and benefit from Hong Kong’s green finance growth.

As a major global asset owner and manager, the Monetary Authority plays a pivotal role in advancing green and sustainable finance to support the global climate agenda. The Monetary Authority has long been a pioneer in responsible investment. Since 2015, it has been spearheading investments in green and sustainable assets, requiring its external investment managers to actively exercise asset ownership rights and integrate environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors into the investment management of the Exchange Fund. Guided by the principle of “preserving capital first, achieving long-term appreciation”1, the Monetary Authority invests prudently, believing that thorough consideration of ESG factors helps mitigate investment risks while unlocking the long-term sustainable value of investments. As one of the first central banks to sign the Principles for Responsible Investment (PRI) and set a “net-zero emissions by 2050”2 target for its portfolio, the Monetary Authority remains committed to advancing its responsible investment journey, with a strong emphasis on sustainability—particularly the urgent issue of climate change—to enhance the resilience of the Exchange Fund and achieve better risk-adjusted long-term returns. As a responsible investor, the Monetary Authority contributes to building a robust green and sustainable finance ecosystem by collaborating with like-minded investors, regulators, and international organizations to develop industry standards and promote the adoption of responsible investment practices within the financial sector and central banking community. Through oversight and collaborative efforts, it strives to foster a future where finance and sustainable development go hand in hand. Illustration 1: The responsible investment journey of the Exchange Fund  Comprehensive and reliable ESG information is essential for integrating sustainability considerations and devising credible climate transition plans aimed at achieving net-zero targets. To fulfill its commitments under the Glasgow Declaration3 of the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) and the strategic plan of the Multi-Agency Task Force on Green and Sustainable Finance, the Monetary Authority has taken proactive steps by preparing this chapter on responsible investment for the Exchange Fund in accordance with recommendations from the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD).3 The Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Financial Secretary, establishes the framework and guiding principles for responsible investment, which are then implemented by the Investment Office of the Exchange Fund in its investment management activities. The primary guiding principle sets the tone for how the Monetary Authority balances responsible investment practices with the Exchange Fund’s investment objectives. The Investment Committee under the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the Monetary Authority, oversees ESG and climate-related risks associated with the Exchange Fund’s investments. It reviews the responsible investment framework and risk management policies, monitoring their implementation through regular reports submitted by the Sustainable Investment Unit within the Investment Office. As illustrated in Illustration 2, the ESG Committee under the Investment Office, chaired by the Chief Strategy Officer, coordinates and supervises all ESG-related activities within the Office. Proposals and progress updates discussed during its quarterly meetings are reported to the Chief Executive of the Investment Office. Additionally, the Green and Sustainable Oversight Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the Monetary Authority and comprising the Chief Executive of the Investment Office and the Chief Strategy Officer, meets semi-annually to provide guidance on ESG policies and measures across various functions of the Monetary Authority, including the Investment Office, in pursuit of its overall ESG objectives. Illustration 2: Governance structure for responsible investment at the Investment Office of the Exchange Fund  As shown in Illustration 1, the Investment Office of the Exchange Fund embarked on its responsible investment journey in 2016, initially focusing on managing ESG risks that could affect the Fund’s financial performance. As sustainability evolved rapidly and became a strategic priority for major institutions worldwide—extending beyond mere risk management—the Investment Office re-evaluated its approach to responsible investment. July 2023 marked another milestone: the Office established a new Business Strategy Division led by the Chief Strategy Officer, tasked with coordinating and steering its strategic development; this division incorporated the former Responsible Investment Unit under the Risk Management and Oversight Department, now renamed the Sustainable Investment Unit. This strategic realignment reflects the Monetary Authority’s shift in emphasizing responsible investment from a risk-based perspective to a more proactive and forward-looking stance in addressing sustainability-related issues in investment practices. The Sustainable Investment Unit collaborates closely with various teams within the Investment Office of the Exchange Fund to integrate ESG factors into investment practices. It also assists senior management at the Investment Office in managing ESG-related risks and opportunities—particularly those related to climate change—across all investment portfolios:    **Public market investments** – The Credit, Regulation, and Oversight Committee, composed of senior officials from the Investment Office, reviews how ESG factors are incorporated into credit risk models, taking into account inputs from the Sustainable Investment Unit. Meanwhile, the Risk Management and Oversight Department regularly reports on the ESG performance of the fixed-income portfolio. Additionally, the Sustainable Investment Unit contributes from an ESG perspective to the selection, appointment, and oversight of external investment managers managing the equity portfolio (see Section 40, “Risk Management,” under “Promoting active ownership” for details). **Private market investments** – The Investment Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the Monetary Authority, considers ESG-related assessments provided by both the private market investment team and the risk management team for each proposed investment. The Monetary Authority recognizes that physical and transition risks4 stemming from climate change, as well as associated opportunities, can significantly impact the long-term performance and value of the Exchange Fund’s investments. According to the United Nations Environment Programme’s *Emissions Gap Report 2023*5, unless greenhouse gas emissions are further reduced worldwide, global average temperatures are projected to rise by 2.5°C to 2.9°C above pre-industrial levels by 2030. The urgent need for more aggressive policies, technological innovation, or behavioral changes to curb this temperature rise may exacerbate transition risks such as asset devaluation or stranded assets. Concurrently, the increasing frequency and severity of extreme weather events pose additional physical risks to investments. The Monetary Authority believes that investing in a greener future aligns with the Exchange Fund’s investment objectives; hence, it places special emphasis on climate-related considerations when integrating ESG factors. In 2022, it set a target for its investment portfolio to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050, underscoring its commitment to global climate efforts. The Authority continues to strengthen its three-pronged approach, with a clear focus on carbon reduction and transition. The following sections elaborate on these measures. **Illustration 3**: The Monetary Authority’s three-pronged approach to responsible investment    In pursuit of its net-zero goal, the Monetary Authority prefers proactive engagement over outright exclusion or divestment from potential investments. First, maintaining a diversified and robust portfolio is vital to fulfilling the Exchange Fund’s primary investment objectives. Excluding entire sectors or industries would narrow the pool of investable opportunities, potentially affecting both returns and risk profiles. Through an inclusive approach, the Monetary Authority can identify opportunities to invest in companies—including those in high-emission industries—that are undergoing transition and possess advanced technologies and sound corporate governance to adapt to evolving global climate trends. Second, addressing climate change necessitates the transition of core “brown” industries. Merely divesting from such sectors fails to resolve the underlying carbon emissions problem. Instead, the Monetary Authority supports these industries by deploying strategic capital and actively exercising asset ownership rights, thereby encouraging them to adopt sustainable and low-carbon practices—benefiting both themselves and the global community. In response to market developments, the Monetary Authority is refining its net-zero investment strategy to adopt a holistic approach that yields transition outcomes aligned with both the Exchange Fund’s goals and global net-zero targets, while adhering to its guiding principles for responsible investment. By integrating ESG factors into investment decisions, it continues to seek sustainable investment opportunities that foster climate transition and enhance the long-term resilience of the Exchange Fund’s portfolio (Illustration 4). In 2023, the Monetary Authority sustained its momentum in responsible investment. In public markets, it launched a new actively managed global equity portfolio focused on sustainability and climate transition, overseen by an external investment manager; it also expanded the use of a customized low-carbon equity index to another portfolio managed externally. Meanwhile, green, social, and sustainability bonds prioritized by the Authority outperformed their benchmarks, exemplifying the principle of “doing good while generating returns.” In private markets, the Monetary Authority actively built a resilient long-term growth portfolio, seizing investment opportunities expected to benefit from long-term economic trends such as climate and energy transition. For instance, this year the Monetary Authority invested in two Asia-focused transition investment funds, demonstrating its commitment to addressing Asia’s climate transition needs. Illustration 4: Ongoing measures to promote ESG investing. The Monetary Authority has invested in a company specializing in producing eco-friendly thermoplastic materials from non-recyclable household waste—including organic matter such as food scraps—and materials that cannot be recycled. Unlike conventional chemical recycling processes, which rely on energy-intensive high-temperature environments to produce plastics, this company has pioneered a low-temperature production method powered entirely by solar arrays. This waste-derived plastic material can serve as a sustainable, versatile alternative to oil-based resins commonly used in retail and consumer goods industries. It is also compatible with existing standard manufacturing processes and cutting-edge technologies such as 3D printing. The company is a staunch advocate of the circular economy. The following diagram illustrates the positive environmental outcomes resulting from its advanced plastic production process: Managed by the International Finance Corporation, the MCPP is an innovative initiative that combines funds from institutional investors with IFC’s own capital to expand sustainable financing for private companies in emerging markets. In 2017 and 2019, the Monetary Authority committed to two tranches of investments under MCPP, each worth USD 10 billion. It further collaborated with IFC to launch “MCPP One Planet,” a new global climate-related investment platform in 2021; this platform is the world’s first cross-sectoral emerging market loan portfolio aligned with the Paris Agreement. Through the MCPP program, the Monetary Authority has pledged to provide financing for 80 sustainable development projects across 38 developing countries, spanning 19 sectors including infrastructure, agriculture, real estate, and manufacturing. The International Finance Corporation has compiled data on MCPP loans. According to IFC’s reports, the Monetary Authority’s loan commitments have provided support to emerging markets and developing countries in various areas such as economic transition and human resource development. Specifically, projects financed by the Monetary Authority are projected to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by approximately 560 million metric tons of CO2 equivalent annually—equivalent to the emissions generated by an average gasoline-powered car traveling 140 billion miles. Illustration 5: Projected average annual benefits of the Monetary Authority’s MCPP loan commitments since 2020. The green and sustainable finance ecosystem serves as a cornerstone for global sustainable development in the future. The Monetary Authority actively collaborates with like-minded investors and partners to promote responsible investing and enhance industry capabilities.

The HKMA is committed to becoming a sustainable organization by taking multiple measures to reduce its carbon footprint, with the goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. Apart from promoting environmental sustainability, the HKMA also attaches great importance to the physical and mental well-being of its staff and corporate social responsibility. It strives to enhance financial inclusion and improve public financial literacy. As a responsible institution, the HKMA has set sustainability goals under three key pillars: the environment, its staff, and social responsibility. The Green and Sustainable Development Steering Committee (the Steering Committee)1, established in October, is chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA and serves as the main decision-making body for all organizational sustainability initiatives. Predecessor to the Steering Committee was the Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainable Development Committee, which guided the HKMA in formulating its vision, strategies, and policies related to sustainability and social responsibility. At the departmental level, the Assistant Chief Executive (Corporate Development and Operations) oversees the implementation of sustainability activities and regularly submits progress reports to the Steering Committee. The Green Office Task Force and the Volunteer Service Group provide support in coordinating sustainability efforts; the former serves as a platform for brainstorming ideas on creating a green working environment, while the latter aims to foster a culture of volunteerism. The HKMA has developed a roadmap to guide its transition toward sustainability. Key priorities include implementing carbon-reduction strategies in its daily operations, such as operating green buildings and data centers, promoting eco-friendly travel, adopting energy-saving measures, digital tools, and greener operational practices, minimizing waste, and cultivating a sustainability-oriented culture. The HKMA also plans to utilize carbon-embedded tools within its own value chain to cut emissions, while employing carbon offset measures for emissions that are difficult to eliminate. Beyond these environmental commitments related to its daily operations, the HKMA continues to introduce greener operational solutions for the broader community, ranging from electronic channels for banks to submit documents and communicate, to electronic payment services and coin-collection programs accessible to the general public. To strengthen and maintain its operational capabilities, the HKMA employs a professional workforce, builds a talent pool, and places great emphasis on staff health and well-being. In terms of social responsibility, the HKMA encourages its staff to participate in volunteer and charitable activities; considers partnering with social enterprises in its procurement processes; promotes financial literacy among consumers; and collaborates with the banking sector to ensure equitable access to basic banking services for all segments of society. The remainder of this chapter details each of these strategies. Under the HKMA’s overall enterprise risk management framework, the Risk Committee chaired by the Chief Executive evaluates potential risks and threats faced by the HKMA in its daily operations, including those arising from climate change. Physical impacts of climate change—such as increased extreme weather events leading to flooding or other damage—could affect the HKMA’s offices and hinder staff mobility. To manage such physical risks, the HKMA regularly updates its business continuity plan to address extreme weather conditions. It also conducts periodic evacuation drills and exercises to activate backup facilities, ensuring staff are prepared to implement continuity measures at all times. Various risk-mitigation measures have been incorporated into the design of its premises. Transition risks may affect the HKMA’s energy consumption, air travel, and waste management practices. The HKMA continuously monitors its exposure to transition risks by tracking its greenhouse gas emissions, waste generation, energy consumption, and paper usage. Its climate goal is to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions across Scope 1, Scope 2, and Scope 3 (air travel) in all aspects of its operations by 2050 or earlier. As near-term targets, the HKMA plans to completely eliminate Scope 1 emissions by transitioning all its existing vehicles to electric ones; and, using 2015 as the baseline year, reduce Scope 2 emission intensity by 63% by 2030 or earlier through various carbon-reduction and offset measures. Despite challenges in accurately measuring Scope 3 emissions, the HKMA will still adopt multiple approaches, within practical limits, to minimize greenhouse gas emissions under this category, including paper usage, waste generation, and air travel. Both its long-term and near-term emission-reduction targets have been established in accordance with the methodology of the Science Based Targets initiative, which has been verified by the Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency. The HKMA has engaged the Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency to verify the emissions, energy consumption, paper usage, and waste data disclosed in this report.6 The scope and baseline of this verification are outlined in the “Verification Statement” section of this report. In 2023, apart from publishing its Annual Report, the HKMA also independently released its first Sustainability Report. The HKMA’s efforts in enhancing ESG reporting were recognized when it won the ESG Award in the “Public Sector” category at the “Best Corporate Governance and ESG Awards 2023” organized by the Hong Kong Institute of Certified Public Accountants. It was the first financial regulatory authority to receive this award in that category. The judging panel commended the HKMA for meeting high ESG standards, noting that the Sustainability Report was clear and easy to read. Furthermore, the appointment of an independent third party to verify its target-setting methodology and the environmental data disclosed in the report reflected the HKMA’s commitment to transparent and accountable reporting. Additionally, in the “2023 Best Annual Report Awards” organized by the Hong Kong Institute of Management, the HKMA received the top Gold Award in the “Non-profit and Charitable Organizations” category. The judging panel praised the Annual Report for presenting comprehensive financial information in a clear manner and for making effective use of infographics, which demonstrated the HKMA’s dedication to improving financial literacy and promoting financial inclusion. To acknowledge the HKMA’s commitment to environmental protection, its staff, and society at large, the Hong Kong Council of Social Service has awarded the HKMA the “15+ Years of Joint Commitment to Caring” badge every year since 2006, marking 17 consecutive years of recognition. The HKMA is committed to minimizing the environmental impact of its operations; its internal Green Office Guidelines provide staff with practical guidance on resource utilization and office waste management. Environmental considerations have been integrated into the design, operation, and maintenance of all its owned and leased offices. During office renovations, every effort is made to reuse existing furniture and materials to reduce waste, and preference is given to environmentally friendly construction and decoration materials. Thanks to this consistent approach, in 2021 and 2022 respectively, certain renovated offices at Two International Finance Centre were awarded LEED7 Gold certification and the “BEAM Plus Indoor Environment Assessment”8 Gold rating. Continued adoption of new and existing technologies to improve energy efficiency remains a key priority for the HKMA. Besides promoting good practices such as turning off unnecessary lights outside working hours to conserve electricity, other energy-saving measures include using LED lighting, motion sensors, maintaining appropriate air-conditioning temperatures, and optimizing energy usage across its IT infrastructure. The HKMA’s energy consumption has been steadily declining; in 2023, it stood at 2.59 MWh per person, representing a 29.7% decrease compared to the 2015 baseline (Figure 1).9 Given the nature of its operations, the HKMA’s greenhouse gas emissions primarily stem from electricity generated using fossil fuels. In 2023, the combined intensity of Scope One and Scope Two emissions—arising from purchased fuel and electricity—was 1.48 tCO₂e per person, a 45.2% reduction from 2015 levels (Figure 2). Beyond standard equipment, office software, and meeting facilities, the HKMA has also adopted digital tools and technologies, automated and streamlined its workflows, and fostered a digital working environment to enhance online collaboration across the organization. 11 Paperless meetings have become the norm at the HKMA. To further reduce paper usage and boost efficiency, most internal administrative processes have been digitized. Moreover, the HKMA encourages its staff to embrace green and digital working practices, replacing paper-based documents and communications with digital alternatives. Work is also underway to implement an electronic record-keeping system. These green and digital initiatives have yielded positive results: in 2023, paper usage intensity at the HKMA stood at 11.55 kg per person, marking a substantial 64.8% drop from 2015 levels (Figure 3). Following the post-pandemic resumption of most international events in physical formats, and in support of Hong Kong’s role as an international financial hub, HKMA staff inevitably need to travel overseas for official duties. To minimize carbon emissions from air travel, the HKMA encourages staff attending overseas events to opt for direct flights whenever feasible and to consolidate multiple trips where possible. At the institutional level, in 2023 the HKMA purchased sustainable aviation fuel to reduce its Scope Three emissions by 126 tCO₂e. In addition, the HKMA participates in the “Gold Standard”12 certified carbon offset program to offset any remaining carbon emissions resulting from staff air travel. This program supports waste-to-energy initiatives, solar power generation, and the provision of efficient and cleaner cooking facilities in developing countries. Similar arrangements will be maintained by the HKMA in 2024. Sustainability and environmental considerations are integral to the HKMA’s procurement processes. As part of a comprehensive review of its procurement policies and procedures, the existing practice of purchasing green products has been formalized and aligned with the environmental specifications outlined in the Government’s “Green Procurement List,” particularly when acquiring electrical appliances and office consumables. Furthermore, ESG criteria and innovative proposals aimed at enhancing productivity and efficiency have been incorporated into tender evaluation criteria. All suppliers are also required to commit to compliance with environmental regulations. Guided by the “4R” principles—Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, and Recycle—the HKMA adopts a three-pronged approach to minimize waste generation and ensure proper waste management. In 2022 and 2023, the HKMA conducted two waste audits to help formulate targeted waste management strategies. A detailed breakdown of non-hazardous waste generated—including general waste sent to landfills and various recyclable materials—is provided in the “Performance Summary” section on page 56. In 2023, the HKMA took part for the first time in a red envelope recycling program organized by the management company of the International Finance Centre. Staff contributed approximately 3,000 used but still intact red envelopes, which were subsequently distributed by an environmental organization to the public for use during the following Lunar New Year. Given that the HKMA’s operations and backup data center account for a significant portion of its total energy consumption, both data centers have been upgraded to meet the highest standards set by the BEAM Plus certification scheme for existing data centers, thereby achieving optimal Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE).13 In 2023, the two HKMA data centers received “Gold” and “Platinum” ratings respectively under the “BEAM Plus Existing Data Centre” assessment guidelines issued in 2021; the HKMA is the first and only organization in Hong Kong to have achieved such ratings. Enhancing the energy efficiency of its data centers has long been a key focus for the HKMA’s technical team. To this end, eco-friendly design principles and energy-efficient operational practices have been implemented during renovation projects, with the aim of lowering PUE and attaining related targets. These efforts include 24-hour monitoring of environmental conditions within the data centers and continuous optimization of factors such as airflow and temperature settings. Recognizing the need for further improvements, the HKMA commissioned an external consultancy in December 2021 to conduct a comprehensive assessment of its data centers’ environmental performance and to provide recommendations for further enhancements. The resulting study was completed in mid-2022, and shortly thereafter the HKMA began preparing for certification as a “Green Data Centre” under the BEAM Plus certification scheme. This certification process is thorough and rigorous. Throughout 2023, the technical team implemented various optimization measures based on the consultancy’s recommendations, focusing on improving energy performance as well as health-related aspects of the working environment within the data centers.

Hong Kong Quality Assurance Bureau has conducted an independent verification of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's ("HKMA") 2023 environmental data ("2023 Data"). The 2023 Data includes total energy consumption in 2023, Scope 1 and Scope 2 greenhouse gas emissions, greenhouse gas emissions from business aviation travel, paper consumption, non-hazardous waste generated (including general waste and recyclable waste sent to landfills), their respective intensities, and the changes in their data compared to 2015 levels. Additionally, the 2023 Data includes the volume of food waste generated during the year, its intensity, and the changes compared to the levels when the HKMA launched its food waste recycling scheme in November 2022. The HKMA's greenhouse gas emissions data is compiled in accordance with the Greenhouse Gas Protocol ("GHG Protocol") jointly published by the World Resources Institute and the World Business Council of Sustainable Development. The scope of verification covers data related to the period from January 1, 2023, to December 31, 2023, as well as relevant data from the period from January 1, 2015, to December 31, 2015, used for annual performance comparison (excluding food waste volume). The scope of verification covers a total of 5 office and warehouse assets, of which 4 offices are located at 1) International Finance Centre Phase II, 2) Hopewell Centre, 3) Taikoo Place Phase I, and 4) Kowloon Trade Centre; the warehouse is located at 5) Loke Sun Industrial Centre in Kwai Chung. The purpose of the verification is to provide reasonable assurance on the accuracy and reliability of the 2023 Data and to confirm the adequacy of the HKMA's data collection mechanism. Within the scope of verification, Hong Kong Quality Assurance Bureau reviewed representative data and supporting evidence selected from the 5 assets. This verification work was performed in accordance with the "International Standard on Assurance Engagements 3000 (Revised)" (Assurance Engagements Other than Audits or Reviews of Historical Financial Information) issued by the International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board. The verification procedures are designed to provide an opinion and summary to obtain a reasonable level of assurance. The verification process is determined according to the requirements of the GHG Protocol. The verification process tests the completeness and accuracy of the data by tracing selected sample data back to their sources, and also reviews the basic procedures for data collection, aggregation, estimation, calculation, and internal checks, and performs reliability testing. The verification process also includes verifying internal data collection and management mechanisms, interviewing representatives responsible for preparing the 2023 Data, and selecting representative data and information for verification. Relevant raw data and supporting evidence were also reviewed in detail during the verification process. The HKMA is responsible for data collection and reporting. Our verification work is absolutely independent and impartial. The Hong Kong Quality Assurance Bureau verification team was not involved in the preparation process of the 2023 Data. Based on the results of this verification, Hong Kong Quality Assurance Bureau provides reasonable assurance on the 2023 Data and concludes: the 2023 Data is substantially accurate and reliable; the HKMA's overall data collection mechanism is adequate. Reviewed by Shen Xiaoyin, Supervisor, Hong Kong Quality Assurance Bureau, April 2024

The threats posed by climate change are imminent, and accelerating global climate action has become a matter of extreme urgency. The World Meteorological Organization confirmed that 2024 was the hottest year on record, and also the first year in which global temperatures exceeded the critical threshold of 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. At the same time, although global greenhouse gas emissions eased slightly during the COVID pandemic, they have recently hit new highs, highlighting the inadequacy of current climate change mitigation measures. In the process of addressing global warming, the emergence of climate-related risks will intensify, and their impact on economic and financial markets will be difficult to predict. Furthermore, current geopolitical tensions, an increasingly fragmented global economic landscape, the potential for worsening energy security issues, and an uncertain economic outlook all present greater challenges for countries in responding to climate change. The process of transitioning to a low-carbon economy requires substantial and sustained financial support. Across the globe, the transition challenges faced by Asia are particularly severe. As noted by the World Economic Forum, Asia is not only the engine of global economic growth but also the region most vulnerable to the impacts of climate change. Therefore, Asia plays a pivotal role in whether the world can successfully achieve net-zero emission goals. As a leading international financial center in Asia, Hong Kong needs to strengthen its leading role and fully leverage the power of finance to support and drive the region's transition. To this end, the HKMA announced the "Sustainable Finance Action Plan" last year, outlining our vision and roadmap for gradually integrating sustainable development concepts into the core of the financial system. Our work focuses on two aspects: enhancing the financial industry's ability to cope with climate-related risks, and assisting the industry in seizing relevant new opportunities. At the same time, we also lead by example to play a guiding role. The HKMA's sustainable development work includes four key areas: supporting the banking sector toward net-zero emissions, investing in a sustainable future, promoting net-zero financing, and advancing more inclusive sustainable development. The banking system plays a critical role in the net-zero transition in Hong Kong and Asia, but it also faces numerous risks during the transition process. In the "Action Plan," we set ambitious targets, requiring all banks to commit to achieving net-zero emissions in their own operations by 2030 or earlier, and achieving net-zero emissions in their financing by 2050 or earlier. Simultaneously, we require all banks to enhance the disclosure of climate-related risks and opportunities. While continuously strengthening the climate risk management of banks, we also provide guidance for the transition planning of banks to help them improve their capacity to respond to the transition and better manage related risks. We are also conducting preparatory work with relevant stakeholders to align Hong Kong's sustainable disclosure requirements with international standards, aiming to further increase the industry's transparency in related activities. Additionally, we are optimizing the Hong Kong Sustainable Finance Taxonomy launched in May last year to include more sustainable activities (including transition activities). We hope to guide more capital toward sustainable and transition-related projects by providing clear guidelines. Climate change brings significant physical and transition risks, which may affect the long-term financial performance and value of the Exchange Fund's investment projects. At the same time, however, it also brings opportunities for the Exchange Fund to achieve growth and drive positive impacts. Our experience proves that investment returns and positive sustainable impacts can be coordinated and do not exist in conflict. With this in mind, we are committed to achieving net-zero emissions for the Exchange Fund's "investment portfolio" by 2050 or earlier, and have committed in the "Action Plan" to support Asia's climate transition through the Exchange Fund's investments. Currently, the proportion of sustainable investments in the "investment portfolio" has already exceeded ten percent. To further promote sustainable investment in the region, the HKMA established strategic partnerships with the Asian Development Bank, the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, and the International Finance Corporation in November last year to accelerate the low-carbon economic transition in Asia through joint investments. Additionally, we published the first "HKMA ESG Expectations" document in September last year to further encourage fund managers to proactively exercise asset ownership and adopt good sustainable investment practices. The flow of capital is particularly important for accelerating the regional transition. As an international financial hub and the preferred location for arranging international sustainable bond issuances for issuers in the Asian region (including provincial and municipal governments in the Mainland), Hong Kong plays a vital role in guiding capital to accelerate the regional transition. The "Action Plan" outlines the vision of developing Hong Kong into the region's preferred sustainable finance platform and the goal of promoting sustainable finance innovation. From leveraging the exemplary role of the "Government Sustainable Bond Programme" to drive green bond innovation (including the issuance of the world's first multi-currency digital bonds in February last year), to expanding the funding scope of the "Green and Sustainable Finance Funding Scheme" to transition finance instruments in May last year, and the launch of the "Digital Bond Funding Scheme" in November last year, we have remained committed to encouraging regional issuers to utilize Hong Kong's financial platform to raise the funds needed for decarbonization transition. To achieve a robust transition, an inclusive and accessible sustainable development ecosystem is required to support capital and innovation. This includes reliable sustainable development data, high-transparency information disclosure, and industry professionals with relevant knowledge and skills. To this end, we committed in the "Action Plan" to support the promotion of high-quality and comprehensive sustainable disclosure, and to work towards filling the gap in sustainable finance talent and knowledge in the region. We have made good progress in assisting relevant stakeholders and facilitating sustainable disclosure, particularly by providing convenient and easy-to-use climate disclosure templates to promote sustainable disclosure for SMEs. We also launched a "Green and Sustainable Finance" professional module under the Banking Professional Qualifications framework in November last year to enhance the relevant knowledge and skills of local banking practitioners. Furthermore, through the inaugural Hong Kong Green Week held in February last year and other events, we have engaged people from all walks of life in discussions on sustainable development, thereby promoting cooperation and innovation. Internally, the HKMA is committed to ensuring that our operations align with the vision of sustainable development. We committed in the "Action Plan" to achieve net-zero emissions in our own operations by 2030 or earlier, which is 20 years ahead of our original commitment. Additionally, we are actively preparing to meet international sustainable disclosure standards in accordance with the roadmap issued by the government. We began adopting electric vehicles in 2024 and incorporated low-carbon emissions as a screening factor in the procurement process. At the same time, we continue to improve work efficiency through digitalization, foster a culture of sustainable development within the institution, and encourage employees to actively participate in sustainable development work. Multilateral cooperation has always been the cornerstone of the global response to climate change, but the reshaping of the international landscape and drastic changes in geopolitics have added variables to global climate action. However, climate change is an indisputable fact and is gradually intensifying. In our work to address climate change, the current situation does not allow us to slacken in the slightest. We firmly believe that promoting an orderly and inclusive transition will help mitigate the impact of climate risks on Hong Kong's financial system and bring opportunities in the process. Stepping into 2025, we will continue to forge ahead, strive to advance sustainable development work, and deepen relationships with like-minded partners. Despite the severe challenges, we will remain committed as always to supporting the construction of a sustainable future for Hong Kong, Asia, and other regions.

Climate change represents a major challenge for our generation. As an international financial centre and a hub for sustainable finance in Asia, Hong Kong is committed to playing a pioneering role in supporting sustainable development both in Asia and globally. In October 2024, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) released the “Sustainable Finance Action Plan” (the “Action Plan”), which outlines the HKMA’s vision in this area, including our future direction, timelines for achieving various objectives, and expectations regarding how the industry can collaborate to advance related efforts. The HKMA aims to strengthen the resilience of Hong Kong’s financial sector and itself against climate-related risks by formulating strategic policies, enhancing regulatory coordination, and improving internal operations, thereby facilitating Asia’s transition to a more sustainable economy. Through active participation in international and regional discussions, the HKMA also seeks to exert influence in shaping green and sustainable finance policies and standards at both regional and global levels. As a banking regulator, the HKMA focuses on enhancing the climate resilience of banks and ensuring their stability as they transition towards net-zero emissions. Our key priorities for 2025 include:   – Conducting a new round of thematic reviews on banks’ climate risk management practices, along with a third round of consultation meetings to assess banks’ compliance with relevant HKMA regulations and further strengthen their climate risk management capabilities;   – Refining efforts to incorporate climate risk stress testing into the HKMA’s regulatory-led stress testing framework;   – Continuing to integrate climate considerations into the HKMA’s regulatory review processes;   – Initiating preparations for formulating regulatory requirements for local banks to implement the upcoming third pillar disclosure framework on climate-related financial risks by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, as well as the International Sustainability Standards Board’s (ISSB) standards;   – Finalizing the development of a new section, GS-2, in the “Regulatory Policy Manual” to provide guidance to banks on transition planning; and   – Sharing with the industry best practices in climate risk management and the application of green fintech solutions.    Beyond its role as a banking regulator, the HKMA also acts as a facilitator, striving to nurture the development of a green and sustainable finance ecosystem and supporting banks in financing the transition process. We have published the first phase of the “Hong Kong Taxonomy for Sustainable Finance”, which serves as a tool for the industry to identify green and sustainable economic activities and promotes the flow of related financing. The HKMA has now commenced work on the second phase of the taxonomy, aiming to expand its scope by incorporating transition-related elements, additional green economic activities, and climate adaptation objectives. Furthermore, building on the success of the third FiNETech event in 2024 and the Green Fintech Challenge in 2023, we will host another Green Fintech event in 2025 to encourage banks to adopt green fintech solutions.    Hong Kong is well-positioned to meet the region’s sustainable financing needs. To reinforce this role, we will continue to assist the Government in implementing the “Government Sustainable Bond Programme”, whose expanded scope will now include sustainable projects such as those with social impact. This move will further foster the development of Hong Kong’s green and sustainable bond market and serve as a model for other potential issuers in the region. Additionally, we will continue to provide funding through the “Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme” to encourage more borrowers in the region to raise sustainable capital via Hong Kong’s financing platforms. We will also intensify promotional efforts to attract more governments, institutions, and enterprises from the Chinese mainland and other regions to raise green funds in Hong Kong. At the same time, we will continue to catalyse and support sustainable financial innovation, including by providing grants to prospective issuers of digital green bonds through the “Digital Bond Grant Scheme”. Although market demand for high-quality sustainability disclosures from institutions and enterprises is on the rise, the capabilities and readiness of different entities to carry out such disclosures vary; some may require additional guidance and support. In light of this, the HKMA will continue to collaborate with other members of the Inter-Agency Steering Group on Green and Sustainable Finance to make sustainability disclosures more accessible and inclusive. For instance, we will continue to provide banks and their clients with a wider range of tools related to climate disclosure, including easy-to-use templates and supporting resources for sustainability reporting. We will also explore how technology can further enhance the usability of existing resources, and partner with major local industry organizations to deliver necessary training. Given the rapidly evolving nature of the sustainable finance market, it is essential to expand the local talent pool and bridge knowledge gaps in Hong Kong and the wider region. In 2025, a key priority for the HKMA will be working with the banking sector to develop professional-level training courses under the “Green and Sustainable Finance” module of the “Banking Professional Qualifications Framework.” Additionally, through the upcoming study on “Future Banking Talent 2026–2030,” we aim to identify areas where further training is needed within the industry. Moreover, we plan to collaborate with key stakeholders to promote the government-funded “Pilot Scheme on Green and Sustainable Finance Training” and review its scope of application. At the regional level, the HKMA will continue to partner with the International Finance Corporation via the “Green Commercial Banking Alliance” to launch targeted initiatives in Asia, including research on green finance, provision of specialized market analysis, targeted skill enhancement and training support, facilitation of community engagement, identification of potential green investment opportunities, and practical guidance to help banks incorporate green finance into their core business strategies. As a responsible investor, the HKMA is committed to ensuring that the Exchange Fund’s portfolio achieves net-zero emissions by 2050, thereby supporting the broader economic transition. We will continuously enhance the sustainability of the Exchange Fund’s investments through pragmatic and rigorous responsible investment practices, focusing primarily on the long-term resilience of our asset portfolio while also exploring investment opportunities that yield positive climate outcomes. The HKMA strives to set an example in corporate sustainability.
